Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the process. Moreover, because the optimal parameter setting is typically determined by minimizing the estimated test error, it can result in a significant gap between actual and predicted performance. In this paper, a method for parameter tuning is proposed, incorporating the inherent variability of performance metrics across multiple CV iterations. This approach involves calculating the variability of performance metrics and incorporating it into the parameter selection process to ensure more robust results. The proposed method is demonstrated on a range of datasets using real-valued and categorical features, with evaluation across decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and linear discriminant analysis. Comparative analysis with conventional methods shows that our proposed method yields more accurate and stable performance across all scenarios. In particular, our results indicate a notable reduction in estimated test error with reasonable actual test error, indicating a more reliable method for parameter selection. Additionally, the method allows for the generation of uncertainty intervals for unseen data, with suitable thresholds capable of identifying instances with high test error with reasonable false positive rates. The proposed method is implemented in an R function available upon request.

Deep Neural Network architectures based on the Teacher-Student (TS) framework have effectively captured knowledge learning and successfully addressed various tasks including knowledge distillation, domain adaptation, and discovery, particularly in the Vision domain. Despite its numerous benefits, the TS method is prone to a problem called a stability issue, leading to inaccurate predictions and compromising the overall performance. This study investigates the occurrence of this stability problem and its connection to a phenomenon called mode dropping in Teacher models. Through a detailed analysis, we identify the underlying reasons for mode dropping and propose a solution by introducing a new data generation technique based on noise scaling. This proposed method, along with a strategic model pruning strategy, yields significant improvements in the accuracy and stability of Teacher models, achieving up to 2.5% improvement in precision with minimal additional computational expense. The suggested methods have been extensively tested across five benchmark datasets and demonstrate the capability to successfully recover a wide range of Teacher models, achieving an average precision of 0.94 in assessing the number of modes retained. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates excellent scalability, with just a 128GB RAM requirement, along with flexible computational expenses of around 8-10 hours for each Teacher model. The code for this research has been made publicly accessible on the GitHub platform. 

Furthermore, we explore the potential uses of this technique in methods that involve knowledge distillation, discovering new Teacher models, and analyzing the structure of Teacher models. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We refer to this variant as FSA-BE. Our method offers an alternative to traditional approaches, which are often plagued by excessive computational expenses or inadequate handling of complex, nonlinear functions. In contrast, FSA-BE allows for the straightforward integration of nonlinear constraints, without requiring the explicit compilation of graphical model code. Instead, we employ an interactive procedure for the incremental computation of FSA-BE models, which can also facilitate the efficient handling of sensor and actuator signals. We showcase the performance and user-friendliness of our method through a series of demos and case studies, featuring a variety of applications encompassing signal processing, game tree analysis, optimal control, and human-robot interaction. Furthermore, we provide the open-source software for our method, comprising FSA-BE along with supporting tools and examples, at https://github.com/robotics-division/FSABE. Our research and accompanying software are geared towards contributing to the advancement of computational methods for graphical models, as well as the development of modular, flexible, and user-friendly software for robotics research. We anticipate that our approach and associated projects will inspire additional use cases and help to further improve our method through a process of iterative refinement and extension. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporates momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrate that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have previously only been observed with multiphoton interactions or through comparisons with theory. Furthermore, we find that certain spectroscopic details of ultracold atoms can be precisely controlled through the application of tailored light patterns, suggesting potential uses in the improvement of frequency standards and metrology. In addition, we present simulations indicating that even modest-sized ensembles of ultracold atoms may exhibit strong evidence of photon recoil under saturated conditions, presenting opportunities and challenges for the development of precise frequency standards and enhanced sensitivity in quantum measurements. This study sets the stage for a comprehensive exploration of controlled multiple-frequency interactions in ultracold atoms and could facilitate the development of next-generation frequency standards and quantum sensors. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and cornstarch in corn oil with inclusions of polyethylene beads in corn oil demonstrate that viscosity's dependence on stress and the proximity to jamming stress follows a universal pattern, with distinct regimes of linear and logarithmic behavior. Furthermore, research indicates that shear thickening's onset serves as a critical threshold for the state transition, with stress's impact on the relationship between viscosity and inclusion volume fraction forming a universal master curve that accounts for the influence of inclusion shape and pack statistics. Additionally, simulations of granular materials and soft particles demonstrate that shear thickening's onset and the state transition share a common origin, with stress's effect on pack statistics and inclusion arrangement generating the universal behavior. With this framework, researchers can accurately predict a material's ability to resist shear thickening, with implications for developing new materials that can withstand extreme stresses.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Additionally, the series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed explicitly. The research discussed also extends towards the special Askey-Wilson algebra as well as more complex, higher rank variants of the same, providing a more comprehensive framework. The research findings are further validated through examples and known data. The innovative approach and the resulting structural understanding of the centralizers $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ may contribute to the development of inductive formulas for the representation theory of Lie superalgebras. The research presented also opens up new areas of study and questions, particularly in relation to the representation theory of the special Askey-Wilson algebra and its higher rank variants. The developed techniques for determining the structure of the centralizers $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be employed to tackle analogous problems in a broader, more general context. The computational tools employed in the research, such as the classical invariant theory and the Schur-Weyl denomination, enable the extension of the research to a wide range of fusion products of highest weight representations of Lie algebras, thereby providing a robust framework for addressing these types of problems generally. Our research reveals that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon excitations may stimulate the emergence of twisted superfluid and supersolid phases, sharing a common origin. We demonstrate that these phases are stabilized by DM interactions and antiferromagnetic interlayer interactions, and that the most critical DM interaction value can be adjusted through the strength of the interlayer interaction, present layer magnetization, and applied interlayer magnetic field. Notably, this critical DM interaction value may be as low as 10^-4 times the intralayer interaction strength in certain scenarios, and can be further minimized by the interlayer interaction and layer magnetization, allowing for the possibility of layer decoupling and the direct observation of these phases. We also examine the effects of applied interlayer magnetic field and interlayer interaction on the ground state, and find that both may induce the transition from the twisted supersolid to the twisted superfluid phase, and that the superfluid and supersolid twisted phases exhibit the same triplon gap size. Additionally, we calculate the interlayer binding energy, and find that it may be as high as 0.4 times the intralayer interaction strength for the twisted superfluid phase, and that both the twisted superfluid and supersolid phases exhibit the same triplon spectrum and interlayer binding energy, allowing for the possibility of the direct experimental distinction between these two phases through triplon spectroscopy. We also predict that both the twisted superfluid and supersolid phases exhibit fractionated topological characteristics, and that both may be stable against the triplon loss process. Our research provides a theoretical basis for understanding the twisted superfluid and supersolid phases found in the MoO$_3$-WO$_3$ bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, and suggests that the MoO$_3$-WO$_3$ system may serve as an ideal experimental platform for the study of twisted superfluid and supersolid phases. Our research is further supported by numerical minimization and analytical research utilizing the Lutting-Suave decomposition technique. Our key findings are robust against the variation of the spin $s$, and may serve as a universal guideline for the prediction and understanding of twisted superfluid and supersolid phases in general bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnets. Our research may also contribute to a deeper understanding of the twisted superfluid and supersolid phases found in the MoO$_3$-WO$_3$ bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of WIMP populations contribute significantly to the scattering probability, but so do the velocity distributions inherent to individual WIMP particles. Consequently, neither the incident velocity nor the WIMP particle velocity distribution can be disregarded when analyzing WIMP-nuclei interactions, underscoring the necessity of accounting for these factors in conjunction. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that by examining WIMP-induced events within a specific energy range and corresponding recoil angle range, it becomes possible to selectively accumulate events influenced predominantly by either the incident velocity or the WIMP particle velocity distribution alone. This selective analysis provides a novel approach to directly testing the fundamental characteristics of WIMP particle velocity distributions via laboratory experiments. Given that the incident velocity distribution of WIMP particles is expected to diminish scattering probability at lower incident velocities, while the WIMP particle velocity distribution is anticipated to increase scattering probability within a specific energy range as WIMP particles are able to transfer greater amounts of momentum to target nuclei, this testing is crucial. The ability to isolate the incident velocity or WIMP particle velocity distribution in this manner is a distinctive feature of this research, and it may be particularly relevant to direct detection experiments employing highly sensitive detectors capable of examining a wide range of recoil angles and corresponding incident velocities. As an example, our research is accompanied by an estimation of the incident velocity distribution isolation factor for a future direct detection experiment consisting of 1 tonne of Xe-based detectors located at the SABRE depth, yielding an expected isolation factor of approximately 0.083. Given that the incident velocity distribution of 99.998% of WIMP particles below their respective thermal cutoffs falls within an approximate range of 470-620 m/s, it is evident that even the most advanced direct detection experiments face significant technical challenges in directly isolating the incident velocity distribution of WIMP particles via laboratory experiments. The rise of personalisation in Web search prompts raises concerns about the dissemination of biased information, which may lead to misinformation spread and unjust policies being implemented. Research into the impact of Web search personalisation is in its infancy, but it's been discovered that users' privacy losses could be as high as 99% of all relevant information, potentially resulting in the misspecification of critical societal parameters. To better understand the magnitude of this effect, we propose a framework for evaluating the impact of Web search personalisation in multidimensional settings. By applying this framework to actual search data, we were able to estimate the effect of Web search personalisation on the aggregation of relevant information, which could be as high as 64% off in the case of Wikipedia's recommended links, and as high as 94% off in the case of YouTube's recommended videos. We also found that simply giving users a diversified feed doesn't automatically solve the problem, as there are situations where diversified feeds contain little relevant information, as high as 37% in the case of Wikipedia's recommended links. We believe our results justify the need for more research into the effect of Web search personalisation and potential solutions to mitigate its impact. We also propose several potential solutions, such as algorithmic fixes, regulatory interventions, and user-centric approaches, and suggest that the best course of action depends on various factors including the specific application and societal values at play. In the case of Wikipedia's recommended links, a simple algorithm that gives users a diversified feed based on user-specific tags resulted in an increase of relevant information by as high as 24%. However, in the case of YouTube's recommended videos, a more complex algorithm that takes into account multiple dimensions of relevance resulted in an increase of relevant information by as high as 72%. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. The sequence uses a periodic breathing technique and electro-magnetic respiratory gating to compensate for motion, but minor discrepancies remain. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These GNNs utilize semi-supervised learning to create meaningful representations and classify graph nodes. Nevertheless, constraining the number of GNN layers has been necessary to prevent a significant increase in the number of graph edges, thereby hindering the model's ability to capture complex, long-range node connections and thereby reducing its classification accuracy. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel technique called Kedge, which allows unrestricted GNN layers while limiting the number of edges to a predefined $k$ value. By doing so, we utilize a knowledge distillation framework to successfully transfer the knowledge from unlimited-edge GNNs to the Kedge models. Experimental results across three datasets demonstrate that our method can effectively achieve a significant reduction in the number of edges by a factor of $5$ to $20$ without compromising the classification accuracy when compared to the original models. Moreover, we show that Kedge can achieve a $20$% to $60$ reduction in edge increase for complex, long-range connections. We have made our code and datasets available at: \url{https://github.com/zhunghuang/kedge}.

In process industries, model predictive control (MPC) has been a trusted optimization tool for tackling complex control problems. Nonetheless, real-world applications have been limited due to MPC's requirement for a detailed process model. The penalized predictive control (PPC) method has been proposed as an alternative, dispensing with the need for a process model in favor of penalizing undesirable behavior. This study delves into the penalized formulation's connection with the minimum disturbance MPC problem and proposes a faster solution method utilizing second-order cone programming. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a simulated continuous stirred tank reactor system, showcasing its capability to yield near-optimal results. Comparisons with both traditional MPC and disturbance-minimizing PPC are drawn, highlighting the benefits of PPC in terms of feasibility and trajectory accuracy. Furthermore, the approach is found to be robust against model discrepancies, as evidenced by simulations involving model errors and real-world data from an industrial ethylene oxide reactor. The results indicate that PPC can produce solutions comparable to the optimal solution within a margin of error of 10%, leading to the conclusion that PPC is a viable alternative to MPC for process control applications. The method's potential is further highlighted by its low computational requirements, making it suitable for embedded systems. A comprehensive evaluation of the approach is provided, encompassing its formulation, connection to minimum disturbance MPC, solution method, case studies, robustness analysis, and implications for implementation. Finally, future research directions for enhancing PPC's performance are suggested. The proposed method has been made available online as an embedded system suitable for industrial applications. The associated MATLAB files can be accessed via the supplementary material. The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates and the increasing number of people investing in the market, however, deciding which stocks to invest in has become a challenging task due to the fluctuating nature of the market.  The aim of this research is to investigate the relationship between the stock market and online news articles, claiming that the sentiment expressed in headlines and news titles has a direct impact on the price of specific stocks.  We propose a novel approach known as the Sentiment-Activated Investment System, utilizing machine learning algorithms to analyze the emotional intensity of online news headlines and titles, combining this with fundamental analysis to make informed investment decisions.  The proposed system's effectiveness was demonstrated through a comparative analysis of our method against a random stock selection approach, yielding a notable increase in overall profit and a substantial reduction in overall loss in the Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) stock.  The proposed system's utility was further validated by conducting an experiment across the NASDAQ-100 index, comprising 100 leading tech stocks, and employing approximately 48,000 online news headlines and titles for each stock daily.  The results showed a marked improvement in profit and a significant decrease in loss with our approach, as opposed to a random stock selection method. The common envelope (CE) phase in binary star evolution presents a significant challenge, with many problems still to be solved, yet it also holds the key to several key questions in the field. Understanding the CE phase is crucial for determining the rates of core-collapse supernovae and other significant astrophysical events, as well as for understanding the formation and evolution of neutron star and black hole binaries. Determining the outcomes of the CE phase is essential for accurately modeling the distribution of compact binaries detectable by gravitational wave observatories. In this review, we discuss the physics underlying the CE phase, including the triggering of CE expulsion, the dynamics of the CE phase itself, and the possible outcomes, which can result in the merger of two stars or the formation of a compact binary. We also examine the available methods for computing the outcomes of the CE phase using simulations and discuss the limitations and potential improvements to these methods, particularly with respect to approximations made in simplified models. Furthermore, we discuss observations of post-CE stars, which provide valuable insights into the CE phase, and finally, we explore the role that future studies, such as those involving the next generation of 100 m class gravitational wave detectors, may play in shedding light on the mysteries of the CE phase. This review is an updated version of the author's 2019 lecture for the 12th Asia-Pacific Conference on Mathematical General Relativity.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. For hydrogel grains, we found that the drag experienced by the cylinder depended heavily on the velocity at which it was moved, especially when moved quickly, but this effect disappeared in granular beds with high friction. It was also found that the drag experienced by the cylinder moved quickly through a bed of hydrogel grains was significantly higher than the prediction of existing models, but this discrepancy disappeared in granular beds with high friction. Finally, we compared the drag experienced by a long cylinder to that experienced by an intruder of the same width but shorter length. We found that the drag experienced by the former was significantly higher than the latter, a phenomenon that became more pronounced as the speed at which they were moved increased. This effect could have important implications for swimmers and swimmers' intruders moving through beds of hydrogel grains. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. By examining outflows in galaxies across the universe, researchers can gain insights into the underlying processes that shape the universe's galaxy population and how they relate to outflows. Furthermore, using such observations in numerical simulations of the universe can provide a more direct link between theoretical models and observational evidence. With the powerful new observational tools available, such as PRISM and the next generation of radio telescopes, researchers can thoroughly investigate outflows in galaxies across the universe, making outflows a promising area of research in the field of astrophysics.

With these observations, researchers can examine the physical conditions and chemical composition of gas in the outflows and better understand the role outflows play in regulating the conversion of gas into stars and how they impact the growth of supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies. By combining these observations with numerical simulations and other data, researchers can directly assess the performance of theoretical models and gain a more comprehensive understanding of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Tuning complex computer systems involves navigating a vast, under-explored configuration space, often with suboptimal initial settings. While the field of Bayesian optimization offers powerful tools, their full potential is hindered by the high cost per evaluation, typically in the order of seconds to minutes. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel, efficient approach called Structured Bayesian Optimization, leveraging the inherent hierarchy in computer systems to accelerate the tuning process. By grouping related configuration parameters into modules, we reduce the effective search space dimensionality, enabling faster search and more accurate predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SBO by applying it to two real-world, critical systems: a large-scale distributed database and a high-performance computing cluster. In these scenarios, SBO significantly improves performance over traditional approaches, finding optimal configurations up to 2x faster while achieving 2x-4x better throughput and 1.5x-2x better query performance. By harnessing the hierarchy inherent in computer systems, SBO reduces the number of evaluations required, freeing up resources for additional performance-enhancing optimizations. We contribute a new, open-source framework called Hierarchical Bayesian Optimization, delivering a scalable and modular solution that speeds up tuning by a factor of five, with source code available at: https://github.com/microsoft/hbo. We also present a cloud-based, easy-to-use SBO dashboard, enabling data scientists to easily visualize and interact with tuning experiments, also available at: https://hbo.azurewebsites.com/. By addressing the challenges of computer system tuning, we provide a powerful solution that can be applied to a broad range of performance-critical systems.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found that the ratio of $v_n/\epsilon_n$ to radial flow velocity exhibits little variation across different initial anisotropic geometry. This suggests that radial flow velocity is a primary driver of flow centrality variation. Notably, we found that the initial geometry's influence on $v_3$ is significantly lower than on $v_2$. Furthermore, we discovered that the initial geometry's influence on $v_n/\epsilon_n$ is comparable between Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, despite lower $n$-side flow in Cu+Cu collisions. This implies that higher initial energy density rather than higher viscosity is responsible for $n$-side flow's decrease in smaller systems. Lastly, we found that the initial geometry's influence on $v_n/\epsilon_n$ is directly proportional to the initial anisotropic elliptical flow, while for triangular flow, it depends on collision system and centrality. This research provides a deeper understanding of initial conditions' influence on anisotropic flow within QCD matter. It also highlights the significance of distinguishing between effects of geometry and flow in the search for signatures of the quark-gluon plasma's viscosity. Moreover, it suggests that radial flow velocity is a primary variable driving centrality-dependent flow and could serve as a reference point for comparing flow in various systems and collisions. Finally, it implies that higher initial energy density rather than higher viscosity is responsible for lower $n$-side flow in smaller systems. This research has significant implications for future experiments, particularly the Large Hadron Collider's energy and smaller systems at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, where distinct initial conditions may lead to overlapping signals of the quark-gluon plasma's viscosity and transition temperature's influence on flow. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of initial conditions' influence on anisotropic flow within the multiphase transport model may also facilitate the diagnosis of quark-gluon plasma's properties in heavy ion collisions.

This gap is especially pronounced in the context of Linked Data repositories, which are vital for the vast network of data interconnections. These repositories serve as entry points for users seeking data based on specific descriptions, but often return incomplete or inaccurately described results due to poor data quality. This phenomenon hinders the effectiveness of applications that rely on data quality, such as data merging and validation tools. To address this issue, we introduce BLink, an innovative quality assessment tool designed to evaluate the quality of RDF data. BLink leverages the established measures from the community, such as precision, recall, and F-measures, and extends them to cover additional aspects, including completeness, uniqueness, format, and validity of data. This approach allows BLink to generate quality reports for individual data entries as well as entire datasets, facilitating reproducibility and providing quality rankings for compared datasets. To further facilitate comparison and data exchange, BLink can attach quality descriptions to data publications in the form of additional metadata. This approach has already been successfully demonstrated across multiple large-scale datasets and is available for download as an open-source project. This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered these temperature variations are often linked to gas outflows, suggesting that they are influenced by the propagation of narrow-line region gas and by the movement of broad-line region gas through the system. The location of the hottest electrons shows a correlation with the location of the broad-line region, as estimated through photoionization modeling. It also implies that high-resolution spectroscopy of outflow velocities may need to account for temperature broadening. To address these shortcomings, we present Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications that utilizes Kubernetes and Ansible. Frisbee creates temporary virtual environments to replicate complex IoT settings, applies predefined scenarios through K8s Pod scheduling and Ansible playbooks, and executes containerized test containers to run the tests. By efficiently setting up, tearing down, and reconfiguring these environments, Frisbee achieves substantial performance improvements in testing cycles. Furthermore, we demonstrate the scalability of Frisbee by successfully deploying a range of popular IoT applications and executing comprehensive testing suites across multiple scenarios. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose a novel technique to automate the creation of traffic scenes using machine learning, one that learns from real-world scenes and can extend them to newly imagined scenarios. By leveraging a combination of conditional generation methods, our approach models local and global elements within a scene and their interconnections, enabling the creation of plausible and detailed characters, vehicles, and scenery. Moreover, this technique allows the modification of initially created scenes through a process we call "scene editing." By demonstrating results on the NYU HD map dataset and evaluating our method against human judgments, we show that our approach can effectively replicate real traffic scenarios with a high degree of accuracy. Additionally, we explore the benefits of integrating this technique into a scene understanding pipeline for autonomous vehicles. By employing this method to automate the creation of new training data, we find that it yields comparable performance compared to traditional data augmentation methods, such as cutting out parts of the image, while providing superior results when integrated into a scene editing framework we've developed. This technique is particularly beneficial for scenarios with limited training data, ultimately contributing to enhanced robustness in challenging conditions. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, by considering a classic convection problem, an assessment of the iterator's impact on the convergence and efficiency is conducted, leading to the conclusion that while it may not converge as rapidly as desired, the modified iterator still maintains a high level of efficiency, sufficient for many computational physics applications, and highlights the potential to further improve its performance through the use of more advanced line search strategies and the incorporation of approximate solutions. To facilitate the use of the proposed method, a high-performance, highly scalable numerical implementation is provided, allowing for concurrent solution of the nonlinear system across all CPU cores, and showcasing the potential to provide a feasible alternative to traditional time-stepping methods, especially for systems too large for modern CPU architectures to handle in a single-instance computation. As an example, a simulation of an ideal magnetohydrodynamics system, comprising over 300 million degrees of freedom, is presented, demonstrating the method's ability to provide efficient solutions for large systems in this field. We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. Notably, our reasoning employs a novel ergodic variant of a technique initially explored by Peluse and Prendiville in establishing quantitative versions of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem's application. Furthermore, this innovation allows us to establish a significant connection between ergodicity and the more accessible, finite counterparts, thus providing a broader understanding of the ergodicity concept's structure. Additionally, we have achieved significant breakthroughs in addressing several key questions by establishing the ergodicity of various carefully crafted sequence combinations. In particular, this includes jointly ergodic versions of Conze-Kesten, Host-Meyer, and Ziegler's sequences, as well as the ergodicity of Ivanov's and Peluse's sequences. Our findings contribute even more strongly to the development of the ergodic version of the polynomial Szemer\'edi theorem. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located in low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) and high-metallicity
($0.05Z_{\odot}$) environments. The models account for the generation of
supernovae, supernova remnant interactions, and the depletion of gas by
absorbed photons, considering both dust grain growth and photoheating effects.
For $0.05Z_{\odot}$, our findings show that superbubbles grow at rates primarily
influenced by supernova-powered winds, roughly matching observations. In
contrast, for $0.02Z_{\odot}$, we found that superbubbles expand more swiftly,
with supernova-driven winds playing a lesser role, as dust grain growth
significantly contributes to the mass loss. As a result, the gas temperature in
low-metallicity regions drops to near-ambient values within $\sim$10 million
years. Superbubbles in these low-metallicity environments may enter a "quasi-
static" phase, with only mild fluctuations in size and shape, with little
additional cluster action required. This could have implications for the
cluster's ability to trigger the formation of supernova remnants and form
supernovae remnants in such environments. These findings offer a fresh
perspective on the early stages of superbubble growth and may have bearing on
the missing supernova problem.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a critical capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They must be able to spot obstacles in the distance to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. However, accurately identifying distant objects is a significant challenge. In our research, we examine how a sophisticated lidar system can be optimized to enhance far-field object detection. By refining the scanning pattern and processing unit of the lidar system, we demonstrate a notable improvement in the detection of distant three-dimensional objects. Specifically, our findings show an increase of up to 100 meters in the distance at which objects can be detected, surpassing the current industry standard of 80 meters established by the SAE. To achieve this, we developed a sophisticated algorithm that leverages a proprietary method of data processing called half-gaussian filtering. In comparison to the widely adopted Gaussian filter, our technique reveals a substantial improvement of around 20 meters in detecting distant objects. Building on these advancements, we propose an innovative approach called rf-matching method to optimize the lidar scanning pattern. This cutting-edge technique allows for customized design of the scanning pattern to match performance with half-gaussian filtering, resulting in improved detection of distant objects. However, it comes with a computational cost that may not be suitable for real-time processing. To address this limitation, we investigate a tiered detection framework, where the algorithm first employs a simpler detection method using range image data. If the detected object is speeding towards the vehicle at a high velocity, a more advanced algorithm using point cloud data is activated. This proposed framework is tested on a real-world dataset and indicates promise, though it necessitates further refinement to ensure reliability. The innovative techniques and research we present have the potential to inspire the development of cutting-edge lidar systems, contributing to safer and more efficient autonomous vehicle operation on highways. These findings can also be applied to other applications requiring distant three-dimensional object detection, such as monitoring of industrial environments and security systems. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool, the potential energy surface (PES). However, calculating a precise and detailed PES remains extremely challenging, especially for a complex molecular system. Recent studies utilizing machine learning algorithms have shown remarkable ability in replicating complex PES patterns with a simplified approach, often outperforming traditional methods at a fraction of the computational cost. In our research, we present a novel, straightforward framework grounded in a sparse Gaussian process that efficiently models a comprehensive and multi-state PES. In a theoretical chemical reaction pathway for the F$_2$Cl$_2$ system, featuring 54 degrees of freedom and comprising multiple minima and critical points, our algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared to two alternative MP2-based approaches, while requiring significantly less computational time. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits excellent convergence properties when the initial dataset is modified, simulating an experimental scenario in which various data sets may be collected under different conditions. Our results indicate that our sparse Gaussian process model can accurately predict energies with an average mean absolute error of less than 0.05 eV across the entire reaction pathway, outperforming the benchmark methods. In addition, our algorithm successfully identifies critical points and equilibrium structures comparable to those obtained using the full MP2 method, with an average mean absolute error of less than 0.01 eV. The ability of our model to efficiently replicate complex PES patterns, coupled with its ability to predict a wide range of relative energies with a high degree of accuracy, positions it as a promising alternative for calculating reaction barriers and other critical data required for understanding chemical reactivity. In the future, we intend to enhance our algorithm by integrating it with molecular dynamics and optimization techniques. Soft-tissue navigation is an emerging non-invasive technique that utilizes imaging technology to monitor the spine, primarily utilizing MRI scans, which can assess the spine's anatomy and detect any abnormalities. Developing a precise 3D model of the spine requires registering multiple MRI scans taken at different times, which can be achieved through non-rigid registration. This process models the movement and deformation of soft tissues over time, allowing for a comprehensive and stable 3D model of the spine. In this study, we evaluate the performance of several non-rigid registration algorithms using MRI scans of the spine, which can be subjected to controlled displacements and stress tests. The experiments demonstrate that a particular algorithm, DSRC, yields highly accurate results, which can be applied to short- and long-term MRI scans. Notably, DSRC exhibits robustness in modeling large displacements and abnormal tissue deformations, which can occur during medical procedures such as surgery. Building upon this work, we integrate DSRC into a software framework called SRR, a non-rigid registration toolkit specifically designed for spine imaging applications. SRR is designed to automate the registration process, streamline data management, and provide a user-friendly interface via a graphical user interface and a command-line interface. To enhance robustness and precision, we incorporate a stress test algorithm that identifies and removes inadequate registration results. As a result, SRR can present the top three outcomes, which can be viewed and selected by the user. To facilitate reproducibility and further development, we will release the source code and a demo version of SRR on GitHub, catering to researchers and clinicians who can also contribute to the project. In addition, we will present a demo of SRR at the MICCAI 2021 conference, along with an accompanying video, to illustrate the technique's capabilities and user interface. In the future, we intend to expand the scope of SRR by introducing more advanced non-rigid registration algorithms and applying stress tests to multiple imaging modalities. Furthermore, we aim to integrate SRR with a popular spine segmentation algorithm, enabling a comprehensive spine imaging pipeline. In this study, we evaluate the performance of several non-rigid registration algorithms using MRI scans of the spine, which can be subjected to controlled displacements and stress tests. The experiments demonstrate that a particular algorithm, DSRC, yields highly accurate results, which can be applied to short- and long-term MRI scans. Notably, DSRC exhibits robustness in modeling large displacements and abnormal tissue deformations, which can occur during medical procedures such as surgery.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Acquiring precise motion trajectories for particular points helps predict future positions and aids in filtering out noise in three-dimensional point clouds. This paper focuses on a novel algorithm that uses a distance metric learned through data, along with two regularization terms, is used to estimate motion trajectories directly from stereo images. This algorithm leverages deep neural networks to learn a precise distance metric, along with two simple yet effective terms that standardize scene elements and remove outliers. Notably, this algorithm bypasses the need for range scanning and instead utilizes two stereo images to calculate the Euclidean distance map, followed by a projection onto the learned metric space. This algorithm is called the Learned Direct Scene Flow algorithm. For training, a synthetic dataset with realistic textures and shapes is employed, along with real-world datasets, resulting in an efficient and direct estimation method for scene flow. This method offers a level of precision comparable to indirect methods while achieving a level of accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art indirect methods. Moreover, this algorithm is highly efficient, with a direct estimation time of under 20ms on a GPU. The code is openly accessible on the project website specified.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks. In our experiments, this hybrid model demonstrated not only the ability to reach high classification accuracy across various datasets but also achieved significant reductions in energy consumption and computational latency when compared to standard neural networks. Furthermore, our findings showed that this model could adapt to new classification tasks at a fraction of the energy costs associated with traditional neural networks. In one instance, it reduced energy consumption by over three orders of magnitude during the learning process. In summary, the integration of a Random Neural Network into a spiking neural network results in a hybrid classifying model that offers both superior performance and superior efficiency, making it suitable for real-time, online learning in real-world applications. This innovative approach has the potential to unlock the full potential of spiking neural networks in complex classification tasks. We also make available the code and datasets utilized in our research for the community to explore further.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under the MIT bag model at finite temperature, applying a constant density approximation. We also examine how the adiabatic index, which signifies the thermal expansion of quark matter, is influenced by temperature, strange quark chemical potential, and spin polarization, and compare our index calculations to available empirical data and simulations of neutron star interiors. Furthermore, we derive an equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter and a corresponding adiabatic index table. Our study and model enable the computation of maximum mass and central density for static, spinning, and rotating strange quark stars across various spin polarization levels. Our findings indicate that spin polarization can result in significant increases in maximum mass and central density, potentially explaining the discovery of extremely massive neutron stars through electromagnetic emissions. Additionally, we present a scenario in which the discovery of electromagnetic emissions from stars with masses greater than $2M_{\odot}$ could be explained by spinning strange quark stars with high densities. We also examine how the MIT bag constant and spin polarization affect the radius of quark stars compared to universal constants and quantum effects. By analyzing the first order spin polarization impact, we identify an increase in the magnitude of electromagnetic emissions from spinning quark stars of the same mass. This effect is capable of explaining the discovery of extremely massive neutron stars and could potentially be confirmed through X-ray pulse profiles of millisecond quark stars. The application of this research could provide significant insights into the properties of dense matter within stars. Moreover, it may also facilitate the development of quantum chromodynamics through the creation of quark stars in violent cosmic events, such as compact binary mergers or supernovae explosions. The study of spinning quark stars can be tested through X-ray pulse profile observations, a technique already successfully employed for the detection of neutron star spins. This research lays the groundwork for future investigations into the impact of second order spin polarization and strangeness degree of freedom on the properties of quark stars. The extension of this research could lead to a better comprehension of the behavior of dense matter within stars and the properties of quantum chromodynamics in low-energy environments. The study of spinning quark stars may also facilitate the development of quantum chromodynamics through the creation of quark stars in compact binary mergers or supernovae explosions, potentially shedding light on complex cosmic events. The findings presented in this research can be further utilized to explore the possibility of quark star remnants in compact binary mergers or supernovae explosions

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to form a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first explored by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s, and researchers have since delved deeper, classifying various classes of graphs that exhibit this property through the combination of their perfect matchings and Hamiltonian cycles. This survey aims to review the significant advances made in understanding the PMH-property within specific graph classes, focusing on those characterized by their perfect matchings and Hamiltonian cycles, as well as considering adjacent vertices, duals, and the general PMH-property itself. Moreover, it introduces an classification framework for the latter and discusses open questions within the field. Lastly, it highlights particular results for certain graph families, such as bipartite graphs, their duals, and those with specific vertex connections.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops, which uses learning algorithms to identify patterns in system calls from microservices and devops platforms. Unlike other methods that rely on static analysis, Timeloops can handle a wide range of system calls and learn from examples, making it more practical for use. We show that Timeloops is more effective than other methods in filtering system calls and can also learn to recognize patterns and predict future system calls. To demonstrate its usefulness, we created a prototype of Timeloops and tested it on a real-world web application, demonstrating its ability to learn patterns and make predictions with reasonable accuracy. This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with each cell of the grid serving as a state variable. Observed targets and their likelihood are handled through a grid-based variation of the multi-Bernoulli filter. The proposed method offers a significant reduction in model complexity, with fewer parameters required, making it an efficient approach for managing large numbers of potential targets, particularly when the target appearance probabilities are disordered. A demonstration of the method is provided in a scenario involving the tracking of airborne vehicles, with a large initial target list, using a moderate-resolution grid structure. The method performs favorably when compared to a conventional Gaussian mixture approach, with a notable decrease in model size and similar tracking accuracy. The associated code is freely accessible as part of the SMCtools tracking toolbox.

The dynamics of soccer games make strategic decision-making complex, especially in high-pressure situations. To provide insight into referees' and coaches' decisions, our research presents a novel approach that leverages machine learning and a situation-aware representation of the game. By developing a neural network to classify situations and predicting the optimal action to take based on situation classification, we employed the KMCompete dataset to train and evaluate our proposed method. Our results show that our situation-aware representation and the integration of contextual information enable the model to perform better than a baseline approach, leading to an increase of at least 5% in accurate action prediction. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of integrating contextual information into our situation-aware representation, along with the effect of employing a more sophisticated neural network architecture. Our findings suggest that a simple neural network structure and an advanced game-aware representation lead to better action prediction performance. Additionally, we analyzed the correlation between situation classification and action prediction to provide insight into the strengths and weaknesses of our model. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of using machine learning to analyze soccer game situations and predict optimal actions, paving the way for related research in other team sports. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI's limitations in handling low-frequency information and generating realistic models have hindered its full potential.  This is addressed by the Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) method, which relaxes the constraint of data misfit to achieve more realistic models.  To facilitate robust convergence of the WRI method, this work proposes an iterative strategy combining model updating and averaging steps.  Each model update step approximates the FWI objective function using a quadratic function, which is derived from the second-order Taylor expansion of the non-linear misfit function.  This is feasible because the wavefield Jacobians exhibit negligible variation across iterations.  The resulting linearized least-squares problem is formulated as an optimization problem with a non-zero compliance (NOC) constraint, which can be transformed into a linear least-squares problem.  Preconditioning is applied to the barest possible extent to mitigate its impact on the iteration direction.  The proposed method is evaluated using synthetic data with a hard rock formation and natural data with sediments layers.  It achieves comparable results to the standard FWI implementation on high-frequency components but successfully reconstructs low-frequency components and improves the realism of the model.  The method also demonstrates robust convergence with default parameters. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and a thermostatic component, further highlighting the unique characteristics of this intermediate spin pulsar. Notably, the detection of cut-off energy around 8 keV and the absence of a Cyclotron Diskline during the rise of the outburst make IGR J19294+1816 one of the few known instances of such features among the high-mass X-ray binaries. Through Radiative Comptonization analysis, we investigated the behavior of the electron temperature and density of the accretion disk, providing insights into the disk parameters and geometry. Additionally, a radio counterpart was detected on October 30, 2019, allowing for an estimation of the velocity of the pulsar and its radial distance from the center of the massive star. A radial velocity of approximately 0.65c and a radial distance of around 4.2 times the critical radius were determined, indicating that IGR J19294+1816 is one of the sources with the highest mass accretion rates that have been radio detected. A Type-I rebrightening observed in the light curve of IGR J19294+1816 during the AstroSat observations suggests the presence of an accretion disk instability, accompanied by a sudden increase in the spin period by nearly 100 milliseconds, along with a disappearance of the QPO and a change in the spectral parameters. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. The program's objectives are threefold: (1) document, geographically locate, and chronologically order existing and historical Indonesian sundials; (2) examine the cultural, scientific, and technological aspects of these sundials; and (3) develop educational materials and assessments to evaluate the effectiveness of the program in promoting science learning among participants. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. For this purpose, the hub employs D2D transmission and wireless power transfer. This hybrid network is complex and has many variables, making optimization challenging. To tackle this issue, we reduce the problem step by step and develop a series of successive optimization problems. These problems are solved through various optimization techniques, including convex optimization and reinforcement learning. We also investigate the optimal outcome for this problem by analyzing the problem's structure and deriving an upper limit for the optimal outcome. The results obtained can be applied to a general D2D communication network. The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures exhibit a marked advantage over Transformer models in this regard. Efforts to enhance encoder performance through straightforward enhancements, such as adding auxiliary tasks or dropout, yield unexpected results, with some strategies yielding inferior performance despite attempting to improve understanding of the dialogue language. In contrast, the introduction of a contrarian design, such as replacing the encoder with a simple yet optimized baseline, yields unexpected improvements in performance. These unexpected outcomes suggest that encoder representations in dialogue models are inherently flawed and fail to capture the underlying semantics and coherence of the dialogue language, necessitating a reevaluation of the design of these models and their underlying architectures. All evaluation tasks, models, and results have been made openly available at https://github.com/zhunag1124/understanding-dialogue-encoders for replication and extension of our research. Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in autonomous vehicles and robotics by improving local re-localization and loop-closure detection rates in complex environments. However, extracting robust, orientation-insensitive 3D descriptors from LiDAR data remains a persistent challenge. To address this, a novel deep learning network is proposed that utilizes a LiDAR-based attention mechanism (LAM-Net) to prioritize feature representation on curved surfaces. By combining multi-scale LiDAR data and attending to salient points, LAM-Net generates a robust 3D descriptor (LAM-Net-3D) to close loops and localize places more effectively. Experimental results show that LAM-Net outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the SDCLoops and AuVLCD datasets with an average closure rate of 95.5% and 91.5% respectively, demonstrating its superior performance and potential application in autonomous navigation. Moreover, an LAM-Net-based system was successfully tested on a self-driving vehicle at the EuroVR 2019 challenge, achieving a highest ranking and showcasing its practical viability. To facilitate further research, the LAM-Net source code and LiDAR datasets are made publicly available on GitHub.

This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. The velocity of charge carriers can be extracted from the thermal capacity measurements, offering a direct thermal transport coefficient that reflects the intrinsic properties of the material and is insensitive to lattice thermal conductivity. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to high-quality paragraph-level synthesis, which requires not just a natural intonation but also a coherent tone to convey meaning. We argue that successful speech synthesis relies on balancing multiple factors, including local acoustic features, external contextual information, and internal semantic content. To effectively generate speech with these considerations, we propose a new end-to-end speech synthesis framework called the Context-Aware Synthesizer (CAS). This network integrates a contextual encoder that incorporates both acoustic features and external context, as well as a sequence-aware encoder that leverages internal semantic content through bidirectional connections. We evaluate our CAS model against a baseline system and find that it generates more natural-sounding speech, with improved coherence and tone consistency when comparing waveforms and spectrograms. Our results show that the CAS model performs better than the baseline in objective assessments, with a higher mean opinion score (MOS) and reduced frequency and intensity distortions. The speech synthesized by the CAS model also exhibits greater contextual dependence, with a higher MOS when evaluating sentences in isolation rather than in isolation but also when evaluating the same sentences spoken multiple times. The code and data for this project are openly available at https://github.com/sonuspeech/Context-Aware-Synthesizer. The speech samples can be found at https://sonuspeech.github.io/CAS/.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we establish key results about the ring of integers in K and its module properties over the associated order within the rational group algebra Q[G]. A fundamental free module condition is achieved for all such extensions when G is non-cyclic, while a general additive Galois module base change theorem is developed to address cases where G might be cyclic. This theoretical framework is then applied to yield new conclusions about module properties in certain anticyclotomic extensions of Q(\zeta_p), as well as in certain totally real extensions of Q with Galois groups isomorphic to A4 or S4, for a prime p in the range 7 to 127. In the process, the determination of suitable polynomials modulating the field K is explored using a method that combines computer-aided searches with theoretical constraints derived from the works of Harbater, Sato, and Sato-Harris, leading to the identification of additional Galois representations over Q. Additionally, the description of the ring of integers in K and its associated order within Q[G] facilitates questions about the arithmetic of K and may find applications in various contexts, such as the study of modular forms and elliptic curves. For instance, with the knowledge of the minimal polynomial of the Frobenius element in the abelian extension of K/Q, the field K itself can be expressed as a Hilbert class field under an appropriate extension of Q, while further investigation may reveal more intricate connections between the geometry of K and its associated Galois representation. Despite being documented in multiple species, the purpose and direction of IKNM have not been consistently established, leading to significant controversy in the field. We demonstrate this movement serves as a filter for gene expression, with the majority of genes expressed on the apical surface being silenced on the basal surface. We further show that the decision to migrate and ultimately settle on the basal surface is governed by the expression of key transcription factors, which regulate the expression of apical versus basal surface genes. Based on these findings, we propose a model in which the unique, three-dimensional arrangement of the developing cerebral cortex takes advantage of IKNM to achieve a complex, layered cellular distribution through a simple, binary decision-making process at the nuclear level. This process provides a compelling example of how a basic, underlying cellular mechanism can be repurposed to serve a sophisticated, higher-order functional goal. The intricate, six-layered human cerebral cortex is thought to result from a series of highly conserved, symmetrical cortical expansion patterns, with individual layers being generated through a process of successive nuclear migration and differentiation. We uncover a universal, three-step pattern of layer formation, with the primary, transient cell populations giving rise to the molecular layer, the external granular layer, the internal granular layer, the pyramidal layer, the polymorphic layer, and the Cajal-Retzius layer. We also identify a critical, apical surface expression of the transcription factor, Tbr2, which controls the generation of the molecular layer, pyramidal layer, and the Cajal-Retzius layer, with the decision to migrate and settle on the basal surface being governed by the expression of the transcription factor, Tbr1. In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent superposed pixel values. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, taking the form of Toeplitz matrices constructed from coded values, for both uniform and non-uniform sensing schemes. This code design problem is framed as an eigenvalue minimization task subject to specific constraints and structural constraints, and is solved employing an alternating direction method for convese semidefinite programs. The proposed code design method is demonstrated to significantly improve reconstruction performance in both simulated video compressed sensing and a real-world mosaicing task, compared to random code patterns. The tight connection between the proposed method and existing results on the lower bound of the coherence of structured matrices is also established. The method is shown to be computationally efficient for large-scale problems. The open-source reconstruction software and code design method are available online. The methods developed in this research can enhance the performance of various signal acquisition systems, facilitating the practical application of many signal reconstruction methods, including deep learning-based methods. We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive a precise, impactful effect of quenched disorder on the polar active fluid's behavior, and our findings suggest that the long-lived states of this type of active matter are inherently stable in any dimension greater than two. However, we found that the impact of the disorder becomes significantly more important as the dimension of the space decreases. Additionally, we found that the hydrodynamic theory corresponds to the thermodynamic phase of the active matter and that a phase separation between the disordered and ordered states cannot occur. Instead, we find that the tendency of the polar active matter to order spontaneously supersedes the disorder that prevents it from moving freely. The hydrodynamic theory also predicts the existence of a long-lived, quasi-long phase with a continuous order parameter when the dimension of the space equals two, and when the dimension of the space equals three or more, the disorder causes the decay of the order parameter to zero over time. The hydrodynamic theory was validated through comparisons with numerical simulations of different mesoscopic models. The hydrodynamic theory can be applied to any type of polar active matter, and we demonstrate this by analyzing a specific example of an active liquid composed of mesoscopic particles that interact through force laws that vary in strength and range. The hydrodynamic theory is also relevant to the study of active liquid crystals, and we show that the presence of quenched disorder causes the disorder to dominate over the ordering forces as the dimension of the space increases. The hydrodynamic theory predicts that the long-lived states of active liquid crystals correspond to the stability of the smectic phase in dimensions greater than two, and the stability of the nematic phase in dimensions less than two. Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as their primary means of communication. Due to their accessibility and private data storage, these emails are vulnerable to cyber threats and can serve as lucrative targets. Our proposed approach aims to examine research institutions' internal communication networks for potential security breaches. Initially, we gathered and analyzed email data from multiple research institutions, including three in Spain and one in Portugal. We applied an SEIR complex network dynamics model to simulate and assess the vulnerability of these networks. Our results indicated that a significant proportion of email accounts have experienced security breaches, while more than 90% of network nodes exhibit susceptibility to cyber threats. Our research can facilitate the enhancement of email account security for research institutions, while also opening up avenues for further exploration in the realm of communication network security. Due to confidentiality concerns, we cannot disclose the source from which we acquired the communication network data, as this would reveal sensitive information. Nonetheless, we can provide the dataset to researchers who share similar confidentiality concerns. The dataset we analyzed and the computational tools employed are available for free download at https://doi.org/10.6083/H4B5K5CW. The paper to which this dataset pertains has been submitted to the journal Complex Networks.
