Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, theorists proposed the idea of an 'exceptional' van Hove singularity to describe the Fermi surface of strongly interacting electron systems. This concept suggests that interactions could break the symmetry of a system with singular behavior at the center of the Fermi surface, instead causing a gap in a region away from the van Hove point. In the case of cuprates, however, experiments indicate that the pseudogap onset temperature follows the Fermi surface, contradicting the exceptional van Hove singularity theory. In this study, we examine an alternative framework that views the Fermi surface as a continuous function of interaction strength. Based on this framework, we calculate the pseudogap onset temperature using a self-consistent diagrammatic approach and show that it behaves linearly with temperature, in alignment with experimental observations. This linear relationship holds for both the hole-doped and electron-doped materials, and we further predict that the ratio of pseudogap onset temperature to critical temperature will decrease with increasing electron interaction strength. These theoretical calculations can be tested using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and also provide a framework for understanding other electron systems exhibiting van Hove singularities near the Fermi surface. The implications of this study extend to materials exhibiting pseudogap phenomena, including heavy-fermion materials where van Hove singularities may contribute to the onset of gap formation. The proposed theoretical framework can be applied to other materials exhibiting pseudogap phenomena, such as the underdoped phase of strontium doped nickel oxide and certain superconducting materials with nodal Fermi surface. In these cases, interactions with a van Hove singularity near the Fermi surface may result in pseudogap formation only when electrons reside on flat regions of the Fermi surface. In contrast, materials with nodal Fermi surface, such as strontium doped iron oxide and heavy-fermion materials, may exhibit pseudogap phenomena due to the presence of nodal points even without the influence of a van Hove singularity. In such cases, the pseudogap onset temperature is expected to behave linearly with temperature, in alignment with experimental observations. This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in the KISO underground laboratory at the Kamioka site, located one kilometer underground in Hokkaido, Japan. The apparatus, known as the Spallation Neutron Drift Detector (SND), is part of the Kamioka Underground Neutrino Observatory (KOTO) and is dedicated to studying the decay of a specific type of subatomic particle called mesons. In order to accomplish this, the apparatus must accurately measure the flux of these mesons as they travel underground and interact with the surrounding rock and water. However, doing so requires dealing with a high background noise level caused by the production of cosmic-ray muons, which can be as frequent as 1000 times a day. Since the SND apparatus is highly sensitive to these muons, the team developed a unique method to use the muons to estimate the neutron yield and validate the performance of the detector in real-time. Furthermore, the team found that the rate of muon production, measured at a rate of 450 per square meter per day, could be used as a reliable and consistent rate meter for the meson flux measurement. The implementation of this technique resulted in a significant reduction in data background noise and enabled the accurate measurement of the meson flux in the KOTO experiment. The effectiveness of this method has been validated through multiple tests and is now an integral part of the standard data processing procedures used in the KOTO experiment. The technique has also been found to be applicable to other similar experiments, such as the Super-Kamiokande experiment, which can benefit from the implementation of this method to improve the accuracy of their measurements. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions are powerful resources, a comprehensive understanding of the solar system requires a multidisciplinary approach, integrating both space and ground-based observations. In this study, we examined candidates from the TESS mission by analyzing the spectra of host stars using the FEROS spectrograph at the ESO. Out of 139 candidates analyzed, we identified 128 planets, including 5 small planets orbiting small, cool stars. Notably, one of these planets, a super-Earth called TIC 45420108.070101, was particularly interesting as it could potentially be a terrestrial planet located in the habitable zone of its host star. In an effort to validate the planet detection, we conducted a series of follow-up observations, including radial velocity measurements with FEROS and a visual inspection of the light curve, but unfortunately, the data did not support the existence of the planet. Instead, we detected a stellar variability in the star's spectrum, demonstrating the importance of using spectroscopic observations to validate planetary findings. In addition, we present the variability characteristics of the stars observed during this study and these observations can be useful in identifying the intrinsic planetary signals from the variable stellar backgrounds. In this context, we discuss the significance of combining space and ground-based observations in the ongoing search for exoplanets. Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. Oscillators with changing driving forces exhibited superposition states, and such conditions may facilitate quantum state manipulation. These findings demonstrate the utility of Monte Carlo simulations for complex quantum systems and suggest they could be adapted for applications involving driven quantum states. Furthermore, this research may contribute to developments in quantum technology by rapidly modeling key systems via classical simulations. 

Keywords: Quantum harmonic oscillator, Monte Carlo simulations, driven quantum systems, quantum states, imaginary time path integral.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be detected through ground-based spectroscopic surveys. By identifying and analyzing objects exhibiting unusual rotational patterns, scientists can determine the parameters of the YORP effect and gain insights into the asteroids' internal structures. Currently, four asteroid categories have been found that are resistant to YORP acceleration, leading to a standstill of their rotation rates due to thermal equilibrium. To expand the YORP inventory, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of slow-down rotations using the Lightcurve Catalogue of Asteroids and found additional nine objects for the YORP list. Furthermore, by cross-referencing the LCAC database with surveys of YORP stars and objects exhibiting stop-rotations or slow-down rotations, we identified 19 candidates awaiting confirmation through lightcurve observations or other methods. The YORP effect's influence on the distribution of rotation rates among small asteroids is evident in a cumulative plot of the number of objects at each rotation rate class. However, the absence of YORP data for objects in the 10-30 km diameter range hinders a more detailed understanding of this relationship. To overcome this limitation, we propose targeting intermediate-sized asteroids with precise rotation rate measurements through a mission that combines the analysis of YORP acceleration and thermal inertia data, which could provide valuable insights into the thermal evolution of these objects and inform strategies for identifying objects most suitable for the Matador sample hunt mission candidates. The optimal targets for this mission would be asteroids with rotation rates at the boundary of YORP acceleration and deceleration, as well as objects with stop-rotations or slow-down rotations, which could significantly enhance the scientific return on investment for the Matador mission. The proposed approach will enable a comprehensive study of the YORP effect's impact on the rotation rates of intermediate-sized asteroids, ultimately shedding light on the prevalence of YORP acceleration or deceleration in this diameter range. The Matador mission is expected to significantly contribute to the expansion of the YORP inventory, as well as lay the groundwork for future in-depth analysis of the YORP effect's mechanisms and its implications for the thermal evolution of small asteroids. The proposed study will also provide valuable insights into the suitability of target asteroids for the Matador sample hunt mission,

The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on users who interact with political content and their connections. We created an experimental framework to analyze the spread of opinions and engagement among users, posting a mix of political and non-political statements to observe user reactions over time. Our results show that political statements provoke more intense, short-term engagement compared to non-political statements, while also generating sustained interest in the long term. Furthermore, users exhibit distinct behavior when interacting with political content, consistently preferring to maintain their initial opinions rather than switching. We also found that users' opinions on political matters tend to diffuse slowly, if at all, indicating a strong presence of echo chambers and confirmation biases. We explored various time-sensitive aspects of the online discussions, studying the time users take to react to political statements, as well as how these reactions fluctuate over time. Our findings indicate that the youth have varying reaction times when encountering political content, with some users quickly posting comments and others taking longer, and also reveal how users' interest in political statements evolves over time, with some statements generating consistent engagement while others' interest either peaks quickly or rises steadily. We analyzed and compared the behavior of users participating in political discussions to that of those discussing other topics, discovering that political discussions attract a larger, more diverse range of users, with faster reaction times, while also exhibiting similar characteristics in terms of echo chambers and biases. We delved into specific policy-related topics, examining online discussions centered on presidential primary candidate debates, observing how users' opinions diffused slowly, if at all, and also studied online discussions centered on environmental issues, discovering how users' interest in these topics fluctuated more significantly. We provided user-centric, community-based recommendations to mitigate echo chambers and biases, proposing methods for generating diverse discussion groups and creating a scoring system to evaluate the level of diversity within these groups, as well as developing a ranking system to prioritize the most diverse, high-scoring groups over time. We demonstrated the practical feasibility of our recommendations through a crowdsourced study, partnering with the Instagram community around the presidential primary debates to encourage participation and provide incentives for users to engage with diverse groups. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This group-theoretic characteristic applies whether the surface is two-dimensional or higher. Our proof explores the underlying properties of these surface-subgroups in a transitive action, combined with recent general results on action topology for surface-subgroups in a higher-dimensional setting. We further establish an analogous non-compactness result for continuous automorphisms of a compact surface's fundamental group, provided that surface's boundary components are not homeomorphic to a sphere. Lastly, we provide a subgroup of homeomorphisms for a specific compact surface configuration, whose action is highly transitive yet topologically compact within a particular surface-subgroup framework. This final example showcases an intriguing interplay between topological compactness and transitivity across multiple levels of action. Our investigation's outcomes extend and refine prior related findings and showcase the intricate complexities that arise in the topology of group actions upon surfaces.

Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which hinders their application to inverse problems. To address this limitation, a new set of linear regression formulas is presented that can be used to solve the inverse problem of stellar properties given apparent magnitudes and spectral types. These formulas were derived from a set of 121 M-dwarf stars with well-characterized parameters and are suitable for the 0.1-4.6 μm wavelength range. The new equations demonstrate improved performance compared to existing empirical relations and can be employed in both forward and inverse calculations via a user-friendly Python module called pyMdwarfs. This module offers a range of features, including calculations of apparent magnitudes and bolometric corrections as well as solving the inverse problem for stellar temperatures, radii, luminosities, and mass-radius relations. To facilitate seamless integration with other astrophysical tools, pyMdwarfs is designed as a Python module with a simple and consistent interface. The module also includes a graphical user interface developed with the Astropy Graphical User Interface (gyper) tool. The new equations and pyMdwarfs are publicly available at https://github.com/kevinwinden/pYMdwarfs. For further information, please contact Kevin Winden at kevin.winden@unige.ch. The new equations and pyMdwarfs are particularly useful for calculating the properties of M-dwarf stars and planets, such as eclipsing binary detections, exoplanet habitability, and mass-radius relations. The module is highly versatile and can be applied across the 0.1-4.6 μm wavelength range, making it a valuable resource for a wide range of astrophysical research and studies. The public availability of pyMdwarfs paves the way for the community to contribute to its development and utilize its features to enhance the understanding of M-dwarf stars and planets. The team is open to collaborations and suggestions can be provided at the GitHub repository. Confining modes at the boundary between two electromagnetic metamaterial surfaces, which share the same properties, have unique propagation characteristics and can't be described by conventional wave theory. By altering the surface's properties gradually, the boundary can support localized modes of continuous wave types, and our research demonstrates that these wave types include both linear and circular forms for both electromagnetic and terahertz fields. We show that linear waves possess unique polarization properties and can convert between different polarization forms as they propagate, while circular waves exhibit increasing intensity at certain points as they travel. Additionally, our research indicates that the energy of line waves is concentrated between the two surfaces, can be manipulated by altering the surface's properties, and line waves may have uses in the creation of localized high-power fields required for electron stimulation. A theoretical model is also presented, along with experimental evidence, showing that line waves can occur in silicon carbide surfaces treated with a silicon dioxide layer, and have a frequency range that is determined by the surface's frequency of resonance. Line waves offer a promising means of creating high-power, localized fields required for electron stimulation, and could enable the development of compact THz emitters. A theoretical model and an experimental case study of a silicon carbide surface treated with a silicon dioxide layer are also presented, showing that both linear and circular wave forms exist within the THz frequency range. Although a key function in database management, query evaluation classification lacks a comprehensive theory when dealing with self-joined queries. Our investigation addresses this gap by examining how self-joins impact the complexity of enumerating database results, focusing on conjunctive queries. By analyzing the relationships between self-joins and structural aspects of queries, we identify both upper and lower bounds for the complexity of enumerating query outcomes based on tree and graph representations of the queries. These findings reveal that complex self-joins can increase the complexity of enumeration by an exponential factor and pinpoint specific structural patterns that contribute to both enumerational and decisional complexity in queries. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the enumerational complexity of certain structures can be tackled through the application of treewidth decompositional techniques. In addition, we introduce novel benchmarks and showcase the practical implications of our theoretical upper bounds by successfully enumerating outcomes for queries with high complexity in a real-world database management system. Overall, our research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the impact of self-joins on query evaluation classification and suggests potential avenues for improving database management algorithms. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, there are infinitely complex functions in this category that cannot be computed by any of these machines. In contrast, for rational functions over finite inputs, there is a well-known equivalence between computability and continuity. This work establishes a similar but distinct equivalence for regular functions over infinite inputs: a function is computable by a single-pass, two-way transducer if and only if it is continuous, enabling the exchange of analytical and algorithmic proofs of correctness. Furthermore, this equivalence is also valid for streaming transducers, allowing the same proof to apply to both two-way transducers and streaming transducers. In addition, we demonstrate that single-pass, two-way transducers can be viewed as a superset of streaming transducers, with some machines making non-deterministic, infinitesimal choices based on the infinite input, leading to infinitesimal increases in computational capacity. Ultimately, this work provides a foundation for exploring decision problems over infinitely long inputs. In support of this research, an open-source tool called SSGenerator has been developed to automatically convert two-way transducer proofs into publicly accessible, interactive SS proofs, facilitating the demonstration of correctness for regularly complex functions over infinite inputs. A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems and can be trained on significantly smaller amounts of data compared to alternative methods. The latest version of this approach simplifies training by minimizing the need to adjust numerous parameters. In a recent experiment involving a highly complex system with distinct time scales and multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, a reservoir computer of the new design demonstrated several advantages over its traditional counterpart. Specifically, it used a much smaller amount of data for training, a much shorter time to adjust its performance, a smaller number of parameters to adjust, and a much higher level of accuracy in predicting patterns of behavior, even when those patterns change rapidly. In addition to this performance, it was able to predict areas of stability accurately, further confirming the benefits of this new algorithm. In order to evaluate the potential of this new algorithm for applications in optics, it was tested using a model based on a photonic reservoir computer, based on a type of laser that can operate at high speeds and is capable of processing large amounts of data in a short time. The results showed that this new algorithm has the potential to effectively control and optimize this type of laser, as well as similar systems, for use in high-performance data processing and other applications. To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. The new algorithm improves upon the efficiency of the first-order sweep method, which has been shown to be an effective solution for first-order hyperbolic problems. We demonstrate the computational benefits of the second-order successsive sweep algorithm by comparing its performance to the first-order method on a sample problem. Furthermore, we apply the algorithm to a large-scale problem involving the optimal control of a quasilinear Euler equation governing fluid dynamics. The results highlight the significant reduction in computational time achieved through the use of the second-order successsive sweep algorithm. The implementation details, including programming language and key parameters, are also provided to facilitate replication of the study. The novel algorithm is made publicly accessible through the open-source package NSPAlg on the MATLAB Central File Exchange. The package comprises the second-order successsive sweep algorithm and a Python-MATLAB interface for the Euler algorithm. The algorithm and software are tested on a HPC cluster and demonstrate excellent scalability. The results show that the second-order successsive sweep algorithm achieves a linear reduction in computational time when using multiple cores. The algorithm and software are freely available at https://www.cima.unlp.edu.ar/~gacarrillo/research/algorithms/NSPAlg and can be replicated with the following parameters: The sample problem was solved with 10 iterations, 1000 mesh points, and 10 cores. The fluid dynamics problem was solved with 5 iterations, 4000 mesh points, and 512 cores. The Python-MATLAB interface was developed using the mex interface. The implementation of the algorithm on the HPC cluster relied on the MATLAB job scheduler. The software was tested on an Ubuntu-based cluster with 64-bit processors. The algorithm is an important step towards developing computational tools for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case conditions in complex systems, informed by real-world applications in the management of oil reservoirs. The research is part of an ongoing project to create a comprehensive computational framework for optimal reservoir management. Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using the periodic activation function, having
a single MLP per dimension has been the standard in these applications.
Employing multiple convolutions in each MLP branch leads to a more
sophisticated representation of data with both local and global characteristics.
Using this approach on two tasks shows that it surpasses the performance of
traditional methods and reduces the dimensionality even further without
compromising accuracy. Furthermore, this signal representation is highly
robust, as demonstrated by applying it to altered versions of the original
input. Additionally, this representation can be utilized for various tasks,
such as mesh generation and the manipulation of light fields and images. 
Utilizing this representation in video data also proves successful, with no
need to retrain the model when switching between different video sequences. 
Lastly, this approach is computationally efficient and easy to deploy, thanks
to the use of a compact, learned encoder. The code for this project is
available at https://github.com/alevanso/dmlp. 

Our work presents a novel, dual multi-layer perceptron architecture called
DMLP, which produces a two-part representation of data. This novel approach
comprises two components: a detail map and a coherence map. The detail map is
a low-dimensional representation containing the primary elements and their
local interactions, while the coherence map holds information about long-range
connections and more complex global characteristics. This two-part representation
facilitates various tasks, such as light field rendering, shape opaqueness and
texture, and image segmentation. Moreover, it can be utilized for video data
and exhibits robustness when subjected to modifications to the input. DMLP
combines multiple convolutional layers with periodic activation functions and
includes a compact, learned encoder that makes it computationally efficient
and easy to deploy. Our findings, including the code at https://github.com/alevanso/dmlp, demonstrate the superiority of DMLP over traditional methods
in terms of both accuracy and dimensionality reduction. Ultimately, this work
proposes DMLP as a versatile signal representation model for images, light fields
and videos.

Research into the neural basis of animacy perception has revealed that the ventral temporal cortex responds to a wide range of non-human biological entities, from simple forms to complex animals and faces. However, the underlying factors driving animacy perception across this continuum remain unclear. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging and a shape manipulation technique, this study measured changes in animacy perception as basic form features were modified to form more intricate forms, and further altered to depict entire animals and then faces, all within the same stimulus class. The findings show a distinct increase in animacy sensitivity across the continuum, with a critical juncture where the addition of local features suddenly amplifies animacy perception. Computational modeling and theoretical frameworks suggest that the ventral temporal cortex processes animacy through an hierarchical combination of entity detection and distinctive feature recognition. This study presents evidence for two hypotheses explaining animacy perception along the continuum: a 'featureless entity' hypothesis applicable to basic forms, and a 'face-like entity' hypothesis applicable to more complex animals and faces, with the critical juncture marking a critical threshold between them. The results indicate that the brain's ability to recognize animacy is a skill that builds upon itself, with each stimulus class contributing uniquely to the whole continuum. The findings also suggest that the brain's ability to recognize faces is an integral part of its ability to recognize animals, and that a comprehensive understanding of the factors driving animacy perception across the continuum is crucial for addressing fundamental questions in the field. Ultimately, this research offers novel insights into the complex and multifaceted nature of animacy perception within the ventral temporal cortex.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. Furthermore, this extension enables the expression of preferences regarding program performance, such as minimizing the number of measurements required, as preferred to achieving a specific computational goal. The "expectations" operator is semantically defined through the use of relational Hoare triples and program transformations, which ensures its soundness. Moreover, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by deriving proofs for a range of quantum programs, including those that utilize unitary transformations, measurements, and classical control, as well as programs consisting of sequential and parallel executions of subprograms. By providing a set of basic rules and deriving derived rules, we have established the practical applicability of this logic to a broad spectrum of quantum programs. Finally, we have explored the potential for implementing this logic through the specification of a judgment algorithm and the identification of challenges related to the verification of programs in the category UCQ(1), which encompasses programs that rely on at most one classical control register and any number of quantum registers. In addition, we have developed a prototype tool that supports the automated proof-search for a limited subset of the full logic, which we plan to further enhance in future developments. Through the incorporation of performance-related expectations into pre-/postconditions and relations, as well as the derivation of proof-rules for a comprehensive range of quantum programs, the extension of quantum relational Hoare logic offers a versatile and effective methodology for the specification and verification of programs within the broad spectrum of weakly entangled programs. This methodology is sufficiently robust to be implemented via an automated proof-search algorithm for a substantial segment of UCQ(0) programs, which encompasses programs that do not employ classical control, as well as programs consisting of unitary transformations, measurements, and any combination of these elements, in isolation or in conjunction. Nevertheless, the verification of programs in UCQ(1) remains a manually intensive process, which necessitates a highly refined and adaptable verification strategy in order to achieve even moderately complex programs. Consequently, we propose a new approach, which involves the integration of performance-related expectations into pre-/postconditions and relations, as well as the derivation of proof-rules for a comprehensive range of weakly entangled programs, which we believe has the potential to effectively address this challenge. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in the early stages of an epidemic, as it significantly amplifies the viruses basic reproduction number ($R_0$) to a degree that rivals traditional contact tracing. Employing a mathematical model that accounts for both super-spreader events and $R_0$, we investigated through numerical simulations and various transmission strategies how the elevated $R_0$ impact from the initial stage of an epidemic is gradually diminished by non-pharmaceutical interventions as the epidemic progresses, ultimately being minimized in proportion to the event's magnitude. We also found that even if the epidemic is initially controlled without immunity, a super-spreader event can trigger sudden virus resurgence if case detection and isolation are relaxed. This phenomenon can be mitigated through enhanced case detection and isolation, as well as a faster implementation of non-pharmaceutical interventions, which can prevent a resurgence by keeping the epidemic's growth rate below unity even if case detection and isolation are later relaxed. This implies a window of opportunity exists for an early, effective response to contain the epidemic's spread. No immunity among the population is necessary for this outcome to materialize; this result holds true even in a model that accounts for a partially immune population. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by investigating the codiskcyclicity of C_0-semigroups comprised of operators. Moreover, we provide a codiskcyclicity criterion for collections of operators aligned with a common gap, specifically focusing on its application to pairs of operators. Lastly, we explore codiskcyclicity within the setting of energy spaces for generation groups, providing codiskcyclicity criteria for collections of operators that are codiskcyclic under the original topology, along with associated proofs. These results are illustrated through codiskcyclicity demonstrations for several concrete examples, encompassing C_0-semigroups, generation groups for second-order differential operators, and Volterra integral operators. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path, but this transformation introduces an additional computational cost that scales with the inverse of the problem's severity. In models like the lattice Hamiltonian, the sign problem's intensity is directly proportional to the filling level and is particularly pronounced in regions with high density. Consequently, the most effective solution for the sign problem would utilize a transformation that minimizes the additional computational overhead while significantly reducing the problem's severity, especially in these high-density areas. In the study, we examine the Lattice Hamiltonian for electrons interacting via a BCS-like pairing force and demonstrate that a simple ring-shape transformation efficiently addresses the sign problem with minimal additional computational cost. By applying this transformation, we successfully perform Monte Carlo simulations at various filling levels, and the results show notable accuracy when compared to exact calculations, with an average error of 0.16. In the most challenging scenario examined (filling level $\nu=3$), the sign problem's intensity was reduced from $e^{\pi^2}$ to $e^{2\pi^2}$, indicating that the computational cost was reduced by a significant $e^{\pi^2}$ factor. Furthermore, we present a detailed analysis of the superfluid phase diagram at various non-zero twist angles for both the Lattice Hamiltonian and the related Bosen-Einstein condensate problem. The study reveals a robustly established phase diagram with isolated islands of superfluidity surrounded by a sea of normal phases. The shape and size of these islands are controlled by the intensity of the sign problem, the severity of which serves as an essential factor in determining the superfluid phase boundary. In the model examined, the superfluid phase is eliminated at high density due to the intense sign problem, but the application of a simple ring-shape transformation yields a substantial improvement in simulations at high density, resulting in the re-emergence of superfluid regions in those areas. The study's findings are complemented by illustrations of the overlap of ground states at different twist angles, which demonstrate spatially coherent regions with high overlap, indicating the robust existence of superfluid phases, in contrast to regions with low overlap, indicating the fleeting nature of non-zero eigenvalues in the twisted boundary conditions. The research presents a novel solution to the sign problem, introducing the ring-shape transformation, and offers a robust framework for phase diagram construction in complex systems. This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula shows the same connection to the Dickman function and and provides an interesting link to the more theoretical estimates derived from the RH. As a result, we are able to improve the current record in a range of $y$ below $(\log x)(\log \log x)^2$ without any assumptions. Under the same conditions, we also derive a formula or an estimate for the count of y-friable integers that are products of at least two prime numbers, further strengthening our main result. By assuming the GRH, we are able to extend this comparison to all $y \ge (\log x)(\log \log x)^{\varepsilon}$, thus breaking through the $\varepsilon$-dependent barrier for the first time ever. In addition to this, we explore and clarify various connections to earlier work by Hildebrand and Saias, as well as the state-of-the-art achieved by Pomerance and his results derived under the same conditions. As a side effect, we are also able to improve the record in the range of $y$ below $(\log x)(\log \log x)^2$ without any assumptions for the count of y-friable integers, or in the range of $y$ below $(\log x)(\log \log x)^{\varepsilon}$ for the count of y-friable integers that are products of at least two prime numbers, assuming the GRH. Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image Y under σ is a subshift composed of words derived from X's elements, with X being the set of inputs for σ. We investigate the complexity classes of Y and X, establishing a connection between their growth rates. Specifically, for left-infinite bi-infinite sequences, if X's complexity function f_X is bounded by a sublinear, non-decreasing function g, then Y's complexity function f_Y is also bounded by g, indicating X's topological entropy equals Y's. If X's complexity function is sublinear, however, we cannot guarantee Y's complexity function is sublinear. Nonetheless, for right-infinite bi-infinite sequences, we can establish a similar connection between Y's and X's complexity functions. Additionally, we examine the relationship between X's and Y's topological entropies, defining them as the supremums of X's and Y's complexity functions over all possible configurations, showing them to be equal. We also explore the impact of left-infinite and right-infinite constraints on X's and Y's topological entropies. Lastly, we provide examples and counter-examples to illustrate our findings. 

Keywords: free monoid morphism, subshift, topological entropy, complexity class.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to yield satisfactory results.
By incorporating an unusual pair-wise ranking step, we rectify the model's performance and achieve significant gains in our experiments.
Notably, using just 300 epochs and a relatively small batch size, ReCross achieved exceptional results on various tasks like T0 and FLAN in both low- and medium-data settings, with results as follows:
For T0 in the low-data setting, ReCross produced 23.2% and 10.2% improvements in GLI scores on Padded-MLM and Whole-Sentence-MLM, respectively, with just a 0.3% decline in Superficial-MLM.
In the medium-data setting, ReCross saw 8.5% and 5.3% gains for those tasks.
For FLAN in the low-data and medium-data settings, ReCross achieved 10.6% and 5.5% gains in GLI scores on Padded-MLM and 3.8% and 2.3% gains in Whole-Sentence-MLM, respectively. 
These breakthroughs showcase the immense potential of unsupervised cross-task generalization in massive language models.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. This computation is further refined to accommodate groups whose homotopy type dependencies are not yet comprehensively mapped. Lastly, we explore connections to rank detection in Coxeter groups via the boolean complex's homotopy type. As a result, several instances of rank detection via discrete Morse theory are resolved, including the fundamental group of the complex itself. In particular, we solve rank detection for the Coxeter group B_n through the homotopy type of its boolean complex, whereas previous approaches to solve this problem were either incomplete or required additional techniques. Our research is capped by investigating the homotopy type of the complex's 1-skeleton. While the general case remains unknown, we demonstrate computational effectiveness of our method by solving rank detection for E_n, F_4, and the Artin group of type A_2 through the homotopy type of the complex's 1-skeleton. In the process, we establish connections between discrete Morse theory and the Lannes' filtration, enabling the application of the latter to compute the homotopy type of the complex's 1-skeleton. In the case of B_n, this computation is further refined to derive the complex's 1-skeleton homotopy type, thereby solving rank detection for B_n via the complex's 1-skeleton homotopy type. As a byproduct, we solve the same problem for D_n and E_n. In contrast, for F_4 and the Artin group of type A_3, while we solve rank detection via the complex's homotopy type, the 1-skeleton homotopy type remains unknown. In the latter case, we establish a connection with the Muñoz's work, and refine its computation to derive the complex's 1-skeleton homotopy type for A_3. In contrast, for A_4 and F_4, while we solve rank detection via the complex's homotopy type, the 1-skeleton homotopy type remains unknown.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency and click-through rates as indicators of online attention, we developed a Hawkes process model to analyze the inter-arrival times of increased attention, as well as a topic-modeling approach to identify the connections between online attention and real-world cases. Our findings revealed that a small group of influential users played a significant role in propagating rumors through retweets, as well as the presence of certain pre-existing conditions that can make users more susceptible to falling prey to rumors. To mitigate the spread of rumors, we recommend targeting users with high influence scores and modifying online platforms to reduce unnecessary exposure to misleading information. The distance to galaxies is often determined by analyzing extragalactic objects with known properties, such as planetary nebulae with well-defined luminosities and spectral classifications. Determining distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae distance ladder relies on measuring the intrinsic luminosities and spectral classifications of individual planetary nebulae. In a study of 11 planetary nebulae in the Large Magellanic Cloud, using data from VMC and the NTT, researchers applied a new, more accurate method to measure the masses of globular clusters based on the dispersion of planetary nebulae. By applying this new approach to previously measured masses of 19 globular clusters in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a systematic bias was identified, resulting in an overestimation of masses by a factor of two. This discovery led to a revision of the masses of these 19 globular clusters and prompted a re-evaluation of the masses of all galaxies in the Magellanic Clouds based on previous measurements, which in turn affected the total mass of these galaxies. A revised mass-luminosity ratio for galaxies in the Local Group was also determined, leading to a re-estimation of the distance to the Large Magellanic Cloud of 61.40 ± 0.32 kpc, a value that can be applied to other similar galaxies, and a new perspective on the mass of the Large Magellanic Cloud and its potential impact on the Milky Way galaxy. Additionally, a new approach to measuring the mass of globular clusters based on the velocity dispersion of planetary nebulae was proposed, involving a theoretical relationship between the velocity dispersion, the mass of the cluster, and the number of planetary nebulae, which can be applied to unsolved cases. Furthermore, a comparison was made between the velocity dispersion of planetary nebulae and stellar velocity dispersion in the Magellanic Clouds, leading to a re-evaluation of the mass-to-light ratio and the mass of globular clusters in these galaxies. A proposed new method for determining distances to galaxies based on planetary nebulae, incorporating a theoretical relationship between the velocity dispersion of planetary nebulae, the mass of globular clusters, and the number of planetary nebulae, could provide more accurate distance measurements and has significant implications for the study of galaxies in the Magellanic Clouds and beyond. This research is based on data collected by VMC and the NTT at the ESO, La Silla, Chile, and is part of a larger study of 11 planetary nebulae

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. Additionally, LifeStream supports popular statistical analysis libraries via its temporal query language, enabling seamless integration with computational biology tools. As an open-source framework, LifeStream facilitates continuous improvement and enables researchers to explore new research opportunities in stream processing, healthcare, and computational biology. We have already successfully applied LifeStream to a range of prominent research projects and showcase its effectiveness through publicly available benchmark results and the source code for LifeStream on the following website: \textbf{https://lifestream.in}.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as the most critical decision in the training process, with popular options including cross-entropy and mean squared error. However, research indicates that a loss function's effectiveness is heavily dependent on data quality, with a proposed framework suggesting five key factors influencing its performance. Through a series of experiments utilizing the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and German Credit datasets, our study demonstrates that a basic neural network can achieve satisfactory classification results when trained with an unsuitable loss function due to overfitting's limited impact. Furthermore, we contend that researchers should be cautious when drawing conclusions from experiments, as issues with loss function selection may confound results and mask the actual effects of other variables. To mitigate this risk, we suggest incorporating loss function robustness as a performance metric in future evaluations. In the context of the German Credit dataset, our findings indicate that a neural network can achieve comparable classification performance using both cross-entropy and mean squared error loss functions, with results suggesting that these datasets may be sufficiently robust to withstand subpar loss function choices. In contrast, the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets appear more susceptible to model overfitting, with a proposed framework placing the former in the non-robust category and the latter in the moderately robust category. In the case of the German Credit dataset, we consider it robust. 

Keywords: Loss function, neural networks, supervised classification, robustness.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and a temperature-dependent diffusive process. This model ensures the preservation of polymer material symmetry and successfully simulates the interplay between crystalline and amorphous regions. To minimize computational complexity, the level set method is integrated with evolutionary laws that respond to mechanical and thermal stimuli. The model's ability is demonstrated through numerical simulations of a uniaxial tension test and a heat transfer test, with results showing its capability to model the interplay between crystalline and amorphous regions under mechanical stress and heat transfer. The model can be found in the accompanying paper, with additional details on its development found in references. The proposed model provides a foundation for investigating strain-induced crystallization in polymers under complex loading conditions and temperature variations. The model is publicly available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/Chen-Yang-Huang/Thermo-Mechanical-LSM. The underlying finite element implementation is based on the FEAPD framework by K.J. Our technique also proves successful on complex datasets like the C4 dataset, a dataset comprising complex scenes and numerous possible actions, as seen in the TSP dataset. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images, but they tend to produce unsatisfactory results when confronted with genuine rainy conditions. This study suggests that this disparity stems from the difference in spectral characteristics between real and artificial rain, which poses a significant obstacle to developing a universal rain removal method. To address this limitation, we present an innovative approach that leverages a complementary technique - deraining and desnowing can be achieved via a shared low-rank decomposition representation, but existing methods overlook the complex nature of natural light. Instead, we propose a new model, inspired by the physics of light dispersion, which involves developing an integral operator to describe the spectral behavior of rain. Nevertheless, formulating an analytical expression for this operator is highly complicated, if not impossible. To circumvent this challenge, we suggest a numerical approach, based on a meta-learning framework, which utilizes a compact expression for the integral operator and can be approximated through a sequential application of two simple convolutional operators. We further extend this approach to tackle multiple snow layers and demonstrate the versatility of our method by applying it to both deraining and desnowing tasks with various input images. Notably, our model exhibits a high degree of interpretability, offering a unique glimpse into the complex nature of natural light through the decomposition of light intensity, snow/snow layers, and the integral operator. Comparative evaluations with prominent rain removal methods, along with detailed component analysis, have been included in the appendix for further review. Our research is openly accessible on MMEditing, and the code can be found on GitHub.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Moreover, our approach proves resilient to various labeling schemes and user interface designs. By exploring both the efficient grouping method and the interactive interface in action, we demonstrate their combined effectiveness in successfully training agents on challenging tasks, achieving performance on par with models utilizing vast amounts of labeled data. Our findings validate the value of human investment in this method, amounting to merely a fraction of the time required for comparative evaluation-based methods. We make the code, data, and human interaction interface publicly accessible.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models utilizing these patterns achieve higher accuracy in evaluating the relationships between previously unconnected conditions and effects. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Finally, we present an alternative construction of the uniform parking distribution based on a recursive updating process. The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence. In particular, the study focuses on the masses of Ω− and θ+ particles to investigate the mass relationships among quarks within these baryons. Additionally, an analysis of diquark masses, obtained by subtracting a quark mass from the sum of two quarks' masses, reveals positive values, confirming the quark nature of these particles. Furthermore, studies examine the charge radii of Ω− and θ+ and evaluate the mass splittings between these particles and their counterparts, the φ and φ∗ mesons. All calculated properties demonstrate consistency with experimental observations and available theoretical estimates. In contrast to other approaches, this study's results show similar mass patterns to those obtained from lattice quantum chromodynamics simulations and confirm the linearity of the Regge trajectory. All calculated properties of the Ω− and θ+ particles are summarized in the appendix for easy reference. Notably, the study finds the mass of the θ+ to be approximately 1.495 GeV, which may indicate that this particle resides within the ground state rather than an excited state of quark systems. In experimentally verifying the existence of the θ+ and accurately determining its properties, a study suggests that further experimental research is needed. If the θ+ is confirmed as a ground state quark state, it may provide valuable evidence supporting the mass relationship among quarks within these baryons. In addition, the study's results on the Ω− and θ+ particles compare favorably with available experimental and theoretical data, thereby validating the employed method of calculation. In conclusion, this study successfully utilizes a quark model with linear confining forces to effectively explore the properties of the Ω− and θ+ particles, providing a useful framework for further research into these particles and potentially other exotic multiquark particles. In order to verify its findings, the study recommends that experimental research be conducted at facilities such as the BESIII, LHCb, or future experiments like the PANDA or the JPSI.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as temperature and humidity effects, which influence the behavior of virus-laden aerosols. To better understand this complex process, we employed a combined numerical method that links computational fluid dynamics and the lattice Boltzmann method to simulate and visualize virus transport in a moving bus under various conditions, including when passengers wear masks. Our findings highlight significant differences in aerosol spread when considering movement and respiration, revealing that turbulent airflow plays a key role in dispersing aerosols and increasing the range of transmission. Additionally, we found that coughing and sneezing can release large droplets which may fall to the ground, but also produce fine virustained aerosols that disseminate widely due to their small size. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of humidity, temperature, and face masks on transmission risk, with results showing that masks significantly reduce the transmission of both large droplets and fine aerosols. Our study provides valuable insights into the factors that contribute to airborne transmission risks in confined spaces and highlights the importance of mask-wearing to reduce transmission risk. Moreover, we propose a risk assessment framework that takes into consideration the critical factors that contribute to transmission risks in different settings and suggests potential mitigation strategies. This framework can be applied to various enclosed environments, such as public transportation, restaurants, and offices, to evaluate transmission risks and inform public health policies. By combining computational modeling with a risk assessment framework, we can provide policymakers with data-driven insights to inform decisions on public health measures and help mitigate the spread of airborne transmitted diseases. As an example, we applied this framework to investigate transmission risks on public transportation, with results showing that wearing masks can reduce transmission risk by at least 60%, and further highlights the significance of social distancing, with a 90% risk reduction, and considers the impact of face masks, with a 60% risk reduction, and humidity effects, with a 20% risk reduction, on transmission risks. With this framework, we can simulate and visualize the complex transmission process of airborne transmitted diseases, with results showing that respiration and coughing/sneezing release different sized droplets with varying transmission risks, and that humidity affects the transmission of fine aerosols. By integrating computational modeling with the lattice Boltzmann method, we can effectively capture the behavior of virus-laden aerosols in confined environments, with results showing that turbulent airflow plays a key role in dispersing aerosols

This note presents the development of an algorithm to identify all single-layer, fully transitive polyhedra in three-dimensional Euclidean space. It also demonstrates the application of this algorithm in determining the structure of such polyhedra using a simplified approach, focusing on cross-sections in specific directions. By utilizing this method, we examine various possibilities for fully transitive polyhedra with single-layer configurations. Additionally, we leverage this approach to construct new examples of fully transitive polyhedra, including one with a hexagonal fundamental vertex figure. To further illustrate the algorithm's effectiveness, we consider an important class of fully transitive polyhedra - those derived from the orbits of vertices under the symmetry group of the dodecahedron - and employ the algorithm to determine new fundamental vertex figures for these polyhedra. One such fundamental vertex figure, obtained for the first time, has a pentagonal base and is characterized by four layers. We discuss the properties of this new fundamental vertex figure, along with two more, and show that the polyhedra constructed from these vertex figures exhibit high symmetry, comparable to that of the snub dodecahedron. Lastly, we explore the implications of using these new fundamental vertex figures in the construction of polyhedra.

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We demonstrate that a standard public-key encryption (PKE) scheme can be modified to possess an unclonable property, albeit it may come at the cost of reduced security in other aspects, such as indistinguishable encryption (DISS). In contrast, incorporating quantum-based PKE (KEM-style) results in a more secure but less versatile outcome.

  - Key Properties: We examine various key properties, including clonability under a different key and whether a copy of the original message can be created from an existing ciphertext, all while considering the restrictions and differences between classical and quantum-based settings.

  - Practical Applications and Efficiency: We also explore potential practical applications and assess the efficiency of existing and proposed schemes in this context. Specifically, we analyze the clonability of the Learning with Error (LWE) problem and propose a new, efficient unclonable encryption scheme based on the Bostrom et al. (Eurocrypt 2010) key exchange scheme, yielding a passively secure KEM-style PKE scheme with an unclonable property while maintaining high computational efficiency. However, this comes at the cost of reduced security in terms of DISS, with at least $2^{\sim n}$ time complexity required to break its security, where n represents the number of bits in the encryption key. Finally, we outline an approach to achieving a positively secure, unclonable encryption scheme based on a quantum-based KEM, but it remains an open question for now. 

  - Definition Expansion and Analysis: We expand upon and analyze several definitions of clonability, including a new definition for a positive-security setting, as well as exploring the relationships and distinctions between different key properties in both classical and quantum-based contexts. 

  - Related Work Discussion: We discuss existing unclonable encryption schemes, focusing on their construction methods, security levels, and efficiency, with additional consideration given to their potential applications and clonability in different settings.

beated. Additionally, we examine the circumstances under which a powerful
transmitter can utilize a variety of modulation techniques, including binary and
continuous options, to provide secure and unambiguous transmission to the
intended recipient. We also provide a means to calculate the capacity of this
communication channel and discuss the impact of an informed adversary on this
interplay. Furthermore, we establish that in the absence of an informed
adversary, a powerful transmitter and communication channel can provide secure
and unambiguous transmission, thereby achieving capacity. However, this
authentication strategy fails when an informed adversary is present, and we
investigate the consequences for a weak transmitter and limited communication
channel as well as consider the impact of an informed adversary on the capacity
under both powerful transmitter and communication channel conditions. These findings
lay the groundwork for a more in-depth examination of this problem in future
research. This study draws on prior work by Ozarow and Lehnert and also
incorporates an unrelated problem that was initially intended for publication.

This paper explores the implications of an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold, where we find that the potential function $f$ must be a constant across the manifold. In addition, the differential of the soliton's potential, amplified by a scalar multiple, can be used to define a non-trivial Killing vector field. Furthermore, the soliton's scalar multiple $\lambda$ is constrained to be either positive or zero, providing a key aspect of its characterization. Along with recent findings from the research of Chen and Wang, our findings further establish the equivalence between conformal gradient Ricci solitons on a Sasakian manifold and their intrinsic soliton form. Moreover, the distinct solutions of the soliton's equation are examined, including both the soliton metrics derived from the Einstein metric and those constructed from the warped product of a manifold with a line. Lastly, the non-existence of conformal Ricci solitons on a compact Sasakian manifold is proven, as is the non-existence of steady or expanding conformal gradient Ricci solitons on a compact manifold.

radiative pressure, in contrast to microobject ejections which are influenced by

loss patterns, whereas the stellar wind's shape is determined by the interplay
between the star's gravitational and radiative forces. By studying these processes
scientists can better understand the evolution and fate of both celestial bodies.

microobject context, with specific applications to the study of exoplanets.

reviewed, with particular attention to those developed to examine the impact of

investigate the magnetospheric environment surrounding microobjects are briefly

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. Our method offers a potential tool for analyzing Mie-type potential-based systems in physics. 

Keywords: Fractional quantum mechanics, Mie-type potential, Bound state solutions, Jumarie type fractional derivative, Approximate solutions, Numerical examples.

Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; however, developing adjustments that cater to an individual's abilities and progress within the game is a complex process. To address this challenge, we propose an approach that leverages machine learning to create tailored modifications to a game that align with a player's capacity for movement, taking into account the automatic assessment of motor skills through reinforcement learning. To support this approach, we introduce a new framework for evaluating the functional ability of players, using a combination of machine learning algorithms and physiological data alongside quantitative performance metrics from the game. By applying this framework to evaluate upper limb rehabilitation through a modified version of the Braid game, we conducted a pilot study with three participants. Our findings show that our approach can effectively create customized adjustments to the game that are responsive to changes in a player's motor skills, and can provide a meaningful measure of functional ability across different levels of the game. Notably, our results indicate that the machine learning algorithms used to create these customized adjustments can generalize across different versions of the game, with implications for the efficient development of upper limb rehabilitation games. Overall, our study presents a novel framework for evaluating functional ability and creating personalized modifications for games used in upper limb rehabilitation, and paves the way for the use of machine learning in developing more effective and engaging rehabilitation tools. Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks. We have previously shown the simplicity and effectiveness of this approximation in a linear elasticity setting. Here, we explore its performance within a nonlinear elasticity framework, represented by a minimum approach to singular contests model, and demonstrate the robustness of our approximation through specific numerical analyses and a computational example. These scenarios highlight how our method successfully captures the piecewise-rigid nature of structures, even in absence of brittle fractures, and we provide a computational strategy to solve this problem using a stabilized augmented Lagrangian scheme. We then validate the accuracy and robustness of our variational approximation through numerical experiments conducted on both discrete and continuous level sets. These experiments demonstrate the capability of our method to accurately model both rigid structures and those with fractures, and we also compare our results to a recent model proposed by the community. Finally, we conclude with potential future directions for this research.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to data from the LHC, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Furthermore, this code can be used to interpret the results of these searches, thereby providing a key contribution to the understanding of quantum chromodynamics within the context of these searches. As the LHC operates at increasingly higher energies in its upcoming phases, this code will be crucial in anticipating the outcomes of searches for vector leptoquarks and informing the design of such searches in future experiments. This code is made publicly available to facilitate the broader utilization of its precision calculations and potential collaborations in this field. By doing so, we aim to contribute to the ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC through collaborative efforts. The code is initially evaluated in conjunction with data from the LHC, operating at a central-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and encompassing the entirety of its operating period. As a result, this code provides the most accurate calculations available for Drell-Yan ditau production at the LHC, taking into account the most intricate aspects of quantum chromodynamics. In addition to vector leptoquarks, this code can also be used to model other exotic particles that couple to ditau final states, such as fourth-generation fermions and leptoquark resonances, which could have a significant impact on the search strategy for vector leptoquarks. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and children, due to insufficient knowledge of radiation effects on a cellular level. DeepLearning-based models, specifically using deep neural networks, have shown potential in estimating radiation doses from PET images, thereby enabling radiation-reduced or replacement imaging protocols. However, a significant challenge lies in training such models using large quantities of data from various sources, given the complex and diverse nature of PET images. A novel framework is proposed, comprising multiple components, including an attention-based network and a generative adversarial network, to develop a highly accurate and transferable model capable of estimating radiation doses from limited training data, while minimizing reliance on external information. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed attention-based network over benchmark models and its ability to successfully apply learned dose estimation patterns to new, unrelated datasets with minimal additional training. Furthermore, the proposed framework effectively tackles the problem of training models on diverse PET image data sets with limited annotations. A case study is also presented to illustrate the practical advantages of the proposed framework in clinical settings. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. By integrating quantum information theory and Lie symmetry, our research provides a novel framework for studying complex many-body systems while uncovering general principles applicable to a wide range of quantum systems. In doing so, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by investigating the operator growth phenomenon across multiple examples, including the SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, for a variety of Krylov complexity measures and information capacity indicators. Ultimately, our analysis confirms that the universal operator growth hypothesis holds true across these systems, predicting an exponential relationship between system size and operator complexity. Furthermore, we identify an intriguing correlation between the rate of this exponential growth and symmetry strength, suggesting that Lie symmetry rate may serve as a fundamental driver of the operator growth phenomenon. In addition, we find that entanglement depth and renormalized average entanglement display distinctive patterns, influenced by the symmetry of the system, while information capacity indicators reveal an exponential relationship with system size, driven by a combination of factors including the rate of operator growth, entanglement depth, and symmetry strength. With this research, we establish a comprehensive theoretical framework that can be applied to an even broader range of systems, making it an invaluable resource for further investigation of the universal operator growth hypothesis across complex many-body systems. In addition, our analysis highlights two-mode coherent states as a powerful tool, capable of extracting fundamental features of the operator growth phenomenon, while also demonstrating the key benefits of leveraging Lie symmetry, including streamlined calculations and enhanced insight into the underlying principles governing these systems. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings.
