This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian. The findings show that zero-shot
learning achieves the best results on both languages, yielding accurate rates of
64.41% and 73.48% for Slovene and Croatian, respectively. Furthermore, the
paper explores the effectiveness of models trained on datasets from a single
language and models trained on datasets from two languages through both zero-shot
and few-shot learning approaches. The initial experiments demonstrate that the
model trained on datasets from two languages yields more reliable results than
those trained on datasets from a single language in zero-shot learning scenarios.
Conversely, few-shot learning on a single language produces more accurate results
than models trained on datasets from two languages in both single-task and multi-
task settings. The paper's supplementary material includes the code required to

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing the reachability of program states and verifying whether certain conditions are met through the use of fence sets. Moreover, we investigate the relationship between fence sets and the coherence protocol's reordering, as well as the potential for optimizing fences within this context. By exploring different orderings of fence sets, we demonstrate the existence of an optimal fence ordering that meets program safety criteria and state-based safety conditions. The existing algorithm for optimal fence ordering determination is suboptimal, leading us to investigate alternative solutions, including a new algorithm with superior performance. However, this improved algorithm's benefit is only realized when the underlying program state meets specific criteria. We also analyze various program examples to demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework and algorithm for optimal fence ordering determination. Lastly, we highlight the potential for integrating our framework with cutting-edge processor technologies. No previous experience with cache coherence protocols is required to comprehend this work, as we approach the subject with a focus on simplicity and clarity. Due to the complex nature of this topic, the development of a practical verification tool for fence ordering still remains an area of ongoing research. The framework, algorithm, and tool demonstrations are available at our project website listed at the appropriate cite. All research and tool implementations are conducted in collaboration with J. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. This improvement comes with a significant increase in the scaling factor, albeit at the cost of a greater complexity in the underlying quantities that define the arithmetic progressions in question. Prior to this work, the best-related frequency theorem, applicable to instances where sumsets have a size near 2k, resulted from the frequency theorem proven by Green and Tao in their celebrated result on the convergence of Kloosterman sums. It's worth noting that the complexity of the underlying quantities in the frequency theorem of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem doesn't significantly increase relative to that of the related frequency theorem of Green and Tao, although the scaling factor does increase substantially. It's also demonstrated in this paper that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every three-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it fails to hold that A and B must exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions, even if we restrict ourselves to very large values of the underlying quantities in question. Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(B^{H}+f)$, particularly proving that if the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ exceeds $Hd$, then its density function is square-integrable, or if $A$'s Hausdorff dimension surpasses $Hd$, then its density function admits a continuous version, thus providing a result already mentioned. Additional results on the singular continuity of the density function, as well as an investigation into the density's pointwise behavior, are also provided. These results significantly expand upon existing knowledge and offer new insights into the properties of the occupation measure's density for modified fractional Brownian motion. Moreover, this research paves the way for exploring more general stochastic processes defined through set operations and may offer new perspectives on the underlying path properties of these processes. Ultimately, this study is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complexity and geometric characteristics of modified fractional Brownian motion's images, particularly its parabolic and Euclidean variants. Lastly, this research is anticipated to lay the groundwork for further investigations into the properties of the occupation measure's density and its potential connections to spectral theory and operator algebras.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable. Furthermore, comparisons are made between our approach and other methods of investigating quantum chaos, including Riemannian chaos and the properties of quantum levels. Additionally, we demonstrate that quantum chaos in the H\'enon-Heiles system is closely related to the emergence of negative modes in classical systems, and that both classical and quantum chaos are equally triggered by changes in the angular momentum of the system. Our analysis provides a clear insight into the complex interplay between quantum effects, classical chaos, and the geometry of systems driven by these forces.

This paper analyzes the Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) issue in object understanding and addresses the high false positive rates associated with it. During the training process, a significant number of incorrect relationships are learned to be plausible, hindering the model's ability to accurately distinguish between true and false relationships. To tackle this problem, we propose the use of a dual-objective loss function that penalizes not only false positives but also limits the number of plausible relationships the model can learn. By constraining the model's capacity for plausible relationships, we leverage the fact that only a limited number of relationships are actually feasible in a given image. By combining a classification loss with a contrastive loss, we ensure the model properly classifies actual relationships while maintaining the ability to generate plausible ones. To further enhance performance, we introduce an asymmetric contrastive loss function that reduces false positives more aggressively than false negatives. Experimental results demonstrate that our method yields a substantial reduction in false positives and outperforms existing methods on the Visual Relationship Detection benchmark. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/zhengyangfeng/PlaNet-ConTris.

This study offers a supervised action recognition method suitable for low-light environments. We utilize a light-guided projection module based on the self-supervised learning technique to extract motion features from a single light source, regardless of the lighting conditions in the training dataset. To enhance robustness, we incorporate a coarse-to-fine processing approach. Additionally, an attention mechanism is implemented to focus on critical areas exhibiting significant movement. Notably, our proposed method overlooks the use of pre-trained models for action classification, instead relying on a basic convolutional neural network. Experiments conducted on the NTU-RGB+D dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, with particular emphasis on its performance in low-light environments. Comparative analyses with existing methods validate the superiority of our proposed technique. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengyf123/Low-light-action-recognition.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on eight diverse data streams. Our research demonstrates the quantum-inspired measurement technique's (MIMI) superiority in terms of average online and offline metrics, as well as the beneficial impact of hyperparameters, which can be efficiently tuned via a grid search. A pivotal question in digital evidence law revolves around a court's authority to require a device password disclosure, a question that various jurisdictions are addressing through different legal frameworks. This research focuses on the English and Welsh approach, specifically the doctrine of "reasonable notice" introduced by the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996, Section 9. By analyzing the line profiles of several light elements - carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, magnesium, and silicon - in the star's atmosphere, we were able to derive their surface abundances. Analysis of the star's oscillations provided information about its internal rotation rate, revealing a 16 km/s difference between the core and the surface. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have shown potential in detecting false information, especially when based on verified data, their effectiveness declines significantly in situations involving new and unforeseen events. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing an approach that utilizes a limited number of labeled examples to identify false information on emerging events. This approach leverages a dual-stage system that first employs a general-purpose false news detector to filter out genuine information from false, based on specific event characteristics. It then employs a specialized deep learning model that learns from a limited number of labeled false articles and relevant natural language processing tools to distinguish false information from true information. The general-purpose false news detector is based on a BERT model that incorporates a pair of additional modules, one for removing unimportant language and the other for identifying key event features. The system's performance was evaluated using Twitter data related to the COVID-19 pandemic and results showed that it effectively reduced the fake news candidates before refining them, resulting in improved performance compared to a single-stage system and traditional approaches. The model and data are available online. 

This paper also presents an open dataset designed to assess the ability of false news detection systems to handle new events quickly, along with accompanying evaluation metrics. The current best approach, despite achieving high accuracy, still fell short of human standards and struggled with more complex events. In one case, it incorrectly identified 32% of false information as true for an event that required further verification. This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation, focusing particularly on those that take the form of quasi-bialgebras. By establishing connections to quasi-triangular quasi-bialgebras and leveraging set-theoretic solution properties, we show that these quantum algebras possess significant properties, including the ability to be equipped with a triangular structure and a specific invariant form. This framework allows us to systematically identify and construct several new quantum algebras, such as U_{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathfrak{g}) and the S-matrix algebra associated with the Faddeev-Takita quantum Yang-Baxter equation, for various simple Lie algebras \mathfrak{g}. Notably, we derive the specific realizations of the Drinfeld quantum double for A_{2n}, C_{2n}, and G_{2}, which differ substantially from their set-theoretic solutions. Furthermore, this framework enables us to determine necessary and sufficient conditions for the associated quantum bialgebras to be coradical-finite, as well as the relationship between these quantum bialgebras and their underlying set-theoretic solutions. Lastly, we explore and construct several new examples of such quantum bialgebras, including those associated with super-algebras and Lie algebras of type D_4. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the structure and properties of the quantum algebras in question, as well as their connections to set-theoretic solutions, while also unveiling numerous new examples and related bialgebras. These findings open up promising avenues for further investigation into the representation theory and deformation of these algebras and bialgebras.

A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are constructible in any four-dimensional space if one of the dimensions is even, while in three-dimensional spaces, possible combinations are limited to certain pairs of odd dimensions. Additionally, in two-dimensional spaces, GCA quadruples are feasible for any pair of dimensions, whereas in three-dimensional spaces, quadruples are only possible when one of the dimensions is two, with the other dimensions being arbitrarily chosen. A central identity is designed to apply to at least four-dimensional spaces, and constructions for five-dimensional GCA pairs and certain quadruples are also provided. Lastly, several constructions are provided for complex GCA in one-dimensional, two-dimensional, three-dimensional spaces, and when one of the dimensions is five, along with challenging scenarios in higher-dimensional complex spaces. To achieve this, silicon must be accurately modified with phosphorus dopants, which requires a deep understanding of the interplay between quantum tunneling and clock pulses. In this research, a precise control method is devised and effectively implemented on a silicon device containing a single phosphorus dopant. The technique utilizes a sequence of pulses to manipulate the overlap between ground and excited states, which is measured through time-energy mapping of quantum emitters. Clock pulse control was successfully demonstrated on a device with a single embedded phosphorus dopant, showing a marked effect on the emission pattern due to the extra quantum coherence created by the pulses. This finding paves the way for developing robust quantum control methods essential for the development of reliable silicon quantum processors. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding the fundamental principles governing their dynamics. To bridge this knowledge gap, we propose a method using temporal graph neural networks that ensures causality and a limited number of hidden units per neuron. By constraining the model using the multilinear rank factorization technique, we can derive a powerful expression for predicting future system states from past observations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the expressiveness of this proposed approach by showing it is equivalent to highly regarded models such as the nonlinear multilinear model and the extensive factorization model. Moreover, our analysis reveals that these models share essential characteristics with fundamental scientific theories, encompassing the ideal gas law and predicting planetary orbits under gravity. Ultimately, our framework provides a unified statistical model that can be applied to various complex systems and paves the way for estimating model parameters using data from experiments and/or simulations. We showcase the effectiveness of this proposal by applying it to three distinct scenarios: a planetary orbit, an ideal gas with an added particle, and a simple chemical reaction between two molecules: hydrogen and oxygen. As the field of graph neural networks and systems science continues to evolve, we hope this work lays the groundwork for developing more advanced predictive models, ultimately driving a deeper understanding of the fundamental principles governing complex systems dynamics. We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable the calculation of homology group ranks for certain constructions in topology. Moreover, they provide a fundamental ingredient for an algorithm to determine the normalized volumes of growing Euclidean subdivisions, a key component in the computation of volumes of high-dimensional spaces. This algorithm is an expansion of the Recursively Calculated Normalized Volume Algorithm, initially developed with a more restrictive application. By showcasing this method, we can evaluate the counts of particular integer partitions up to a given size, while also computing the ranks of abelian groups associated with these constructions. However, the algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through a simpler case, as the most effective implementation would likely require a more efficient algorithm for computing the underlying M\"obius function. As a practical application, we employ this algorithm to compute the homology group ranks for a specific family of complexes, establishing connections to existing results and suggesting potential directions for further research. Furthermore, we provide a step-by-step description of the algorithm's recursive formula derivation, accompanied by a sample calculation to illustrate its application. Lastly, we pose questions and suggest potential extensions related to the algebraic framework underlying our calculations. Lastly, we note that the algorithm's most effective implementation would likely necessitate a more efficient algorithm for computing the underlying M\"obius function, while also exploring the broader implications of these calculations within the context of graded polynomial rings.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by using MRI images before and after the procedure. However, these evaluations can be complicated by the presence of scar tissue and other abnormalities in the MRI images, making it difficult to define the boundaries of the treated brain area. In an attempt to resolve this challenge, we developed a mathematical method to accurately identify the boundaries of the treated brain area based on pre- and post-treatment MRI images, without relying on external references or predefined formulas. This new approach was successfully tested on simulated brain images and real-world data, yielding precise boundary definitions compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrated a high level of consistency in its outcomes when applied to different sets of MRI images. In contrast to other brain segmentation algorithms, our method operates within a comprehensive framework that can be adapted to accommodate various imaging modalities and different measurement units. Consequently, this algorithm may be a valuable tool for analyzing post-LITT brain images, ultimately contributing to the assessment of LITT treatment efficacy. In its current form, this algorithm is accessible as a part of the 3D Slicer software package. In future iterations, we intend to enhance its performance by incorporating additional processing techniques and comparing it to other related methods. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite product states that cannot be extended to a full set of nonlocal properties using local measurements. We focus on finding strong nonlocality in unextendible product bases (UPBs), a key resource for this phenomenon. UPBs consist of multiple product states that cannot be combined into a full set using local measurements. Our research aims to identify whether all UPBs contain strong nonlocality and if so, determine the relationship between strong nonlocality and UPBs. To achieve this, we develop a new criterion for strong nonlocality based on its connection to UPBs and apply it to already known UPBs. Furthermore, we demonstrate a direct method for detecting strong nonlocality within UPBs consisting of multiple states. Using these methods, we examine the relationship between strong nonlocality and UPBs in 2-qubit, 3-qubit, and 4-qubit systems. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to easily capture complex, recursive program relationships.
However, efficiently evaluating GP 2 programs poses a challenge due to the potential for deep graph nesting.
To overcome this limitation, GP 2 incorporates a rooting mechanism, limiting program structure to a finite depth of branching.
In addition to a rooting mechanism, GP 2 features a unique method for handling unbounded recursion via a 'call stack,' which replaces infinite graph depth with a finite sequence of references.
By combining rooting and call tracking, GP 2 programs are transformed into a new, flat graph representation called Pre-GP 2, allowing for lightweight evaluation using a minimal set of rules.
In our research, we develop a method for converting GP 2 programs into Pre-GP 2 with call tracking and demonstrate its effectiveness through the implementation of a GP 2 compiler, showcasing the benefits of GP 2's architecture through benchmarking of actual GP 2 programs. 
Our results indicate a significant performance gain, achieving evaluation speeds comparable to those of GP 2 programs with shallow nesting, and also achieving substantial memory reductions in programs with deep nesting due to the rooting mechanism. 
Furthermore, we explore the potential applications of GP 2 and its compiler as a back-end for various programming languages, including JSON, XML, and database query languages. 
Our research paves the way for a more in-depth investigation of GP 2's capabilities and efficiency in program analysis and verification. 
In addition, our GP 2 compiler is publicly available for download and provides an innovative solution for evaluating recursive programs with complex structures. 
Our research also offers an original approach to handling unbounded recursion via call tracking, an innovative method that can be adapted to other graph-based languages. 
In our research, we explore the relationship between GP 2 programs and Pre-GP 2 programs via call tracking, demonstrating its soundness and completeness through a formal proof. 
Our research is part of an ongoing project to evaluate recursive programs with complex structures, combining rooting and call tracking for efficient program analysis and verification.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Furthermore, these graphs possess a degree that grows in proportion to the square of the number of orbits under automorphism group action, and this degree of dependence is precise. Locally arc-transitive graphs exhibiting quasiprimitive behavior on multiple orbits do not exist. Additionally, a limit is placed on the number of orbits within locally arc-transitive graphs, and this limit is directly proportional to the degree of the graph when the degree grows large, conforming to a specific standard. This finding is further illustrated by a new infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs with a high degree, and these sequences are derived from infinite families of twisted star graphs and line graphs, respectively. Lastly, a local anti-transversal set of minimum size for certain members of these sequences is calculated, and this includes a new minimum local anti-transversal size for the Grasshelley graph. Lastly, several unsolved questions are posed regarding the twisted star graphs, including the determination of local anti-transversal size for certain members, as well as the classification of quasiprimitive action within these graphs. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superiority in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits computational efficiency, requiring less time than other competitors. As an illustrative example, we apply this algorithm to a real-world dataset consisting of morphological characteristics and combat outcomes of ancient Greek warships. The methodology described can be applied to any dataset that combines continuous and categorical variables. The algorithm's code and the accompanying data for the examples are available at the link provided. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks, yet their limited generalization capacity beyond their training data remains a significant concern. To enhance the versatility of these models, there is growing interest in leveraging external structured knowledge for various NLP tasks. In this work, we differentiate between two methods of incorporating knowledge: using natural language descriptions and employing knowledge graphs. We argue that the latter offers several advantages, including more precise and concise information, better handling of semantic relationships, and reduced noise. To facilitate easy access to knowledge graphs, we introduce T5-KG, a type of large language models that can draw from knowledge graphs through a proposed multi-hop retrieval framework. This framework allows us to build a prototype of few-shot named entity disambiguation and to conduct experiments on the efficacy of using knowledge graphs for natural language inference, revealing a notable gain of over 20% in accuracy compared to traditional data. Moreover, we demonstrate the potential of this approach for low-resource languages and observe a 10% improvement in inference when utilizing knowledge graphs rather than language descriptions. The code and knowledge graphs are available at https://github.com/ghrua/T5-KG.

This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. These analyses demonstrate how inhomogeneous boundary conditions can be viewed as limiting cases of the nonlocal equations, with certain conditions on the fractional parameter. Furthermore, the article discusses how inhomogeneous boundary conditions can be perceived as an outcome of the nonlocal equations, given specific requirements on the fractional parameter. These results provide a framework for understanding the relationship between inhomogeneous boundary conditions and nonlocal equations, addressing concerns and solutions presented in recent research articles.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas affected by Parkinson's disease, centered on the substantia nigra pars compacta and basal ganglia. The model incorporates the autoregressive integral method to generate realistic neural activity patterns, based on the Friston's DOPAMINE hypothesis. The model consists of two key components: the autoregressive integral models for neural populations and a dopaminergic system that self-regulates according to the intensity of its release. The autoregressive integral models are defined by equations that incorporate neural activity, external inputs, and past activities, with the goal of mimicking the characteristics of local field potentials. The dopaminergic system, in turn, exerts a modulating influence on the neural populations through a cost function that influences the autoregressive parameters. The model's ability to mimic the effects of dopaminergic medication was tested using a computational simulation, with the results showing a significant and clinically-relevant improvement in the reduction of tremor-like activity in the affected areas. The model's potential for contributing to the development of targeted brain stimulation therapies is also discussed. The code for this model is available online as an open-source repository.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase or decrease smoothly. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original operator's characteristics, including smoothness and compatibility with second-order derivatives. It has been mathematically proven that the modified operator converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling the accurate reconstruction of a function even when using a large interpolation interval. This is demonstrated numerically through the solution of an ordinary differential equation and the evaluation of a non-smooth function, showcasing the method's efficiency and effectiveness.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
The experimental model is a basic implementation of the U-Net structure, and we experiment with conventional training, data augmentation, and a limited dataset to establish key findings:
using the RFS dataset, a diverse set of weather conditions can be accurately classified without additional preprocessing techniques;
both horizontal and vertical flips are ineffective data augmentation methods;
horizontal rotation and carefully applied data augmentation lead to significant performance improvement;
utilizing a limited dataset still yields a satisfactory classification rate. 
Our research indicates that a basic U-Net structure is capable of effectively classifying the RFS dataset without relying on complex weather features, and that the model's performance is resilient to limited data scenarios.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns and accurately estimates the associated heat transfer scaling when employing a prism-shaped cell. Notably, the precision of these predictions rivals that achieved by sophisticated mass-flux schemes and the comprehensive analytical theory. The suggested two-fluid model also demonstrates the ability to capture the effects of horizontal extension on convection through increased residual stresses and subsequent increases in heat transfer rates. The straightforward nature of the model makes it suitable for integration into general circulation models, with the first exploratory studies on multi-fluid GCMs already underway. The model has the added benefit of facilitating a deeper understanding of the interactions between convection and potential atmospheric superrotation by incorporating a suitable boundary condition. The implications of this research on the advection of potential temperature and moisture are also discussed, paving the way for further investigation in numerical simulations of global convection. The publicly accessible code for the model can be obtained from an open-source repository. The present paper provides the theoretical basis for the model and documents the results of a series of numerical experiments, with the code serving as a tool for subsequent model development and refinement. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Using event horizon radius data from gravitational wave events and electromagnetic observations of black hole candidates, a statistical examination was conducted to identify whether their dimensions are linked to an intrinsic temperature and entropy in a manner consistent with standard holographic principles across various mass ranges. Additional analysis into the relationship between the surface gravity of these objects and their dimensions revealed potential biases that could impact inferences about thermodynamic phase transitions, with dimensions exhibiting distinct behavior at specific critical points that may be tied to mass transitions in black holes. Furthermore, a minimum critical mass was estimated below which the dimensions of the objects in question would not exhibit the characteristic behavior seen in more massive black holes, and this finding is interpreted in the context of the information paradox and the role of firewalls in mass transition transitions. Lastly, the statistical significance of the findings was evaluated in relation to potential systematic errors in the data used.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since field experiments typically have a limited number of replicated trials, the results lack sufficient data, which hinders the adoption of these methods by practicing farmers and industry stakeholders. To address this challenge, we investigate the application of Bayesian methods to analyze a single trial outcome and its limitations in comparing multiple treatments. In addition, we explore the use of a Bayesian expected value approach to determine the certainty equivalent of each treatment directly from the posterior distribution of mean yields, which provides a more accurate and reliable measure of expected values. To validate our approach, we conduct a field experiment using a series of fungicide treatments on a wheat crop under natural disease pressure. The results show that the Bayesian expected value approach yields robust and reliable measures of expected values even with a limited number of trials, which can be a valuable tool for industry stakeholders and farmers to compare the efficacy of multiple treatments directly from a single trial outcome. 360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences, particularly in virtual tourism, by allowing users to explore destinations naturally. However, these videos demand high bandwidth, making them expensive to stream and limiting their accessibility. To address this challenge, a deep learning framework has been developed to enhance 360-degree streaming videos by fusing multiple frames into a single streamable video. This framework utilizes a 360-degree attention mechanism and convolutional neural networks to predict user views from video streams and correct any desynchronization. Fusing multiple frames increases the perceived quality, while bandwidth requirements remain similar, making it a cost-effective solution. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves significant quality gains with reduced bandwidth, outperforming alternative techniques. Furthermore, user evaluations indicate a preference for the proposed method, demonstrating increased viewing satisfaction. This framework has been applied to improve the viewing experience for two prominent 360-degree streaming video platforms. In collaboration with these platforms, we have identified key factors influencing user view predictions and validated our approach with real-world data, paving the way for further research and potential applications. In virtual tourism, streaming video field trials have been conducted, yielding promising results, and the proposed method is deemed viable for large-scale, commercial 360-degree video streaming applications. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/zhengzhengchen/360FusionStream, along with the trial data mentioned in the paper. This work has been accepted for presentation at IEEE ICME 2022. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This project uses data from the Microscope experiment to examine these frequencies for any signs of a phenomenon that could indicate a violation of the weak equivalence principle, taking into account the experimental errors associated with each individual frequency. By analyzing these results in the context of the experiment's overall sensitivity, we place limits on the magnitude of any potential violations of the weak equivalence principle. These limits apply equally to both local and non-local violations, as they fall within the experiment's detectable range. In this case, the experiment places these frequencies within its detectable range, resulting in tightened limits on the magnitude of violations of the weak equivalence principle at frequencies below 73.3 $\mu$Hz, a value that surpasses previous records set by ground-based experiments. Furthermore, the narrow window in which the experiment operates its most sensitive tests allows it to set lower limits on the frequency at which any potential violations of the weak equivalence principle should occur, raising this threshold to 2.5 times $10^{-18}$ times the Earth's gravitational acceleration, a record that exceeds the capabilities of ground-based experiments by a significant margin. Additionally, this experiment places a universal mass acceleration sensitivity limit of $7.8\times10^{-16}$g$_{\rm c}}$ and a local mass acceleration limit of $1.4\times10^{-17}$g$_{\rm c}}$ at a frequency of 38.6$\mu$Hz. We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, while others exhibit mixed behaviors, all of which are dictated by the dimer's overall directionality. This directionality can be manipulated through the displacement of the dimer within a narrow range, offering the possibility of controlling the movement of dimer-shaped cells through the management of their internal asymmetry. This research offers an initial exploration into the fundamental properties of active colloidal dimers and highlights the significance of studying dimer-like structures over individual active particles. It also highlights the potential for future studies to advance our current understanding of active matter. Specifically, we analyze k-hops strong shortest path covers in polynomial time for series-parallel graphs and show an NP-hardness proof for k-hops strong shortest path covers in the class of n-node series-parallel graphs. On the other hand, we provide a k-hops cover of size n for series-parallel graphs, and demonstrate a (n/2) + 1 approximation for all graphs through a greedy algorithm. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for compressing deep neural networks, enabling a smaller model to acquire the probabilistic and decision-making characteristics of a larger, more complex model. Traditionally, this approach relies on the assumption that the teacher model produces accurate and relevant knowledge, but real-world applications may involve a teacher model contaminated with errors or irrelevant information. In response, we introduce a new framework called heterogeneous distillation transfer, addressing scenarios where the teacher and student models share different source and target data characteristics. Through the incorporation of a noise factor that allows for the generation of synthetic data, our framework is capable of extracting valuable knowledge from the teacher model and eliminating any noise or bias. With the incorporation of a joint training approach for the teacher and student models, our framework produces a student model that not only possesses the same probabilistic characteristics as the teacher but also performs better in terms of accuracy and bias reduction. Extensive experimental evidence confirms the superiority of our approach over conventional distillation methods in scenarios with label noise and bias. Additionally, our framework's ability to leverage unsupervised knowledge transfer is demonstrated. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyang762/hdtx.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific subset of vertices~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including hypergraphs, which do not allow parallel edges, as well as cliques and trees. Further, a fixed-parameter complexity analysis of SGR is performed in relation to parameter~$k$, which indicates that this problem contains a fixed-parameter algorithm based on vertex inclusion, but not based on vertex exclusion. A fixed-parameter algorithm is developed for the Strong Geodetic Generalized version (SGG) of the problem, which involves determining the minimum number of vertices required for a strong geodetic subset, as well as identifying this subset, within a graph~$G$ and its subgraphs. This research is an extension of previous studies on geodetic subsets of graphs. It provides new insights and fixed-parameter algorithms for the SG and SGG problems, which can be useful for developing more effective algorithms. In particular, a fixed-parameter algorithm is proposed for the parameter~$k$, which could be employed to address NP-hardness issues. In addition, this research compares computational complexities across various graph types, including hypergraphs, cliques, and trees. It is acknowledged that geodetic subsets have diverse applications in biology, physics, and computer science, among other disciplines. Therefore, further research is recommended to explore the properties and algorithms for geodetic subsets, as well as the Strong Geodetic problem, and its generalizations. In particular, research is suggested on computational complexity, fixed-parameter complexity, and NP-completeness, as well as the development of fixed-parameter algorithms and heuristic approaches, and the investigation of the Strong Geodetic problem within different graph types, including hypergraphs, cliques, and trees. We examine several methods for estimating the policy and evaluate them on complex MultiArmedBandit and gridworld problems. The findings indicate that imitating diverse actions results in a superior policy when compared to standard approaches, while also providing insight into the scalabilty of different methods. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly boosted through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function prediction to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a simple grid world and more complex MultiAgentChainWorld environments, showing that co-imitation learning can yield superior performance compared to imitation learning from individual data and even surpass traditional reinforcement learning performance. Moreover, our analysis reveals the challenges posed by agents imitating each other, including the risk of being "fooled" by peer agents' suboptimal policies. Our findings suggest that co-imitation learning can be an innovative solution for addressing the data scarcity issue in reinforcement learning. Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large size of the action space, specifically the vast vocabulary in the translation decoder. This study investigates the hypothesis that reducing the action space's size (ASLS) enhances RL's effectiveness. We first present an analytical model highlighting ASLS's benefits in terms of action concentration and target word coverage. Empirical results across three language pairs demonstrate that both a limited starting vocabulary and dynamic sub-vocab selection yield substantial improvements (up to +2.5 BLEU points) when combined with RL training. Furthermore, our findings show that dynamic sub-vocab selection's performance can be further optimized by incorporating a simple threshold-based strategy, along with characteristics of target words, to select more accurate sub-vocab sets (up to +1.3 BLEU points). All experimental settings and data were conducted within the TPUv2-8 and TPUv3-8 frameworks. The proposed methods' efficacy is evident, and they introduce straightforward, computationally light techniques that can be readily integrated into current RL-based NMT pipelines. Source code and additional data/implementation details are available at this link: https://github.com/zheng062/ASLS-RL-NMT.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of these context-free languages, we show the simplicity of their combined form's context-free nature. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more complex than solving the space complexity of these context-free languages. We also establish that the universal version of V's word problem, when restricted to inputs where one side is filled, is not in NP by reducing from the NP-complete circuit satisfiability problem. This indicates that solving V's word problem deterministically, even for finite inputs, cannot be accomplished in NP time. This result is achieved without employing any non-deterministic techniques. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between Weingarten type operators and the biharmonic equation itself, discovering that specific operators such as the shape operator play a crucial role in determining whether a hypersurface is biharmonic. Additionally, within the context of the Euclidean space, we establish that the shape operator and its components behave identically to the Jacobi operator and its components, when the operator itself is a recurrent curvature operator within a certain subset of the Euclidean space. Building upon this finding, we prove that any biharmonic hypersurface, which has an intrinsic type point somewhere, will have a widespread presence of intrinsic type points. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis of dark matter creation within its own parameters. As a result, we find that the model naturally produces the appropriate amount of dark matter through a combination of processes including neutrino-induced axion production, as well as the creation of sterile neutrinos within the core of axion stars and bombs, and finally, through the primordial depletion of axion plasma within these objects as they move through the dense early universe. Additionally, we analyze the possibility of these objects serving as dark matter within our own universe, estimating the minimum mass required for their stability and the duration they spend doing so. Furthermore, we investigate the characteristics of these objects as they interact with each other and the surrounding dark matter through both non-perturbative and perturbative means. As a result, we are able to estimate the minimum mass of axion stars, as well as their lifespan, and we find that primordial axion bombs possess an extremely low mass, likely below $10^{5}$ grams. We also find that the density of axion stars and bombs in our universe does not exceed $10^{-6}$ times the density of dark matter. Nevertheless, we anticipate that the direct detection of these objects or their antimatter counterparts through antimatter sensors in future experiments such as XENONnT and DARWIN may become feasible in the near future. The axion star scenario also presents an opportunity to observe the diffused annihilation radiation from these objects as they move through our galaxy's halo, potentially making them detectable through the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. The future development of multi-messenger observations and a deeper understanding of the universe's dark matter structure may make it possible to locate these objects directly through gravitational lensing or gravitational waves. The time period during which axion stars and bombs exist as dark matter is estimated to be on the order of $10^{-3}$ times the present-day age of the universe. In image recognition, distinct types of elements (edges and pixels) contribute uniquely to the recognition process. While edges provide a visual outline and characterize an image's shape, pixels represent the actual building blocks of an image. Our research focuses on edge-based recognition within the context of medical imaging, specifically using an artificial neural network, as conventional boundary detection methods are not sufficiently advanced to substitute edge-based information for pixel-based information. By incorporating edge attention into a neural network, our model enhances the network's ability to utilize edge information for accurate diagnosis. We experimentally compared edge-based attention to standard attention and found that edge-based attention outperforms the alternative by achieving a 1.2% improvement in the case of K-nearest neighbors and a 7.4% improvement in support vector machines, ultimately demonstrating the potential for edge-based attention to be applied across a broader range of machine learning algorithms. Additionally, we observed reduced overfitting with edge-based attention as an important factor. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengfengs/Edge-Attention.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols to identify potential vulnerabilities and weaknesses. In an experimental analysis, we assessed the effectiveness of transactions across various deployment scenarios and encountered instances of failed transactions and inconsistent document state. To address these issues, we proposed and implemented a method to detect and analyze the effects of MongoDB transactions, especially focusing on transactions that failed or exhibited inconsistent document state. Our approach involves using the MVAPID tool to create modified versions of the database and apply successful transactions, and we demonstrated its usability and effectiveness through an evaluation of our method. We intend to contribute our transaction analysis framework to the community to facilitate further exploration and development of effective techniques for analyzing MongoDB transactions.

Furthermore, we connect the underlying statistics to Desnaney-O'Connell (2009) and analyze the $e$-positivity of related functions. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. Moreover, a theoretical model explaining the benefits of this approach is developed and its performance analyzed under varying conditions. The implementation of a dynamic baseline model further facilitates an in-depth examination of the proposed approach's benefits. Ultimately, the successful application of this method to an additional task indicates its potential for adaptability across different scenarios and tasks. In conclusion, the presented real-time domain adaptation method yields superior results and may serve as a foundation for further research into advanced techniques. The code and data utilized in this research are openly accessible for replication and exploration by the community. 

Keywords: speech-emotion recognition, real-time domain adaptation, reinforcement learning, policy gradient, multi-task learning.

BFTO exhibits magnetic order origin stemming from the Fe$^{3+}$ ions for T$\leq$5.5 K, and our findings reveal a notable increases in magnetic order with enhanced pressure, accompanied by a shift in the critical pressure from 4 to 7.5 GPa for magnetic order disappearance upon cooling under pressure. Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors like
air traffic, weather, and aircraft performance. Current approaches to this problem use
a two-step process, with initial discrete optimization followed by continuous global
optimization. The choice of network density affects the results of the latter, with
implicit implications on discrete optimization. This study proposes a method to
explicitly control network density based on a density threshold, which enables flexible
management of the discretization error. The proposed method is validated using
real-world data and aircraft performance data, with results showing that controlling
network density according to the error threshold leads to more efficient computation,
with reduced running times and fewer iterations, while producing comparable results
in terms of optimal route distances. However, the approach may not be suitable for
networks with significant variations in local density, with power-law distribution. 
The proposed method is particularly useful for flight planning, as it enables dynamic
adjustment of network density to mimic the effects of air traffic, with reduced running
times. The method can also be adapted to other continuous shortest path problems in
spatial networks.

with an example input file specified in the README file.

library for global optimization, with the network generation based on the Vickers
model. The research is supported by the European Union's Horizon 2020 research

A persistent issue in signal processing research stems from the diversity of methods used to analyze time series data, particularly when comparing results across different techniques. To address this, it's essential to verify the validity of analyzing time series data before drawing conclusions. The proposed method involves assessing the convergence of estimates from different techniques, such as autoregressive modeling, fractal analysis, and embedding dimensions from delay plots, in the study of a highly nonlinear system driven by white Gaussian noise. The system's time series data presents challenges due to its nonstationary nature and the need to distinguish it from stationary systems driven by noise, which requires special consideration in practical applications. The findings indicate that while most methods converge for the driven system, they yield inconsistent estimates for the nonlinear system, highlighting the importance of accounting for the system's drive mechanism and system type when interpreting results. The method's effectiveness is further demonstrated through the analysis of a renowned chaotic dataset. In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate voltage due to the quantized charging energy's impact. The observed phenomenon is consistent with theoretical predictions and holds significant potential for applying quantum randomness randomly switching a quantum state on and off. Furthermore, we propose potential applications for this phenomenon in random telegraph signal generation and adjustable scanning resistance in SIS mixers. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of Josephson devices as reliable random number generators, with the added benefit of adjustable generation rates controlled by the gate voltage. Additionally, we investigate the threshold temperature's spatial uniformity across different locations on the wafer, with a focus on identifying potential sources of threshold distribution disparities. Our research provides valuable insights into the phase behavior of Josephson junctions and suggests the potential for developing robust random number generators with adjustable rates, offering a promising path for utilizing quantum randomness in a controlled manner.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures. Furthermore, boundary temperature-dependent non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are computed, and the impact of a finite aether-like constant on the non-abelian Casimir effect is explored through numerical estimation with SU(N) gauge groups, for both zero and finite temperatures. Additionally, the influence of a non-abelian aether-like term on the deconfinement temperature within finite temperature quantum field theory is investigated. Lastly, discussions on the possibility of testing Lorentz symmetry violation through the non-abelian Casimir effect in confined spaces are presented.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is defined and analyzed in the context of a general European option. Subsequent sections apply this framework to specific options, including calls, puts, digital options, binary options, lookback options with a general minimization or maximization path, and options with an Asian strike that mimics the arithmetic or geometric average of the underlying asset's past values. Furthermore, the study provides a method for calculating the expected hedging cost over a specified time period, as well as an upper limit for at-the-money options, providing the option price divided by its volatility times the square root of the time period. The results can be employed to determine the option price, volatility, or hedging cost, given the other parameters, through a system of nested Newton-Raphson iterations. The study also verifies the accuracy of these formulas through direct simulation, as well as examining the validity of the approximation when time steps are large. Finally, the research illustrates the method's application via examples of the options mentioned above. The associated algorithm and a Python implementation of the method are included as supplementary materials. The paper's results can be of particular interest to option pricing theorists, numerical analysts employing the method, and practitioners responsible for implementing the method in a production environment. The study's method is versatile, addressing a wide range of options, and the associated algorithm exhibits acceptable computational efficiency. However, further research is required to extend the method to options that cannot be handled through the established method, as well as exploring alternative hedging strategies. By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic level. The material's macroscopic behavior is characterized by an uncoupled mixture of two phases, and our analysis provides a method for determining the limiting phase structure. The strength of the material's microstructure is reflected in the coercivity of its magnetization, and our approach enables the study of this phenomenon. The results can be interpreted through the calibration of a magnetization constraint in favor of the material's mechanical properties. The analysis is grounded in the minimization of a functional that includes the squared gradient of a magnetization field, and we investigate this problem under both constrained and unconstrained conditions. The key concepts are explored through the calculation of lower bounds for the coercivity, and we consider two specific material configurations: a composite material with alternating layers, and a material with a two-dimensional tree-like structure. The results for these structures demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in quantifying the energy storage within high-contrast composite materials. The research is set within the broader framework of the nonlinear elasticity model and contributes to the ongoing study of the impact of structural defects on the material's macroscopic behavior. The results for the material with layers yield a lower bound of $\frac{1}{3}\varepsilon_0$ for the coercivity, and for the tree-like structure, the lower bound is $\left(\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}}\right)\varepsilon_0$. The results for the composite material with layers and the tree-like structure have a practical application in the development of high-performance magnetic shape memory alloys and nitinol. The research also explores the effect of constraint and volume fraction on the coercivity, and the results indicate that the coercivity can be optimized through the manipulation of the material's microstructure and geometry. The research is relevant to the development of nitinol with high coercivity and could contribute to the improvement of nitinol's performance in biomedical applications, such as in the development of self-healing coatings and in the treatment of cerebral aneurysms. The research can also contribute to the improvement of nitinol's biocompatibility and resistance to fatigue failure. The study of the coercivity of the material's microstructure and geometry could also contribute to the improvement of the sensitivity and accuracy of nitinol-based sensors and actuators. Our analysis revealed that roughly 25 percent of 2664 galaxy samples, selected from the SDSS, exhibited distinct tidal features with a flux fraction exceeding one percent, constraining our tidal feature detection method to achieve a similar accuracy as the original study by Joerson et al. For the first time, we delved into the detailed properties of these tidal features, establishing a relationship between their mass-to-light ratio, radius, and flux fraction. Our findings indicate that low-density regions surrounding early-type galaxies tend to possess tidal features with shorter radii and lower mass-to-light ratio when compared to more dense areas. Additionally, we observed a linear connection between the radius and flux fraction of tidal features, providing a means to predict radii based on given flux fractions or the reverse. This statistical analysis paves the way for investigating tidal features in specific galaxy samples, providing a robust framework for comparing mass distributions within and outside galaxy borders. To explore this dynamic, an simple model incorporating inheritance and education has been developed. Furthermore, the model estimates the impact of inherited wealth on education, as well as the effects of education on wealth, both across and within generations. Interestingly, despite significantly improving education outcomes, the recent decline in mobility rates in the US cannot be attributed to changes in the effects of inheritance on education. Instead, the model suggests an increasing influence of inherited wealth on education, particularly in the US, which can be linked to intensified social identity and intensified upper-class access to top universities, as observed in the UK. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share data securely to overcome communication limitations. The algorithm ensures that the optimal solution can be accurately reached, despite the presence of malicious nodes attempting to disrupt the process. Moreover, our approach detects and excludes the impact of adverse behavior from the remaining good nodes. The algorithm's performance is analyzed in terms of convergence rate and reliability, as well as how it handles node failures. Interestingly, the algorithm can distinguish between good and bad nodes without prior knowledge of the system, which is an important feature. The detection capability of the algorithm is showcased through an experiment conducted on a cooperative last-mile solution for 5G cellular networks. The results demonstrate the ability of the algorithm to identify and exclude the impact of adverse behavior from good nodes, achieving optimal performance as a result. The algorithm's performance is also compared to other renowned distributed optimization algorithms in the presence of good nodes only, as well as with the influence of bad nodes removed. The technical advancements discussed in this paper can be applied to a broad range of optimization problems in the context of multi-agent systems. The associated code for the algorithm proposed in this paper is openly accessible on an online repository noted in the paper's supplementary materials. The code is written in Python and utilizes the PyTOCSIM library for simulation purposes. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain and phasors for mock data sets for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments that sample the sky with multi-polarised bolometric detectors. This framework is built on top of the HEALPIX library for spherical harmonic analysis and enables's4cmb' to efficiently generate realistic data streams that incorporate systematic effects of instrumental nature, before producing simulated raw data streams. As an example, we illustrate the capabilities of a mock instrument designed to resemble the S4 experiment. This instrument is then used to investigate the impact of several key design choices on the systematic effects present in the simulated data. Finally,'s4cmb' is used to investigate the impact of instrumental systematic effects on the estimation of the CMB anisotropies' power spectra with approximate cross-correlation with actual data streams showing a correlation of 0.97 in most cases, highlighting the need for realistic systematic effects modelling included in's4cmb' to be taken into consideration in future simulations and data analysis techniques before they can be applied to actual data sets. This framework is an open-source Python tool that is available on GitHub at https://github.com/raoulwolf/s4cmb with the code to replicate the results presented in this paper included in the repository.
