In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. To facilitate future research, we introduce a new task and provide associated data and guidelines. Our experiments involving linear models, transformer models, and self-supervised pre-training techniques yield notable gains, which shed light on issues such as the effectiveness of pre-training and supervised fine-tuning in this context. The exceptional performance of BART prompts us to delve into a more in-depth comparison with its source code, which we make available for public access. Our findings also suggest enhancements can be achieved by leveraging the pre-trained language model's knowledge and utilizing it for this word ordering task. Consequently, we propose a related new task known as partial tree linearization, conduct associated experiments, and provide data and guidelines for this task. Ultimately, our research presents a comparison with linear models, transformer models, and self-supervised techniques and includes a comparison with BART's source code, which we make available for public access at https://github.com/abhiramag1/word_ordering_bart. The data and guidelines for the new task can be found at https://github.com/abhiramag1/word_ordering_bart/tree/main/data.

The creation and dissemination of deepfakes pose a threat to the spread of misinformation, particularly in areas like politics and celebrity culture. Developing effective methods for detecting deepfakes in real-time is crucial. Current approaches primarily focus on analyzing frequency-based features, but they fall short in utilizing a combination of spatial and frequency information. This study builds upon the success of the PloflierNet network, a real-time deepfake detection model, by enhancing the network's ability to extract complementary spatial and frequency features. The modified network, dubbed PloflierNet-2, incorporates an additional convolutional layer and a Convolutional Neural Mobile Network (CMNN) module to extract distinct spatial and frequency-based features, respectively. By combining these features through a convolutional layer with a summation operation, PloflierNet-2 is capable of capturing more complex and discriminative information. This technique allows the generation of activation maps with clear patterns, facilitating the network's ability to focus on critical features and reject noise. Comparative evaluations against prominent real-time deepfake detection models, conducted on the FaceForeniscs++ and Deepfake Detection Dataset, demonstrate the performance superiority of PloflierNet-2 in terms of accuracy, outperforming the baseline by a significant margin. Notably, PloflierNet-2 achieves a notable 95.5% accuracy on the FF++ dataset without the use of pre-trained weights. The enhanced model, PloflierNet-2, exhibits enhanced performance, efficiency, and interpretability when compared to the network, with a parameter count reduction of 10 million while maintaining a comparable inference speed. The source code for the proposed method has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository. 

Keywords: Deepfake detection, real-time detection, convolutional neural networks, spatial and frequency information combination.

This research examines the impact of degree correlations in probabilistic low-density parity-check (LDPc) codes on the binary erasure channel. By analyzing and solving a simplified correlation-based optimization problem, we found that the optimal degree distributions do not necessarily occur at the minimum of the corresponding rate equation. Instead, they may be influenced by an equilibrium point affected by degree correlations. We tested various practical decoding algorithms and found that even though correlated LDPC codes perform poorly, irregular ensembles with optimal degree distributions can achieve high performance. Furthermore, our results suggest that the density evolution equation can be solved efficiently using a fixed-point iteration method, and this method is effective for large degrees. We also observed that the performance of LDPC codes is significantly degraded by degree correlations, and this degradation becomes more pronounced as the correlation between degrees increases. In addition, we investigated the effect of degree correlations on the distribution of degrees and found that they influence the minimum distance of LDPC codes significantly. Finally, we proposed a new LDPC code construction method that generates codes with optimal minimum distance and high performance. These codes outperform conventional LDPC codes, especially in the high-rate regime, and can be efficiently decoded using the belief propagation algorithm. We also demonstrated the feasibility of this code construction method by an example of a rate-5/6 code with a very large size. Moreover, we developed a general correlation-based density evolution equation and solved it analytically for a specific case, providing an exact solution for a particular type of degree distribution. This led to an innovative LDPC code construction method that yields high-performance codes, and we reported specific code ensembles with exceptional error-correction capabilities. Moreover, we designed a general framework for generating a variety of LDPC code ensembles with distinct degree distributions and correlations, and this framework is adaptable to various channel models. Finally, we presented an innovative approach to enhancing the performance of LDPC codes, and we claimed that this approach has the potential to create exceptionally high-performance codes, but further research is needed to fully explore its capabilities.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the proposed attack's success depends on the number of system users and suggests that adding random polarization rotation may hinder the attack's effectiveness. Finally, our research indicates that the required complexity of quantum hacking attacks is vastly inferior to that of optimally efficient attacks, implying that the latter may be practically achievable with minimal effort. As such, we contend that multi-user phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states, particularly those employing random polarization rotation, are highly susceptible to hacking and should be treated with a critical and cautious approach.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate the efficacy of these methods, showing significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, with scaling techniques producing particular gains from decreased energy usage. Furthermore, we observe that, under certain conditions, our proposed methods yield near-optimal results. By exploring these strategies and related research areas, we lay the groundwork for developing more sophisticated solutions and addressing key challenges in Future MNs. This work is part of an ongoing research project, with potential applications extending beyond mobile networks to other edge computing environments, such as industrial networks, and presenting opportunities for interdisciplinary research in the field of edge computing and networking. As this is a developing area, there are several open questions that require further investigation. To facilitate collaboration, we outline specific research problems and potential solutions, with areas of interest including performance modeling, security, and collaborative data processing in Future MNs. By exploring these challenges and opportunities, we aim to contribute to the advancement of Future MNs and invite the research community to join this project through joint contributions and collaborative discussion.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Moreover, it also addresses an additional problem he had considered unanswerable, while also introducing a key theorem that facilitates the topological characterization of spaces with angle functions resembling the structure of Euclidean spaces. This line of inquiry belongs to the broader field of hyperoperative topology, which explores the topological properties of spaces defined through the concept of betweenness and angle functions. These spaces, often described as metric without metrics, present a distinct framework that diverges from the traditional understanding of metric spaces. This article represents the first comprehensive exploration of its kind, offering a detailed review of the underlying concept of betweenness and providing several examples of spaces with angle functions, while also establishing the foundational theoretical framework for the associated topological characteristics. It also addresses specific problems concerning the embeddability of these spaces within Euclidean structures. In doing so, it introduces novel terminology and techniques, along with geometric interpretations, to present a clear and approachable examination of these complex topological spaces. In particular, this article introduces a new concept of geometric homogeneity for a given dimension, alongside an investigation into the geometric homogeneity of specific spaces and the conditions under which it applies. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Furthermore, we explore connections to Hilbert's 12th problem and the Brauer-Manin reciprocity for homogeneous spaces defined by actions of groups on homogeneous spaces. Lastly, we examine the set of fields $K$ for which there exists an order $\mathcal{O}$ such that the only non-trivial relation among the successive minima is $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1\lambda_2^{-1}$, and generalize this finding to ideals in number fields and curves. We also investigate the diophantine properties of systems of equations defined by these minima relations and present several results on the solubility of systems of equations of this type over rings of integers and power residues, inspired by earlier work of several mathematicians. Additionally, we establish the property of being in $\mathcal{S}$ being decidable for fields $K$ of degree $2$ or $3$ and provide a computational verification for various instances of degree $4$. Lastly, we outline an approach to extending these results to higher degree fields $K$ of degree up to $7$.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of offline schemes, as well as the vast reach of modern digital platforms, the true extent of these scams is often unknown. Our investigation focuses on the cryptocurrency-based pyramid scheme, Diamond, which exploited the Ethereum network to deceive investors and recruit field representatives from 2013 to 2018. With the help of Ethereum's transparent and publicly accessible data, we analyzed Diamond's activities and uncovered its worldwide reach, as well as the intricate network of participants and the distribution of funds within the scheme. Our research reveals the geographical hotspots and key players involved in Diamond, as well as the frequency and amount of cryptocurrency being invested in the scheme over time. By presenting various visual representations of Diamond's network, recruitment patterns, and payment structures, our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of a modern cryptocurrency-based pyramid scheme and its operations. Our research used the Ethereum network, but it could also serve as a framework for examining other cryptocurrency-based pyramid schemes and multi-level marketing scams. With the increasing difficulty of detecting hidden networks through transaction analysis, our research introduces new approaches for identifying and exploring complex pyramidal structures. Our study is now available as an interactive visualization at [1]. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates within the Galactic bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. By calculating the total extinction in each candidate's field and assuming a uniform range of reddening within the bulge, we were able to correct the diagrams and derive parallaxes for likely members of each cluster, classifying them as intermediate or low-mass objects in the process. Among the 19 candidates, 13 were validated through the detection of RR Lyrae stars and double main sequence turnoff features, while the remaining six candidates required further observation to determine their status. We present updated RR Lyrae specific period-luminosity-metallicity relations for the bulge and a new formula estimating the RR0 Abundance from period measurements. Four of the validated candidates showed metal contents similar to average bulge values, while three had higher metal contents and multi-turnoff patterns, suggesting a younger population in the inner bulge. Two candidates, VVV DR1 108 and VVV DR1 111, exhibited low reddening levels, indicating these clusters reside outside the bulge and could be part of the stellar halo. We estimate the ranges of reddening and extinction in each candidate's field, suggesting that extinction in the Galactic bulge can exceed 3 magnitudes in some areas. This research highlights the significance of the VVV survey in identifying new globular clusters and sheds light on the complex structure of the Galactic bulge. It also underscores the need for additional observations to determine the status of the six remaining candidates and confirm the findings presented here. Ultimately, a more comprehensive catalog of globular clusters in the Galactic bulge will require the analysis of more candidates and additional data from upcoming surveys. In this work, we examine the relationship between approximate holographic tensor networks and quantum error-correcting codes. We demonstrate that any approximate holographic tensor network can serve as a quantum error-correcting code, with properties including the ability to perform erasure correction and certain forms of protection against depolarizing noise. We also show that such codes maintain a specific form of quantum channel simulation, which amounts to a kind of fault-tolerant quantum computation. Notably, we find that roughly half of all quantum error-correcting codes exhibit properties of holographic tensor networks, suggesting a fundamental connection between approximate holographic tensor networks and quantum error-correcting codes. This relationship could potentially inform the design of new codes inspired by tensor networks. We illustrate this concept with a specific example of a pentagon code, which can be described as both a holographic tensor network and a approximate Majorana beam splitting network. This framework provides a new perspective on the study of quantum error-correcting codes, positioning them within the broader context of tensor network research. As such, it may facilitate the discovery of new codes drawing from other areas of study, such as those related to the Majorana beam splitting network collection. Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of Graph Neural Networks for predicting future event sequences
in processes. Our findings demonstrate that compared to traditional RNNs,
Graph Neural Networks exhibit enhanced performance. Furthermore, among the GNN
variants tested, the multi-layer permutation-invariant model yielded the best
results, outperforming both fixed-hidden-size GNNs and the traditional RNN. We
also present an insightful analysis of predicted trajectories and examine the
impact of process characteristics, such as linearity and temporal dynamics, on GNN
performance. All experimental settings, models, and data, are openly available
at the provided repository. As processes continually evolve over time, our
research proposes methods for enhancing GNN predictions by integrating new data
and adjusting weights based on temporal dynamics and process characteristics. We
also introduce an adjustable time-window parameter to capture recent and more
distant predictions' influence, resulting in more accurate predictions in complex
processes. The proposed techniques demonstrate potential, and we suggest future
directions for improving GNN predictions in processes. Despite the promising
outcomes, there are several issues that require attention, not least the lack
of transparency and robustness in GNNs, especially when predicting critical
events. Consequently, we emphasize the necessity for further research into
these topics and the availability of publicly accessible datasets containing
critical event predictions. In conclusion, our research contributes novel,

Turkey is prone to seismic activities and lies in a high-risk earthquake region. Possible future earthquakes pose a significant threat not only to the population but also to the country's infrastructure and the national economy. Given the likelihood of an impending earthquake, it is essential to develop effective strategies for crisis management and public relations. These sectors can leverage social media platforms to disseminate critical information, address public concerns, and promote relief efforts. In this research, we examine the current social media presence of government institutions, companies, and emergency services in Turkey, along with their capacity to utilize these platforms for crisis communication. A network analysis of Twitter followers and engagement metrics with these entities provides valuable insights into their social media performance. Furthermore, we investigate the content being shared among these actors' Twitter accounts to assess their capacity for providing informative and helpful information during an earthquake crisis. These findings offer practical recommendations for enhancing social media-based crisis communication and facilitating collaboration among these stakeholders. Ultimately, this research offers a framework for monitoring and evaluating the effectiveness of social media-based crisis communication and could be applied to other crisis situations in other regions.

White-light stellar flares offer valuable insights into planetary host stars, particularly useful information to assess exoplanetary biosignatures, even if they're rare. However, the necessary ultraviolet observations are often missing from existing datasets. By analyzing data from the Kepler mission, we identified 82 solar-like stars with detected flares, including 24 planetary hosts. We applied a new method to estimate the UV energy release during their white-light flares and radio counterparts, utilizing their spectral energy distributions and considering the temperature and radius changes. The results show a wide range of energy distributions, from 5.5 to 108 times the solar value, with no significant differences found between small and large flares in these distributions. The estimated radii during the most energetic stages of the flares exceeded twice the radius of the host stars. One host star, K2-25, showed unusually high UV energy release during its flares, indicating superflares that could pose a significant threat to potential exoplanetary biosignatures. By comparing our UV estimates with previous ones and those derived from Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams, we found the latter to be the most reliable method to assess the potential impact of stellar flares on exoplanetary atmospheres. Our study provides a larger dataset of UV energy releases from stellar flares, with implications for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the stability of stellar habitable zones. Moreover, it highlights the significance of using space-based spectroscopic ultraviolet observations to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of the interactions between host stars and their exoplanets.

The connection between gene regulatory networks and the second law of thermodynamics is explored through a dynamic model that highlights the interplay between activation and repression mechanisms within a network of Boolean functions. We focus on analyzing the thermodynamic properties of network dynamics, taking into consideration the costs associated with gene expression and repression. It is demonstrated that, in order to avoid uncontrolled growth, the network must operate in a state of homeostasis, with an average expression cost equal to an average repression cost. Furthermore, it is shown that in networks with an adequate number of nodes and appropriate connectivity, there are multiple stable states, and that these states can only be reached through transient dynamics. The reason for this transient behavior lies in the network's ability to respond to external signals through bidirectional information flow. The implications of these findings are considered in the context of cancer biology. 

In this work, the benefits of network complexity are reevaluated by comparing the simplicity of repressilac2 with the actual biological networks, such as the E. coli transcription network, which involves around 2000 genes. Additionally, several of the network's properties have been replicated in a larger-scale version, with implications for our understanding of cancer development and treatment. The research was conducted using the publicly available repressilac2 platform, and the source code for the projects described is freely available upon request.

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems. Utilizing a real-space approach, our method bypasses the use of creation and annihilation operators in favor of direct, straightforward calculations that directly utilize the underlying single-particle energies and quasiparticle gaps obtained from HFB theory. Consequently, this approach renders our formulation extremely versatile and efficient for computing various physical properties, including two-body matrix elements, across the entire nuclear chart without requiring substantial computational resources. As an illustration, we employ our compact formulae to calculate positive and negative parity low-lying states in $^{192}$Pt. Additionally, we investigate the impact of assuming axial symmetry within our calculations, comparing rotating HFB configurations to true rotational states obtained via HFB+RPA+BCS treatments. Our findings highlight the importance of considering non-axial shapes in potential energy minima when analyzing collective properties under axial symmetry constraints. Moreover, our results show that substantial overestimation of excitation energies can result from calculations that assume axial symmetry, leading to the emergence of collective states at incorrect energies. Nonetheless, the overall collective behavior, characterized by collective inertness and shape-stabilized states, remains largely intact when axial symmetry is imposed. Our research paves the way for future extensions of this work to more complex nuclear systems, such as multi-rotational states and studies of high-spin states, particularly given the recent advancements in computational power and numerical linear and algebraic solvers. As an aside, our compact formulae can be applied to any wave function configuration, making them immediately applicable to post-processing calculations following more sophisticated many-body treatments that employ HFB parent states, such as the Pairing Collective Model (PCM) or the Pairing Deformed Quantum Phase Transition (PDQPT). With such frameworks often exhibiting complex phase diagrams and potential critical points, such as first-order phase transitions or quantum critical points, our derived expressions enable efficient computation of collective states, potential critical points, and phase transition lines across the entire nuclear chart with minimal computational expense. As an example, we demonstrate this capability for PCM and its quantum critical point within the $^{150}$Nd mass region. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-critical domains but have been found vulnerable to manipulations such as rotation and flipping. To address this limitation, our research expands the scope to three-dimensional transformations, classifying them into zooming, bending, and twisting. We develop a testing framework that generates diverse transformation scenarios and applies them to models through a wrapper, ensuring input validity. By conducting extensive experiments on popular point cloud models, we observe a significant increase in error rates across various datasets, demonstrating the critical need for robustness enhancements in point cloud processing. Alongside our findings, we highlight strategies for mitigating these vulnerabilities through data augmentation, yet these measures prove insufficient. Consequently, we advocate for the incorporation of security considerations into model evaluation and propose refining the testing framework to assess robustness through adversarial attacks. Ultimately, our research paves the way for the exploration of secure and trustworthy point cloud models. The code is available at: https://github.com/zheng0620/robustness-testing-point-cloud. The paper has been accepted for presentation at ICASSP 2023.

We're examining a wireless radar network that utilizes ISM bandwidth for data transmission, with nodes employing Clear Channel Assessment (CCA) to detect availability before transmitting and adapting their transmission probability accordingly. However, CCA's effectiveness is compromised when the network suffers from real-time delays, a common issue in high-frequency applications. In this study, we analyze the expected CCA outcomes under Rayleigh fading conditions and derive an energy efficiency optimization problem for radar networks affected by delay. Our analysis yields an approximate solution through a weighted sum approach, with results indicating that optimal performance is achieved when transmission probabilities are set in proportion to the square of the fading coefficients, with energy efficiency benefiting from tighter frequency reuse. A fully distributed algorithm is also proposed to achieve optimal performance through local optimization, with simulation data verifying its efficacy. Notably, our findings demonstrate that ad-hoc CCA-based transmission schemes can achieve near-optimal performance, with some cases even surpassing the optimal efficiency by up to 10%. As such, these schemes are viable alternatives for radar networks operating with ISM bandwidth. As for the impact of fading distributions and CCA delays on network performance, a case study of the K-factor in Rayleigh fading conditions provides valuable insights, with further research into the effects of CCA in other fading conditions yet to be explored. As such, this study offers a fundamental framework for understanding the effects of CCA in radar networks, with room for more in-depth analysis in other fading conditions. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework to provide a more comprehensive time context.
Our proposed framework exhibits superior performance when compared to existing methods
in predicting event and temporal knowledge graph connections, as supported by our
experiments and results. All code and data resources are available for replication
and further development at our repository link.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to identify complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, and resonance mechanisms. Furthermore, studies indicate that the resonance's primary component originates from a stable RPA pole located at approximately 18.5 MeV, supported by data from electron scattering and relativistic models. Prior to this research, the Jost function method had only been utilized to investigate RPA poles up to $^{16}$O; the team's work represents a significant milestone in this field. Additionally, the development of a robust algorithm enabled the location of poles with very small imaginary parts, a challenge that had been a major obstacle in this type of research. As a result of this breakthrough, new insights have been gained into the complex energy plane dynamics of excited states and a new approach has been established for solving complex RPA equations, opening up new avenues for the investigation of bound states, quasi-bound states, resonances, and threshold phenomena. As an example, the study of $^{16}$O's ground state and low-lying states, including alpha particle configurations, was conducted with this method and the results were consistent with established knowledge. As research in this field continues to evolve, the ability to solve complex RPA equations will provide opportunities to gain a deeper understanding of excited states and potentially uncover new physics within atomic nuclei. As a complementary approach, the study of complex RPA eigenenergies can be combined with other many-body theories such as large-scale configuration interaction calculations, heavy-ion collision research, and electron scattering data analysis. As a result, new research directions have been explored, including the investigation of complex RPA poles in heavy nuclei, the study of rotating nuclei, and the extension of this approach to relativistic RPA models. As an example, the investigation of $^{16}$O's rotating nuclei was conducted with this method and the results were consistent with established knowledge. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often exhibit dynamic characteristics that affect clustering methods, yet traditional techniques overlook this aspect. In this work, we present a novel approach that leverages dynamical properties to create meaningful clusters, drawing from the concept of conditional independence in probabilistic models. This method is both scalable and appealing due to its intuitive representation of cluster structure. To evaluate its effectiveness, we present a range of benchmarks featuring synthetic and real-world data. Our results demonstrate that our approach not only rivals the performance of competing methods but also offers a more succinct and visually appealing solution, thereby facilitating cluster exploration. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The ability of SparseGAN to generate compact sentence representations also facilitates applications such as inference acceleration and improved sentence encoding. We observe that the representations produced by SparseGAN exhibit semantic coherence and can be interpreted through the identification of key word embeddings in the selected code. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of the dispersal of microorganisms, the model is pitted against various observational scenarios using real-data examples from the Kepler survey, only to find that even in the best-case scenarios, the necessary data falls short of being sufficient to test the hypothesis of interstellar panspermia. Nevertheless, as surveys and the detection of exoplanets become increasingly more refined, there is hope that one day we may be able to verify the possibility of life dispersing between star systems. Research on species' habitat selection, a key component of wildlife management,  often employs resource selection functions (RSFs) to quantify and analyze habitat  preference. However, implementing and validating RSFs can be complicated,  especially when using spatially explicit models with autocorrelated residuals.  We present an integrated approach using Bayesian methods to model autocorrelated  residuals, incorporate environmental covariates, and estimate resource selection  probabilities. This approach leverages prior expertise and relevant ecological  literature to inform the model, simultaneously addressing residual autocorrelation,  unobserved covariates, and model coefficients. To demonstrate this approach,  we applied it to study the habitat preferences of a threatened species, the northern  Aplomado falcon, using location data and environmental covariates in the Sonoran  Desert, Arizona, USA. Our analysis utilized location data from 2015 to 2019, with a total  of 4393 unique location records from 11 individual birds. We fit three Bayesian  mixed-effects models to estimate resource selection probabilities and evaluated the  approach through model selection, with a focus on habitat categories and spatial  autocorrelation. We found that the Bayesian approach performed better than the  conventional likelihood-based model, with support from the Akaike information criterion.  The best-performing Bayesian model identified several habitat categories that the  falcons selected or avoided, as well as the effects of distance on resource selection,  with a notable avoidance of areas within 1000 meters of other falcons. Our findings  highlight the importance of incorporating spatial autocorrelation in resource selection  analyses and suggest that the threatened Aplomado falcon may adjust its habitat use in  response to other individuals, with implications for conservation and management.  This study provides an example of an integrated approach to modeling resource  selection that can be applied to other research questions and species, and is  particularly relevant for research involving radio-marked individuals. In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm for this problem has been previously developed under more general conditions. However, whether a constant-factor approximation algorithm exists for the more restricted case of undirected graphs has remained an open question. Here, we address this question by providing an O(log k)-approximation algorithm for Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths within undirected graphs, thus demonstrating improved approximation performance compared to existing k-approximation algorithms while addressing the specific case of undirected graphs. Furthermore, our analysis yields an O(log k)-approximation algorithm for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem in undirected multigraphs. Our approach leverages an An-Yen rounding scheme, combined with an examination of the large-minimum-degree subgraphs in a limited extent, to achieve these results. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between approximability and the underlying structure of graph types.

The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding the spread of information, disease, and other processes on networks. It describes the phenomenon where a random activation on a network becomes concentrated in a small number of nodes after repeated applications. Researchers studied a simple local update rule on a model network derived from the Cayley tree, demonstrating that nodal activity enhances the localization of dynamical processes, while disorder has a contrasting effect that hinders localization. However, when the network is highly connected, the effects of nodal activity and disorder are outweighed by another mechanism that promotes localization, originating from the competition between nearest-neighbor hoppings. This competition creates an effective long-range hopping effect that accelerates the spread of activation on the network, leading to further localization. An analytical approach to quantify the activation distribution revealed that the degree of localization is influenced by the activation of specific nodes, while mean-field approximations were validated through comparisons with exact results on the Cayley tree structure. Furthermore, the promotion of localization through the competition of hoppings was shown to occur not just on the Cayley tree but also on other model networks, indicating a general phenomenon. Additionally, simulations on a small-world network demonstrated that the competition of hoppings can drive activation localization more effectively than on the model networks. The activation distribution was found to exhibit power-law behavior, with the index depending on the network's connectivity parameters. The results provide insights into the localization of dynamical processes on networks and may have implications for understanding the spread of information, disease, and other processes. The model and associated methods developed in this study can also be applied to investigate other problems involving local update rules and network structure. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports is complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball, based solely on the location of all players involved. However, these earlier approaches overlooked crucial aspects such as the speed at which players are moving and the time left in the game. To address these limitations, we propose the use of a visual-spatial representation called the 2D spatial speed timeline graph, which takes into account the x-y coordinates of player positions, their corresponding speed values and time intervals. By incorporating speed and time, we enhance the predictive model's ability to capture more nuanced aspects of game events. To validate our approach, we conducted an experiment using data from 1,023 NBA games. By comparing the proposed method using the 2D spatial speed timeline graph to a baseline approach using a simpler representation, we demonstrated significant improvements in prediction accuracy. Our findings show that the proposed method yields a 21.5% absolute increase in mean absolute error and a 32.5% absolute increase in mean squared error when predicting defensive strategies in the NBA, showcasing the importance of speed and time in this context. Furthermore, we applied this approach to analyze the defensive strategies of NBA teams during the 2018-2019 season, and our results provide valuable insights into the performance of various teams. By considering the spatial, temporal, and dynamic aspects of game events, we offer the sports analytics community a comprehensive framework for assessing defensive strategies in team sports. This approach can be applied to other sports, such as football, where players have the ability to move freely in two-dimensional space, and is particularly suitable for analyzing data from individual game events with associated time intervals. Additionally, we believe that this approach has the potential to contribute to more advanced applications, such as providing real-time defensive strategy recommendations to players during games. To facilitate replication and further exploration of this research, we have made the basketball dataset and the proposed method available online. Through this research, we aim to address the methodological limitations in evaluating defensive strategies in team sports and provide a framework that is applicable to other sports with similar dynamics. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the ongoing discussion in the sports analytics community about the most effective methods for assessing the performance of teams in team sports. Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwritten text, and their connections. This approach can operate with limited training data and is versatile in handling different forms, whether old or new. What sets it apart is the ability to execute field-label connections without additional training. Our method has been put into practice and yielded effective results when tested with a range of forms, including old and new images containing deteriorated and clean data, respectively. This has been demonstrated through experiments conducted with the ICDAR Robust Reading Challenge and WIComp Vision Challenge datasets. Our research has shown significant improvements over existing methods, and the code is available for public access at https://github.com/ananth-hub/ann-wassstein. This work has been presented at the 14th International Conference on Document Analysis and Recognition, Thessaloniki, Greece. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel model that uses a compact set of latent factors to influence systems with distinct patterns. By combining RSSMs and factor models, HiP-RSSMs provide a unified framework for multiple interconnected dynamical systems, with a compact representation that significantly reduces the need for data compared to traditional approaches. Through thorough experimentation and comparative analysis on various scientific and engineering time series tasks, HiP-RSSMs have demonstrated superior performance, with code and experiments available at the link provided.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. The principles of asymptotic freeness and conditional freeness form the basis for demonstrating the convergence of a sequence of unitarily invariant random matrices with a specific distribution, and for establishing the convergence of the largest eigenvalue and the corresponding eigenvector for a specific class of unitarily invariant random matrices meeting certain conditions. Furthermore, this leads to secondary findings such as the convergence of the largest conditional eigenvalue and the corresponding conditional eigenvector for a specific class of matrices meeting certain conditions. Lastly, this results in the convergence of the largest eigenvalue and the corresponding eigenvector for a sequence of independent but not necessarily invariant random matrices under specific conditions. Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to assess polarization in social networks through structural analysis, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the distribution of the measurement itself conformed more closely to a standard bell curve, thereby enhancing the methods' reliability and consistency. Our research encompasses a comprehensive evaluation of the methods, including both unnormalized and normalized versions, to facilitate informed method selection for various analytical goals. Additionally, we present a user-friendly online tool that allows users to determine the best measurement method based on their specific research requirements. This tool is accessible at the website listed in the text.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. We demonstrate the success of this representation by investigating the formation of synchronized states and stability in the presence of internal node dynamics. Furthermore, we investigate a scenario where interlayer connections are added or removed, and analyze the impact on synchronization by utilizing these new methods, in addition to numerical simulations and strategic node degree adjustments. The proposed method can be an effective tool for analyzing and understanding the intricate dynamics of multilayer networks.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempting to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator leads to the theory of gravity. The parametrization of the Nijenhuis operator results in the theory of Nijenhuis tensors. The parametrization of the Virasoro operator yields minimal gravity in a manifold with one complex dimension. Attempting the same in two complex dimensions leads to consideration of the full Weyl differential operator rather than the Virasoro operator. This change causes a failure of the parametrization to be minimal, leading to an infinite number of additional gauge parameters in minimal gravity in this higher dimension. This issue first arises in String theory's consideration of this scenario. The failure of the parametrization to be minimal may provide a solution to the cosmological constant problem in this dimension. The failure to consider a torus in the energy calculation of Yang-Mills theory, albeit with an infinite dimensional gauge group, results in an infinite energy in the vacuum state. This phenomenon does not occur when the gauge group is finite. The cause of the infinite energy is the infinite dimension of the gauge group rather than topological factors such as in gravity. This is concluded through an analysis of the Dirac operator's spectrum in a torus. The investigation of the bulk energy of the Yang-Mills theory on a torus is analogous to the investigation of the Laplace operator's spectrum on the same torus. The latter is well-studied. The Dirac operator's spectrum on a torus is studied in the context of heterotic String theory. The consideration of Yang-Mills theory's bulk energy on a torus is studied in the context of the brane world scenario. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing framework that can be applied to a broad range of programming languages and systems, even those with intricate data structures and concurrent functionality. This framework is capable of generating relevant test cases by analyzing the unreachability problems identified through the application of zBDD-based set operations, in addition to verifying whether the generated test cases indeed pose a threat to the program's dependability. Furthermore, this framework can also pinpoint the exact locations within the program where errors are likely to occur. By integrating this approach with tools from the formal verification community, we can acquire a more comprehensive understanding of the dependability flaws present in the program, allowing for prioritization of test cases to be carried out in an optimal order to ensure maximum effectiveness in revealing close-to-the-bug locations during the testing process. Our proposed approach has been put into practical use through the development of a prototype testing tool, F3T, which is capable of supporting the Racket programming language. Andean, a geometric model checker integrated with F3T, has successfully uncovered close-to-the-bug locations in Racket programs, as validated by comparative analysis with other testing techniques. Andean has also been applied to the evaluation of safety-critical concurrent algorithms, yielding promising results. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, HyperNetworks are responsible for producing task-specific attention weights, mask vectors, and positional encodings in a module-wise manner. By doing so, HyperPrompt enables efficient task-specific feature mapping in language models by creating custom self-attention mechanisms that can effectively map input tokens to semantic vectors associated with each task. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a more modular design compared to previous methods, and our experiments demonstrate its capability to achieve high performance on both few-shot and zero-shot settings for various NLP tasks while employing a significantly reduced additional parameter count. Evaluations across eight text classification, three sentiment analysis, and three paraphrasing tasks back up our claim of HyperPrompt's efficacy. The code is openly accessible on GitHub, and we have published our findings in the form of detailed notebooks on the Hugging Face Transformers hub. Moreover, an in-depth analysis of HyperPrompt's performance, along with comparative results to prominent competitors, is included in the supplementary material accompanying this document.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena. It also paves the way for applying symmetry protection principles to improve the performance of quantum devices operating in this regime. Moreover, this finding suggests the potential for creating a source of two-photon emissions through a simple and controlled method. This could lead to the development of a efficient and reliable device for generating two-photon entangled states, a crucial resource for quantum applications, including quantum simulations and the testing of quantum local realism. This device could potentially be applied to other multi-quanta emissions, such as three-photon emissions, which are essential for quantum engineering and communications. It is also possible that this emission of protected multi-quanta states could be used to develop a new approach to quantum metrology, among other quantum technologies. Finally, this research suggests that protected emission of multi-quanta states could be achieved in other ultrastrongly coupled systems, such as superconducting microresonators connected to a quantum well or Josephson junctions coupled to a quantum well, among others. It is also possible to control the parity symmetry in these systems with an external magnetic field, a capacitance, or a voltage, among other options. It is worth noting that this research is at an early stage, and further investigation is required to fully understand the protected multi-quanta emission phenomenon and its applications. It is also important to note that this research is focused on cavity QED, and it is unclear at this point whether protected multi-quanta emission phenomenon could occur in other systems, such as chemical or molecular systems, or in systems based on SQUIDs, among others. It is also important to note that this research is not without challenges, and one of the main difficulties is achieving the ultrastrong coupling regime in a stable and reliable manner.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the network freely. Our algorithm achieves accurate approximations of the network's size in the presence of an arbitrary number of malicious nodes, provided that the remaining nodes constitute at least a two-thirds majority, in a network characterized by undirected and symmetric connections between nodes. We leverage this estimation capability to develop a subsequent algorithm that can detect the presence of malicious nodes within the same network parameters. Both of these algorithms can be executed in a distributed manner among the network's nodes, with no requirement for a trusted third party. Our approach involves a combination of deterministic and probabilistic techniques to ensure the accuracy of our results. In contrast to previous studies, we are able to handle a higher proportion of malicious nodes than existing literature. For instance, the team proposed an innovative method for approximating network size, achieving a two-thirds majority of genuine nodes as opposed to previous methods' one-half majority. Furthermore, our research introduces novel techniques for verifying the accuracy of network size approximations and identifying malicious nodes. In collaboration with Hendrika Joanne van der Pol, I coauthored an enhanced version of these algorithms, now published as EWMA-Net-SizerV2 and EWMA-Net-MaliciousNodesV2, with improved performance and tolerability of up to three-quarters malicious nodes due to an expanded use of hedge protocols. This advancement enables accurate approximations of network size even in highly compromised environments. As an added feature, the upgraded algorithm includes a modified version of malicious node detection, now capable of handling a majority of genuine nodes as ten percent, as demonstrated in our accompanying research. In this experiment, we explore the effectiveness of these algorithms when executed in an environment with a significant presence of malicious nodes. Our results show that the original algorithm still yields reliable approximations and accurately identifies malicious nodes even when the network contains an arbitrary number of malicious nodes, as long as genuine nodes comprise at least a two-thirds majority. However, in ten-fold simulations, the upgraded algorithm performed no better than the original when the network contains an arbitrary number of malicious nodes. Nevertheless, we do observe the upgraded algorithm's increased tolerance for malicious nodes of ten in both network size approximation and malicious node detection, as opposed to the original algorithm's zero tolerance. This gain in tolerance comes at no additional computational cost, as both algorithms have the same average execution time. Notably

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for simulations involving charged matter or spinng sources, where separating the conformal connection from the Weyl tensor fails due to the loss of simplicity in such cases. Our method substitutes an algebraic Hamiltonian constraint with one that depends on the Weyl tensor, allowing for direct integration of sources within the 2nd order Newman-Penrose equations. This approach is demonstrated by constructing a pair of rotating black hole mergers in a non-equilibrium state, with one hole having a nonzero angular momentum while the other remains stationary. Our method is shown to effectively produce accurate results in such complex scenarios. Furthermore, our method exhibits a significant advantage in computational efficiency, with a substantial reduction in computational time required to produce the same results. This is an important development, given the enormous computational demands of simulating high-energy gravitational waves in the context of General Relativity. Our method is sure to play a crucial role in making such simulations more feasible in the future. This research is an essential step towards developing the capability to accurately model binary black hole and neutron star mergers, especially in the high-spin regime. Our method is already being explored for potential applications in solving similar constraints in other Einstein field theories that incorporate matter configurations. Given its innovative nature, we believe our approach deserves further investigation by the scientific community. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce. In this research, we focus on the antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Ni$_{3}$-Ga antiperovskite layer, now reclassified as NiGa in a study, situated within the Co$_{2}$-Ga$_{2}$ framework, both of which possess the B2 cubic crystal structure. The measurements of anomalous Nernst coefficient $\alpha_a$ and anomalous Hall coefficient RHAE are determined as the electron temperature increases, accompanied by measurements of electrical transport and heat diffusion in the NiGa material. By comparing with theoretical models, we infer that the anomalous Nernst effect in NiGa is dominated by the scattering of electrons by the magnetic atoms and the antiferromagnetic order, as well as the availability of holes. The quantitative analysis of $\alpha_a$/$RHAE versus J-c curves allows for direct correlation between the anomalous Nernst and anomalous Hall effects, suggesting that the latter could be manipulated through the control of electron heat transport. Notably, the ratio of $\alpha_a$/$RHAE$ is independent of the electron temperature and electron mobility, implying that the extrinsic contribution governs the anomalous Nernst effect in NiGa. The discovery of the $α_a$/$RHAE versus J-c curves, along with the determination of the ratio of $\alpha_a$/$RHAE$, provides a crucial foundation for further research into the interrelation between the anomalous Nernst and anomalous Hall effects in NiGa and similar materials. Moreover, this study paves the way for a comprehensive investigation of the thermal and electronic transport phenomena in antiferromagnetic materials, enabling precise control of these effects and, ultimately, the development of advanced spin calorimetry techniques. Ultimately, this research may facilitate the discovery of novel antiferromagnetic materials with anomalous Nernst and anomalous Hall effects of significant magnitude, thus unlocking their vast potential for technological applications.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Source code and further details are available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/Knowledge-Transfer-Ranking.

This lecture will provide an elementary overview of both transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics, in addition to key beam loss phenomena in circular accelerators, catering to attendees with minimal to no prior understanding of this topic. We aim to convey the significance and practical applications of this knowledge through discussions of available diagnostic tools and examples from the particle physics community. Furthermore, we will highlight the importance of this subject in relation to the design and operation of future colliders and experiments, specifically the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) and future lepton colliders like ILC and CLIC, which will require precise management of beam loss to ensure the safety and effectiveness of these facilities. Given the technical nature of the topic, the content will be presented in an accessible manner, with key concepts illustrated through basic diagrams to facilitate understanding. We anticipate around 30 minutes of presentation time, followed by a 30-minute Q&A session, to clarify any further points of interest. 

Presentation Outline:

1. Introduction to Beam Dynamics and Loss Phenomena (10 minutes)
2. Transverse Beam Dynamics (20 minutes)
3. Longitudinal Beam Dynamics (20 minutes)
4. Key Loss Phenomena and Diagnostic Tools (20 minutes)
5. Conclusion and Future Directions (10 minutes)

We intend to maintain an interactive session with the audience through open-ended questions to gauge their understanding and address any misconceptions. In preparation, we invite participants to come equipped with their own definitions and explanations of key beam dynamics terminology. 

In addition to the primary objective, we also seek to explore the possibility of creating a comprehensive, easily accessible online reference in relation to this topic, given the limited written material currently available. Any suggestions or contributions towards this goal are welcome. 

We look forward to engaging with the audience and sharing our knowledge on this fascinating subject of beam dynamics and loss phenomena.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, forcing researchers to settle for limited statistics due to time-consuming and experimental-limited access. Machine learning tools, particularly automated scripts and advanced methods like active learning, can efficiently navigate this challenge by targeting and re-imaging materials to yield more useful data. A study presents an active learning framework incorporating a neural network expert and a sampling committee to prioritize and refine the characterization of materials. The framework leverages a neural network's expertise to evaluate the material's properties and rank sampling candidates, with support from a diverse set of simple Bayesian sampling suggestions to prevent bias. An analysis of an idealized scenario using a neural network expert and multiple diverse sampling rules in an scenario of increasing complexity demonstrates the method's effectiveness. Furthermore, the proposal of an idealized scenario and an associated work flow demonstrate how this approach can be applied to real-world problems. A concrete example using a neural network and experimental NMR data for a superconductor also illustrates the method's performance, with the discovery of a critical material property through only 10 characterizations out of a possible 50. A complementary software code is available at an indicated repository.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio. Additionally, a regime is identified where GAMs become unstable in the core region, facilitated by the presence of a shear Alfven wave drive. A dimensionless parameter, $\Delta_{\mathrm{A}}$, is defined to characterize the anisotropy effect, which could be relevant in contexts like ion cyclotron resonance heating. Further, the influence of a magnetic field on the direction of geodesic curvature and its impact on the mode frequency is explored, which could be significant in smaller devices like the JT-60U but less important in larger machines like JET and J-TEXT. The proposed analysis can be applied to various devices, including tokamaks, stellarators, and spherical tori. The findings from linear research demonstrate the necessity for nonlinear investigations into the anomalous GAM frequency shifts observed across different machines. The developed linear theory provides a foundation for further investigation into the potential influence of ion distribution anisotropy on GAM turbulence and associated heat transport. The proposed study can be expanded to consider the interplay between GAMs and other geodesic modes, as well as the impact of fast ions on ion distribution anisotropy. The framework presented can be combined with other models, such as the total turbulence model, to better comprehend the complex interplay between GAMs and balanced turbulence in fusion devices. The research outlined paves the way for exploring the potential of GAMs as an diagnostic tool, providing insights into ion thermal diffusion and turbulence and potentially influencing the development of advanced plasma confinement modes. The study of geodesic acoustic modes, fueled by the JT-60U experience, may contribute significantly to the advancement of plasma science and fusion research. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. However, the driver Hamiltonian's annealing schedule and strength are critical factors that significantly impact the quantum annealer's performance. In this study, we investigate the impact of adding weak anti-ferromagnetic interactions within a linear spin chain, as well as the effect of a non-integrable perturbation, on the quantum annealer's schedule and driver Hamiltonian's strength. Our findings indicate that quantum annealer's acceptance probability exhibits intricate patterns related to the number of quantum annealing steps, as well as the strength and annealing schedule of the driver Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain regions of the phase diagram exhibit complex structure, including regions of high acceptance probability and discrete phase transitions. Additionally, we observe that the presence of weak anti-ferromagnetic interactions leads to an increase in the quantum annealer's success rate for certain Hamiltonian parameters, resulting in solutions found more quickly than classical annealing. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the laboratory's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the laboratory was on the cusp of a significant breakthrough, with the Near Stars project on the verge of producing results. However, van Rhijn's leadership was marked by a prolonged struggle to publish the findings, which was compounded by his own lack of interest in the research and his distant management style. Additionally, van Rhijn's priorities shifted towards his directorate at Leiden University and his own astronomical research, leaving the laboratory's affairs largely to the staff. In 1945, with the project finally nearing completion, van Rhijn secured the support of the university to publish the results. However, his untimely death in 1960 delayed the publication, which was ultimately secured by his successor. The essay delves into the intricacies of van Rhijn's leadership and his relationship with the staff, particularly his struggles with Adriaan Blaauw, who would go on to become a prominent figure in the field of astronomy. The essay also examines the legacy of van Rhijn, the impact of World War II on the laboratory, and the eventual publication of the Near Stars project, which led to a substantial contribution to the Henry Draper Catalogue. The struggle to publish the research during van Rhijn's tenure had far-reaching consequences, propelling the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory into the forefront of the emerging field of galactic research in the 1950s and 1960s. The essay concludes with an examination of the laboratory's achievements during this period, including the research of Adriaan Blaauw, Jan Oort, and Hendrik van Rhijn's own contributions, which cemented the laboratory's position as a leading centre for the study of the galaxy. The legacy of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory during this period has had a lasting impact on the development of the European Southern Observatory's 2dF/QUIPP project at the AAO and the KAGRA gravitational wave project at the AEO. The essay offers a fresh perspective on a significant period in the history of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory and positions the laboratory's contributions within the broader context of the development of the galaxy research field. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the method enhances convergence rate and stability. A theoretical analysis is provided to demonstrate how the proposed method can be viewed as an application of the proximal operator framework. In addition, the paper derives a dynamic parameter update scheme that accurately accounts for model-parallel delays. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms traditional model-parallel training on convergence rate, stability, and final accuracy in both fully connected and convolutional neural network architectures. Source code is available at https://github.com/hk6204/LCTMP-learn.
