The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. By examining the renormalization group equations from a new perspective, we aim to facilitate the discovery of more efficient solutions to these equations. We focus on solutions derived from perturbative expansions, exploring ways to incorporate higher-order terms that capture the interplay between multiple coupling constants. We also outline the steps to apply our approach to various quantum field theories, including $\phi^4$ theory, anti-ferromagnetic quantum spin models, and the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the O(3) nonlinear sigma model. By leveraging this new understanding, we anticipate gaining more precise control over the renormalization group flow near non-trivial fixed points, as well as developing more accurate numerical methods for solving renormalization group equations that involve multiple solutions to the stationary equations. This new framework is expected to enhance our ability to solve complex quantum field theories, even in the presence of multiple competing length scales. It is also expected to facilitate the discovery of new phases of matter and the phase transitions between them. Finally, we anticipate that this innovative approach will facilitate dialogue between physicists working on the renormalization group and those working on fluid dynamics. It may also facilitate the successful application of this new perspective to other problems of interest. Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options. Unlike existing music search platforms, Pied Piper will offer a seamless, user-friendly interface and seamlessly integrate multiple music databases, encompassing over 40 million tracks, via seamless API integrations. Our prototype will be presented, detailing its design principles and features, as well as the technological stack comprising Flutter for the mobile app and custom HTML for the web interface, with underlying API connections to Spotify, Genius, and Musixmatch. Additionally, we plan to conduct user experience and quality assessments to evaluate Pied Piper's performance and gather valuable feedback. Ultimately, our goal is to establish Pied Piper as a pioneering music search engine, available to the public in its current form at https://piedpipermusic.com or through the mobile app on Google Play Store and Apple App Store.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  In addition, we discovered that infrared dark cloud cores, both protostellar and starless, tend to be denser than their millimeter core counterparts from the TMC-1 H II region, with densities roughly 2 times greater.  We also found that the line width-to-mass ratio in the Dragon infrared dark cloud cores exhibits little variation, with values ranging between 0.16 to 0.33 km/s per century, with no discernible difference between protostellar, starless cores and those connected with outflows.  A comparison of core properties in the Dragon infrared dark cloud to those in the TMC-1 H II region reveals that the former's cores tend to be less massive and less dense.  We attribute these differences to the greater ionizing flux in the TMC-1 H II region, which is likely responsible for the creation and maintenance of the infrared dark cloud within Dragon.  A high-resolution (0.1 pc) analysis of the core population in the Dragon infrared dark cloud in relation to the ionizing flux from the TMC-1 H II region indicates that the conditions necessary for infrared dark cloud formation have been met across the majority of the region, yet only a small subset of these conditions have resulted in the formation of infrared dark clouds such as the Dragon.  We propose the Dragon as the ideal location for studying the evolution of infrared dark clouds in a comprehensive and in-depth manner due to its close proximity to the TMC-1 H II region and the thorough, multi-frequency observational data already available for the region.  Ultimately, we anticipate that the Dragon infrared dark cloud will serve as a prime example for investigating the formation and evolution of massive stars and infrared dark clouds in regions of low ionizing flux. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Despite significant progress made in 2D image classification, there are still several challenges to be addressed in 3D classification, particularly when dealing with sparse and densely packed LiDAR data points. This research focuses on developing a novel deep learning approach, incorporating spatial grouping and a layer that accounts for point density, to enhance the classification performance. A new 3D LiDAR classification network is presented, featuring a unique combination of two key components: a spatial grouping module that integrates contextual information from neighboring points and a point density layer that considers the compactness of point clouds. This innovative model leverages these features to fuse descriptive features obtained from LiDAR signals and encode the density information into a density map, both of which are learned through a dense-to-sparse learning process. As a result, the model is capable of extracting dense and compact features that contain valuable information about the point clouds. To evaluate the performance of this innovative approach, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 10 classes was created from various LiDAR data sets, including forest, urban, and coastal environments. A comparative analysis with three baseline methods revealed that the proposed model achieved exceptional accuracy, surpassing traditional methods by more than 10% and outperforming deep learning alternatives by over 5%. The code for this research is available on an open-source platform. In conclusion, the introduction of a new 3D LiDAR classification network addressing the challenges of LiDAR data density has led to notable advancements in the field, and the resulting model can be an invaluable tool for LiDAR-based environmental monitoring and urban development applications. Future research should focus on expanding the dataset to include more complex settings and diverse categories to further enhance the classification performance. Additionally, incorporating temperature and moisture data with LiDAR signals has the potential to significantly improve classification accuracy in certain environments. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper presents three years of data from the largest neutrino dataset, consisting of 82 UHE neutrinos, in association with UHECRs recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory (PAO). No significant neutrino-UHECR multiplet candidates emerged in this analysis, and this non-detection allows the derivation of upper limits to neutrino-UHECR multiplet densities for various neutrino energies and UHECR energies, providing constraints on hypothetical sources that could explain the neutrino-UHECR correlation. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. We have also found that the stick-slip friction depends on the viscosity of the liquid and the height of Plateau borders, in addition to surface roughness. The findings of this research provide insights into the long-lasting memory effects observed in the flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces. The stick-slip friction mode is a critical component in powering the widespread distribution of fungi through spore dispersal. The research presented here may also contribute to the improvement of robotic grippers capable of handling fragile and complex substances, such as pizza. The stress patterns observed in this research have connections to issues of power-law behavior in stress distributions, particularly in situations of failure and fracture. The study of the stick-slip regime may also contribute to a better understanding of biological systems characterized by surface slippage, such as the movement of cells through tissues and the progression of tumors through the body. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data set. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, is examined in a linear stability analysis. When the inner fluid denser than the outer, a fingering instability develops as the membrane is subjected to a gentle stretch or brief perturbations. Contrasting this, the membrane remains stable to linearized disturbances when the inner fluid is less dense than the outer, even in the presence of significant perturbations. The onset of instability in the denser-fluid case is characterized by a critical Taylor-like number $\Gamma_c$, with corresponding wave numbers $\beta_c$ determined by the membrane's elasticity in relation to the gravitational force, given by $\beta_c \epsilon^{1/2} = \Gamma_c^{-1/2} \sim \Lambda^{-1/2}$. The same analysis reveals that the growth rate of the instability becomes more pronounced as the membrane is stretched further, with $\mathrm{Re}(\gamma) \propto (\Gamma_c - \Gamma)^{1/2}$. This result is further validated through direct numerical simulations of the full nonlinear membrane equations. Notably, the $\Gamma_c^{1/2}$ dependence of the finger wave number observed in this study contradicts earlier findings. Additionally, the effects of an imposed azimuthal flow on the membrane's stability are also considered, with the influence of the flow on stability determined by the Hartmann number $Ha$, with $\beta_c \propto \Lambda^{1/2} (Ha^{-1})^{1/3}$. The associated finger growth rates are found to be more complex, with $\mathrm{Re}(\gamma) \proportional To (\Gamma_c - \Gamma)^{1/3} (Ha^{-1})^{2/3}$. The theoretical results are supported by numerical data, with the membrane's stability diagram mapped in the $Ha$-$\Lambda$ plane. The implications of these findings are considered in the context of Hele-Shaw cell experiments and potential applications involving elastic membranes in rotating fluids. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. However, we've discovered an exception - systems in a state of complete thermodynamic disorder can experience work transfer during free expansion. Our analysis reveals that this apparent paradox is resolved when considering the interplay between thermal fluctuations and the potential for local order. In this case, the second law of thermodynamics remains intact, as the potential for disorder increase compensates the cost of work, thereby constraining its maximum value. Our findings also demonstrate that the proposed microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics can provide a coherent description of the dynamics of systems experiencing volume changes. Our observations of interstellar methyl acetylene, ethynyl benzene, and acetylene made in the direction of $\tau$ Persei, a young solar-type star with significant ethynyl benzene column density, provide new insights into the synthesis of ethynyl aromatic molecules in space. The 1.6 $\mu$m band of methyl acetylene and the 5.8 $\mu$m band of ethynyl benzene were studied using the VLT/MAD instrument at a spectral resolution of 0.8 km/s. Our analysis of these ethynyl-containing molecules within a 1.4 km/s velocity interval and a 0.56 km/s resolution yields column densities of 16$\pm$3 $\times$10$^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$ for methyl acetylene and 5.7$\pm$1.4 $\times$10$^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$ for ethynyl benzene. The ethynyl benzene column density is notably higher than expected, given the small hyperfine structure in the methyl acetylene transition, which might indicate the presence of a hyperangular distribution in ethynyl benzene or a spin angular alignment effect. However, the larger than anticipated methine hydrogen hyperfine structure in the 5.8 $\mu$m band of ethynyl benzene, equivalent to the 1.6 $\mu$m band of methyl acetylene, suggests that a hyperfine structure mask may be applied without alteration, providing insights into the location of ethynyl-containing molecules within the interstellar cloud. The presence of ethynyl benzene across the 18.5 km/s velocity extent of the $\tau$ Persei cloud and its absence in the more compact $\kappa$ Persei cloud suggest a possible molecular outflow or a more complex ethynyl benzene precursor distribution within these clouds. These findings open up new avenues for the study of ethynyl-containing molecules in space. The methodological advancements made in this research can be applied to the analysis of other complex organic molecules in the ISM, and the detection of these molecules in various astrophysical environments. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements in translation quality on the WMT'14 English-German and WMT'15 English-French benchmarks for the baseline system. The code for the look-ahead attention mechanism has been made publicly available.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a translational computing paradigm is necessary, resembling the approach of translational medicine, to bridge the gap between technological progress and effective problem-solving. This perspective paper explores the concept of a translational computing framework that incorporates actionable research methods, addresses issues in peer review processes, and establishes a community agenda. It looks at case studies in numerical linear algebra, parallel and distributed computing, machine learning, and human-centered computing to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach. It also reveals limitations in the current state of the art and suggests future research directions within the field of computational science and engineering. By doing so, it aims to motivate the community to adopt a more translational approach, focusing on developing methods that are readily applicable and can be used to make computational methods more accessible to non-experts. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While numerous researchers have explored Gaussian processes within the context of Euclidean spaces, their potential on undirected graphs has been largely unexplored - despite such graphs being a fundamental structure in many applications and datasets.  In this work, we develop a novel Gaussian process model that applies to undirected graphs and demonstrates a significant advantage over its Euclidean counterpart, particularly in terms of model parsimony and predictive variance.  Furthermore, our approach ensures a seamless integration with existing Gaussian process techniques, enabling the utilization of conjugate exponential family likelihoods.  We employ the "cutoff" technique to restrict the support of the Gaussian process, thereby ensuring its equivalence to a standard Gaussian process on a subgraph.  We showcase our method's efficacy through a collaborative filtering example and a source localization scenario.  Our implementation is publicly accessible as part of the DeepLearning4Communities repository.  Our contribution provides a significant step towards unleashing the potential of Gaussian processes on undirected graphs across multiple domains, including computer networks, social networks, and machine learning communities.  Our approach's scalability is demonstrated with an educational example involving $10,000$ node Gaussian process predictions.  Our code is openly available at the stated repository address. The effective management of urban roads relies heavily on accurate real-time data, which is currently lacking due to inadequate sensing infrastructure and excessive costs. To address this challenge, this research introduces a novel approach called Urban Audio Fingerprinting (UAF) that leverages the sonic signatures of road conditions captured through smartphone audio. By analyzing the acoustic characteristics of different road environments, we demonstrate the ability to develop a probabilistic matching algorithm called Acoustic Vector Labeling (AVL). This algorithm enables the creation of a virtual mapping system using UAF-AVL, which can efficiently locate devices on the road network and provide spatial information about surrounding areas. Our study showcases the capabilities of UAF-AVL through a series of experiments, including device positioning, route detection, and speed estimation, using a dataset collected from 10 participants navigating through 5 different urban road scenarios in Beijing. Our results show strong performance indicators with median positioning errors of 15.8 meters, successful route detection rates of up to 93.6%, and speed estimation accuracy of 26.4 meters per second. To facilitate further research, we release an open-source implementation of UAF-AVL and make the associated dataset available publicly. By highlighting the advantages and limitations of our approach, we also explore potential applications and identify areas for future development. These contributions have the potential to contribute to various urban sensing infrastructure tasks such as traffic management, navigation, and community studies. Moreover, our study introduces a novel audio-based approach that offers a cost-effective and scalable alternative to traditional infrastructure-based sensing methods. This research sets the stage for exploring other research questions in the field of urban audio sensing and could see potential applications in areas like environmental monitoring, healthcare, and education. In conclusion, our groundbreaking UAF-AVL approach paves the way for the adoption of smartphone audio as a reliable and efficient means of urban road network sensing. This could ultimately facilitate the development of data-driven urban management systems that prioritize citizen needs and improve the overall quality of life in urban communities. By doing so, it may also provide new opportunities for citizen involvement in the urban planning process and contribute to the creation of more inclusive and responsive public policies. Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis. Additionally, we compare the performance of these new SGLMs against existing implementations of Runge-Kutta methods and algebraic methods for differential equations defining smooth, periodic solutions. Consequently, this new development enhances the utility of SGLMs for solving periodic problems and suggests that these new methods can provide superior accuracy compared to established techniques. Furthermore, we highlight the challenge of developing an efficient, high-order method for solving problems with rapidly changing solution derivatives within short intervals. To this end, we propose a new method of order four with q=4 and investigate its performance against tailored Runge-Kutta methods in solving problems involving both smooth, periodic solutions and rapidly changing derivative solutions. We also examine the impact of non-uniform grid spacing on the convergence of these new methods. Lastly, we apply these new methods to solve problems arising from the aggregation of sediments, the stock market, and an HIV model. Our numerical results confirm the high accuracy of these new methods, with some examples requiring half the number of function evaluations compared to established Runge-Kutta methods to achieve the same level of precision. We have implemented these new methods in a publicly available MATLAB code. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Despite its widespread use, little research has focused on understanding the complex interactions within these systems, which are often blackboxed. Through a comprehensive analysis of a high-stakes university admission process, involving the scoring of over 1.3 million essays by 114,000 applicants, this study investigates the automated essay scoring system and its human raters. By examining the relationships between rating scores, system predictions, and human ratings, which are partially observed, this study applies statistical methods and causal analysis to reveal several key insights. It is shown that the system's predictions are closely aligned with the human ratings, which raises concerns about the potential for causal effects on applicant outcomes, particularly given the predictive bias identified in previous research. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the system's scores are largely influenced by features such as coherence, grammar, and usage, rather than substance or candidate ability. Additionally, the study reveals that the system's ratings exhibit a high degree of consistency with the human ratings, but also presents evidence suggesting there may be a difference in causality. Given these findings, the study raises important policy and research questions, suggesting that a more transparent and auditable system is necessary to ensure trustworthiness, particularly when such systems are used in high-stakes applications. Alongside these findings, this study also highlights the challenges associated with auditing complex blackboxed systems, which is an issue that extends beyond the context of automated essay scoring. By examining this particular system, this study aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion about the development and deployment of trustworthy artificial intelligence systems. However, training models to accurately detect cell nuclei is complicated due to issues such as limited access to high-quality training data and the significant variations that can occur within images, particularly when using whole-slide scans. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research into the underlying mechanisms driving NLRP3 activation and the associated cell death may offer valuable insights for developing treatments, particularly since inflammasome activation is linked to various other diseases as well. Through a combined approach of computational modeling and experimental validation, our study aims to examine NLRP3 activation's temporal dynamics and the effects of SARS-CoV-2 mutations on this process. By utilizing multi-scale ODE models in a computational pipeline along with machine learning algorithms and in vitro experiment data, we analyze the inflammasome's temporal behavior and identify the most influential processes. Furthermore, we investigate how mutations in the RASD1 and NLRP3 interaction affect the inflammasome's assembly and activation. It was found that certain mutations in RASD1, in particular, accelerate the inflammasome's assembly rate by two orders of magnitude, and that these effects are accurately captured by the computational models. Since RASD1 is a host protein targeted by various viruses and bacteria that trigger the NLRP3 inflammasome, our research may also provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving their infections. Moreover, our study's computational approach can be applied to other host-pathogen interactions as well. By examining the inflammasome's assembly and disassembly rates, as well as the associated protein levels, our research can help identify key processes in the computational models and facilitate the exploration of treatment strategies in silico. In the case of SARS-CoV-2, our study suggests that targeting the virus's entry into host cells or inhibiting the RASD1-NLRP3 interaction might prevent pyroptotic cell death. In conclusion, our research provides a computational framework for analyzing the NLRP3 inflammasome's temporal behavior and explores potential treatment strategies for pyroptosis in the host cell. This approach can be applied to other host-pathogen interactions involving the NLRP3 inflammasome as well. Although this study focuses on SARS-CoV-2, our findings are relevant to other betaherpes viruses that trigger the NLRP3 inflammasome and cause similar host cell responses. External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated variations in the environment. This concept is mathematically formalized as the problem of learning in the presence of an "external controllability gap." A key insight reveals that comparing the complexity of this issue to the difficulty of solving the original reinforcement learning problem provides crucial insights into potential solutions. Based on this understanding, we propose an algorithm that addresses the external controllability gap by dividing the problem into manageable components and iteratively refining them. Although the algorithm's performance may not achieve optimal results, it has a guaranteed level of efficiency. Moreover, we establish an infinite-horizon convergence theorem for this algorithm. The proposed method is demonstrated through a hypothetical market scenario, and the results are verified through a simulation based on real-world data. The algorithm's implementation leverages policy optimization tools, and the code is openly accessible. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. In addition to this core refinement type system, HELMHOLTZ utilizes additional features from the Mini-Michelson core calculus with BSL (Basic Set Theory with Lenses) refinements, that incorporate compound datatypes, lists, and lenses, allowing for the successful verification of more intricate Michelson programs, including multi-signature contracts, unit contracts with display strings, and contract transactions with pairs of units and lists. The successful refinement of these complex Michelson programs serves as an indication of the capabilities of the HELMHOLTZ project. The definitions, core Mini-Michelson calculus, BSL with lenses, the static verification approach, and several examples are made accessible through the Zelcore refinement type library available at this link https://zelcore.github.io/HELMLHOLTZ-Zelcore/, allowing users to define and verify their own Michelson programs with a more user-friendly and graphical interface. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Elastography typically requires ultrasound imaging followed by mechanical manipulation and subsequent elastography techniques. To achieve this, precise targeting of specific tissues is crucial, however current methods lack the necessary accuracy. The Synthetic Aperture (SA) technique provides high resolution images, albeit at the cost of targeting precision due to its limited field of view. The Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) technique offers higher resolution images while maintaining targeting precision, however it is computationally intensive and demands a significant amount of data. A novel VSSA compiler is proposed, leveraging a data parallelisation method through the use of multiple Hardware Accelerators (HWs), resulting in the successful implementation of VSSA on a Hardware Accelerator with a single DAQA (Data Acquisition and Amplification) unit. The proposed compiler enables the VSSA technique for real-time elastography, addressing the challenge of targeting specific tissues, in addition to providing high resolution images, and facilitating the mechanical manipulation of tissues, thus propelling elastography into real-time elastography. The novel compiler is compared to a reference compiler through a benchmark test, resulting in a VSSA compilation time of 0.65s as opposed to 11.76s for the reference compiler, indicating a significant improvement in computational efficiency through the use of multiple Hardware Accelerators. The proposed VSSA method is validated through the imaging of a tissue-mimicking phantom and a rabbit elastography, resulting in high resolution images, accurately depicting tissue structures. The VSSA method demonstrates superior targeting precision when compared to the SA technique, allowing for precise targeting of specific tissues, mechanical manipulation, and successful elastography, indicating a significant advancement in the development of real-time elastography. The proposed compiler and VSSA method are made publicly available through an open-source repository. Through the use of a 128-element DAQA unit and four Hardware Accelerators, the VSSA method achieves high resolution images at a frame rate of 0.5Hz, demonstrating the computational efficiency of the proposed compiler. The use of a mechanical manipulation technique results in the successful depiction of tissue structures, along with the successful elastography of tissues, resulting in the accurate identification of tissue pathology. The proposed VSSA method provides high resolution images, precise targeting, along with successful elastography, allowing for the accurate identification of tissue pathology, thus propelling elastography into real-time elastography. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. The benefits of this hierarchy are further highlighted in scenarios featuring dynamic grid transformations and hidden agent movements. Our findings suggest a significant potential for hierarchical models to reduce the substantial computational overhead often associated with grid world PEGs, while also laying a theoretical groundwork for future research and potential applications to larger, more complex environments.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area is the cycleGAN, which utilizes a one-way transformation between images of high and low doses. However, it typically requires two separate networks, translating low-dose images to high-dose images and vice versa. These networks must be carefully trained to ensure the cycle consistency constraint is satisfied, which can be challenging. In response to these difficulties, we propose a new adaptation of the cycleGAN, using a single switchable generator that can switch between these two tasks. By sharing the architecture and parameters of the two networks, we simplify the training process and improve the stability of the training. Additionally, we investigate the effects of the switchable generator on training stability and image quality. Compared to the original cycleGAN, our method achieves comparable performance on public datasets while significantly reducing the number of parameters. Our results also demonstrate the effectiveness of the switchable generator, leading to improved images with fewer artifacts when applied to clinical low-dose CT images. To facilitate future research, we release our code and methods publicly. As an example application of our method, we utilize our low-dose CT image denoising algorithm to enhance images for an automatic lesion detection task, achieving a high AUC-ROC score of 0.963. Our code is available online at https://github.com/CheneyShih/LDCT-SRGAN.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-trained models like BERT, specifically when fine-tuned for these tasks. However, these models are limited by their linear architectures, hindering their ability to handle complex interactions and share knowledge across multiple layers. To circumvent this limitation, we propose a tree-structured pre-trained conversation model, aptly named TCM, which leverages a deep neural network architecture while minimizing unnecessary model parameters through sparse connectivity. TCM maintains a balanced representation of unidirectionality and bidirectionality in its tree structure, enabling it to participate in both generation and classification tasks in dialog understanding. By constructing a sparse tree structure with minimal depth, TCM reduces training data requirements while preventing overfitting. Comparative evaluations of our approach against multiple strong baselines have shown superior performance across open-domain conversational dialog, multi-turn closed-domain dialog, and paraphrasing tasks, with evaluations conducted on the WikiConv, T5-ADT, and ParaConv datasets. The code and model have been made publicly available at this link: https://github.com/zhengyunw/TCM. With TCM, we have achieved notable gains of +4.4 F1, +1.3 F1, and 0.91 p-value less than 0.01 (t-test) on the WikiConv, T5-ADT, and ParaConv datasets respectively, outperforming the current state-of-the-art models. Moreover, TCM has demonstrated the ability to generate more accurate and diverse responses while minimizing the generation of irrelevant information, as evident from the generated examples and evaluation metrics including BLEU, METEOR, and FLORES-101. Through thorough analysis and experimentation, we have validated the efficacy of TCM in employing local memory nodes to preserve contextual understanding and incorporate domain-specific knowledge from generation to classification tasks. Moreover, TCM has successfully avoided the challenge of training deep neural network architectures by employing a tree structure with minimal depth and sparse connectivity. As a result, TCM has achieved impressive performance without incurring additional training complexities. With its exceptional performance and efficient training capabilities, TCM has immense potential to contribute positively to various applications involving dialog understanding, including human-computer interaction, customer service, and personal assistance. Ultimately, the innovative tree-structured architecture proposed in TCM can serve as a pioneering model for exploring the possibilities of deep neural network architectures in dialog understanding tasks. To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, a new approach is introduced, involving a deformed Lagrange multiplier technique within the framework of deformed relativistic mean-field theory. By applying this approach to isotonic chains of $^{48}$Mg to $^{68}$Mg and calculating energy spectra and intrinsic wave functions for a wide range of angular momenta, researchers can directly observe the transition from deformed halo to spherical shell filling. The results indicate that adding protons to $^{48}$Mg, specifically up to $^{51}$Mg, involves a combination of both mechanisms, whereas in the $^{52}$Mg to $^{54}$Mg range, the spherical shell-filling effect dominates, and with $^{55}$Mg to $^{68}$Mg, the dominant influence becomes the distorted halo model. Monte Carlo shell model calculations are used to validate the theoretical approach and results, utilizing an interaction effective field theory for white box effective interactions. The study reveals that the 1f$_{7/2}$ shell filling in $^{51}$Mg exhibits rotational characteristics similar to those found in $^{42}$Ca and $^{54}$Ca, and for $^{54}$Mg to $^{68}$Mg, the rotational patterns are influenced by core excitation and shape coexistence. The research provides a theoretical basis for predicting excitation energies and intrinsic wave functions of rotational states in distorted halo nuclei. The results can be utilized to guide the development of effective interactions for Monte Carlo shell model calculations for medium mass and heavy nuclei. The study offers a new framework for investigating rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei and can be an important tool in understanding the complex structures of these nuclei. The approach is applicable to a wide range of nuclei with distorted halo properties and can provide valuable insights to support ongoing and future experimental studies using relativistic and radioactive ion beam facilities. The research is highly relevant to ongoing and planned experiments at the RIBF, FAIR, and HIRSE, and the theoretical approach can be employed to investigate other phenomena, such as shape coexistence, triaxiality, and superdeformability in heavy nuclei. The results can also contribute to a better comprehension of the ground states of light and medium mass nuclei and provide valuable input for research on astrophysical applications, such as stellar stability and big bang nucleosynthesis. The study offers a new framework for investigating rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei and can be an important tool in understanding the complex structures of these nuclei.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the use of a recurrent structure, with the nestedSKIP model being one of the top-performing variants, which employs a skip connection and incorporates a non-expansive operator in its recurrent formula to maintain detail preservation. However, this approach still faces challenges, such as motion and light effects not being well-modelled and video processing being inefficient due to the limited use of external information. To address these limitations, we introduce the MS-SkipVideo model, which builds upon the nestedSKIP model by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, along with the integration of an external light encoder. By leveraging external light information and incorporating a boundary-aware alignment module, we are able to capture light effects and improve boundary detail preservation. By using a second-order grid propagation method, we reduce grid-related artefacts and achieve more natural results. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single dynamics model learned from combined state and action data does not
necessarily lead to a boost in performance when compared to training individual
dynamics models for each task. However, we also discovered that training a
dynamics model on relevant states and actions can indeed facilitate transfer
learning and accelerate learning on new tasks. To overcome the limitations of
this intuitive approach, we developed an alternative strategy, involving (1)
training separate dynamics models for each task and (2) leveraging a task-agnostic
state representation learned through an autoencoder, resulting in a model-based
multi-task reinforcement learning framework. Our proposed method, MB-MTPR, uses
these representations to construct an augmented state space for each task, thus
enabling the efficient exploration of new states and the exploitation of known
states in the corresponding task space. The effectiveness of our approach is
validated through experiments on both simple gridworld and complex Vizdoom video
game environments, yielding superior performance when compared to a baseline model,
along with a notable boost in performance when compared to a method employing a
shared dynamics model. The code for our research is available online at https://github.com/ChenChen314/MB-MTPR.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. In our combined framework, these theorems demonstrate the capacity of any formal, sufficiently robust axiomatic system to either harbor a knowingly false axiom or generate an internally inconsistent derivative system within its own language. Furthermore, we derive a 'Modified Incompleteness Theorem for Inner Inconsistency', which states that from any such formal system, we can formulate a statement indicative of the system's internal contradiction within the language itself. In addition, we explore the constraints imposed on our theorems by the limited expressive capabilities of first-order logic. Finally, we examine potential extensions to our results within more expansive logical frameworks. 

Keywords: Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem, Tarski's Undefinability Theorem, Formal Systems, Axiomatic Systems, Inconsistent Theories, Self-Reference, First-Order Logic.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Given that a non-trivial, monogenic function u is given within three distinct balls in R^n+1, all having the same radius, if the corresponding Laplace transform Δu diverges at some point, then there exists at least one point in common where the functions u do not vanish. Similar conclusions can be drawn for functions f that are polyanalytic, quasianalytic, or harmonic. Furthermore, this theorem is shown to be an equivalence statement. Additionally, we prove that the set of monogenic functions within three-dimensional Euclidean space can be expressed as the union of countably infinite, mutually exclusive sets, each corresponding to unique values of the singular value parameter λ. Moreover, this parameter determines the maximum and minimum values of the L^2 norm of the differential operator Δ. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability and interconnectedness of these results to harmonic, quasianalytic, and polyanalytic functions within R^n+1 space.

When the population is not fully known in advance, sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm chooses successive mini-batches that, when combined, produce a balanced sample. It achieves this by selecting the most informative mini-batch relative to all previous ones, as measured by its expected distance or variance. The algorithm can be applied to a broad range of discrete population types and may also be used to select sequential, non-balanced samples. We examine the algorithm's performance using simulated data and show that it compares favorably to other methods, as evaluated through the sum of squared deviations from a desired balance level in each category. The algorithm has a favorable computational cost of $O(n + b^2)$ per mini-batch selection, where $n$ is the size of the population and $b$ is the size of the mini-batch. We also discuss how the algorithm can be modified to accommodate changing population characteristics over time. As an example, we use it to create a balanced sample from a set of genes that are associated with particular biological categories, as identified in a genome-wide study in Finland. The data consists of 529,452 FinnGen genes, grouped into 1,822 categories, and we select a balanced sample of 10,000 genes within these categories for each of three different scenarios. The code and data for the gene selection are publicly available on the R-forge website. As an additional example, we use it to select a non-balanced sample of 10,000 genes based on their significance levels in a set of 14,028 genome-wide association studies (GWAS), as conducted by the University of Michigan GWAS group. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting a pose directly from the image, another using a intermediate representation to guide a traditional method, and a third approach employing a model that considers both image and 3D information. Evaluating these approaches using a robust metric for uncertainty in a variety of real-world scenarios revealed that combining an attention-based network with the traditional method yielded the best results, outperforming direct prediction methods and demonstrating improved performance when considering uncertainty. By incorporating the results from multiple views and addressing issues of data limitations, we were able to achieve accurate and robust estimates, successfully applying this approach to a physical camera after the model had been trained virtually. The successful implementation of this approach enabled us to integrate an artificial intelligence-based camera calibration system into a robotic control framework, successfully demonstrating the method's effectiveness in sequential control scenarios. The method being proposed tackles the challenge of camera calibration through the use of an eye-in-hand camera in complex and dynamic environments, addressing issues of data quality, noise, and limited training sets. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering the likely image, but rather on generating a set of samples representative of the underlying truth, drawn from its posterior distribution. Although advances in deep learning such as generative models have simplified the creation of such samples, evaluating their accuracy remains a challenge. In this work, we investigate using the Monte-Carlo estimate of the Bayesian risk as a way to assess the performance of these samples. This approach involves evaluating a large number of mock measurements to determine how well the generated images match the true images. Since this is computationally expensive, we propose a more efficient alternative based on a single instance evaluation, augmented by a statistical test to account for any bias. We examine this method on synthetic MRI and natural image inversion problems. Our results show that it's possible to evaluate the performance of neural network-generated samples without generating explicit images, and that the estimates are accurate when tested against the desired performance metric. The source code for this work is available online at https://github.com/romghoul/BC-Eval.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Lastly, we provide guidance on accessing conditions for invariant lines and parabolas through numerical tools. These discussions aim to facilitate dynamic system analyses utilizing reduced systems defined along identified invariant sets. We illustrate this approach with a sample fractional-order system exhibiting an invariant line, demonstrating the efficacy of this method in simplifying high-dimensional systems and expediting computations. We also emphasize potential avenues for exploring this research in the context of economic dynamics.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Although Terahertz communication offers high bandwidth, implementing it on a large scale is hindered by the complexity of producing low-cost and high-performance transceivers. To overcome this limitation, researchers have been exploring the potential of using deep learning to enhance Terahertz communication performance. This paper delves into a novel, efficient, and scalable approach that leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) to enhance Terahertz channel performance. Unlike conventional approaches that focus on optimizing receiver performance, this work directly aims to enhance performance at the transmitter end. Through simulations, it's shown that the proposed GAN-based system outperforms conventional multiuser Terahertz communication systems while requiring minimal training data and low computational complexity at the transmitter end. This suggests that deep learning models like the one proposed can effectively improve Terahertz communication performance on a large scale while minimizing costs. Further analysis of this paper's findings includes examining GAN performance under various scenario conditions, comparing the proposed approach with conventional communication systems, analyzing scalability with respect to bandwidth and user numbers, and discussing implementation feasibility using current technology. This work has the potential to contribute to the development of next-generation wireless communication systems that utilize high-frequency bands and could enable the widespread adoption of Terahertz communication. This research is currently being presented as an extended abstract at the IEEE International Conference on Communications, and it awaits full review and revision. The final version of this work has been submitted to an appropriate journal for further consideration.

The interstellar medium contains scattering screens made of tiny particles that distort and fade starlight, particularly affecting blue and violet colors. Understanding these screens is crucial in determining the path and origins of cosmic objects, such as supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. Researchers have proposed using virtual screens based on the laws of physics to fill in missing data, and they have suggested using machine learning to identify these screens directly from observations. Here, we present a new technique that utilizes a generative model to analyze data and predict the screens, and this approach is applied to studying the screens in the Milky Way's central region using data from the Euclid satellite. The model's performance is assessed by analyzing its accuracy and bias in predicting screen density and size, and it is compared to a more simplified model. The results show that the model is highly accurate and has a low bias, and it is more effective than the simpler model in capturing the screens' patterns and sizes. Additionally, the model can identify the screens' density and size at specific locations, such as near the Galactic center, and it can distinguish between small and large screens. This technique has the potential to study the screens in other regions of the galaxy using future data from the James Webb Space Telescope and the Square Kilometre Array. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of machine learning in studying complex astrophysical phenomena through a machine learning-screen-sky model, and it paves the way for further research in this innovative area. The code for this research is available online for other scientists to use and adapt. 

This work is an extension of an earlier research project presented at the 2021 European Physical Society (EPS) conference. Since then, the researchers have refined the model and applied it to a larger dataset, and they have compared it to a more basic model to validate its effectiveness. The code for this research is available online for other scientists to use and adapt.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as a conditional generative model. However, its pitch control is constrained by the length of its conditioning input. In contrast, our QPNet uses multiple conditioning inputs with different network dilation factors to generate various periodic components at distinct pitches. This approach allows for flexible pitch control without increasing the number of parameters. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed QPNet surpasses WN in terms of pitch control and overall audio quality. Additionally, our method successfully generates multiple periodic components within a single audio signal, paving the way for the development of complex quasi-periodic signals in music generation. The code is openly available at https://github.com/linguisticnlp/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

Planets similar to Earth, orbiting nearby stars with reduced energy output, are being extensively studied and several are suited for further analysis. Focusing on temperate worlds surrounded by thick H2 atmospheres, our models follow chemical transformations and power production as we examine potential bio-signatures in gas giants resembling Kepler-452b. Considering seven host stars with lower energy output, four of which are GSC, K2-155, K2-440, TRAPPIST-1 and Epsilon Indus, we investigate how atmospheric chemistry evolves when methane and ammonia interact under intense stellar radiation. Analyzing this process in detail, our research reveals a plethora of photochemical compounds formed through the interaction of ammonia and water in low-pressure atmospheres. These compounds include hydrogen cyanide, cyanide, cyanoacetylene, ammonia, cyano-polysynes and cyano-methyl-polysynes. As we ascend to higher pressures, where supercritical water exists, we find the formation of additional compounds such as methylamine, ethylamine, dimethylamine, methanol, ethanol, propanol and dimethylethylamine. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/vlasiosound/source-localization.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Moreover, LGCN showcases improved robustness against noisy edges and outperforms existing methods on semi-supervised classification tasks. The source code of LGCN is publicly available at: https://github.com/zheng062/lcgn.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, utilizing the example of a two-level system. We demonstrate the equivalence of average energy calculations using both the normal temperature distribution and the Dirac distribution at negative temperatures. Additionally, we examine the time-dependent behavior of such a system when initially held at a negative temperature and then allowed to reach equilibrium at a higher positive temperature. Our findings reveal that, under these conditions, the system's temperature undergoes a transition from the negative state before eventually stabilizing at the positive equilibrium temperature. This scenario is represented numerically using a two-level system with external resonant irradiation as an example. We also derive an analytical solution for an arbitrary number of energy levels, providing further insight into this phenomenon. This scenario may be applicable to systems of N two-level particles, multi-level systems with selective population and no spontaneous decay between levels, and systems with a wide energy spacing between levels. We anticipate that this report will contribute to a deeper understanding and visualization of negative temperature concepts.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. It can be particularly beneficial for developing multi-class classification models capable of identifying various degrees of dysplasia and distinguishing benign and malignant lesions. Moreover, UniToPatho includes a limited set of adenoma-specific samples to facilitate the development of more precise models in this area. The dataset has been thoroughly evaluated using multiple deep learning architectures to validate its effectiveness and provide valuable insights for future research in this area. In line with relevant medical board guidelines, we emphasize that UniToPatho should be utilized to develop data-driven solutions for improving patient care, with strict adherence to patient data confidentiality protocols. As the largest available dataset for colorectal polyp and adenoma characterization, we believe UniToPatho presents an opportune chance for cutting-edge deep learning researchers to contribute to life-critical applications. The dataset is openly accessible at https://www.unito.it/richieste-di-dati/colorectal-pathology-dataset, accompanied by thorough documentation and marking guidelines available at https://github.com/alecghini/UniToPatho-annotating-guidelines. With advancements in deep learning and computational power, incorporating additional datasets, and addressing issues of overfitting, we are confident that UniToPatho will play a pivotal role in pushing the boundaries of precision in medical pattern recognition, ultimately contributing to better patient outcomes. As such, we invite researchers to join us in evaluating UniToPatho and exploring its capabilities in this area. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thus circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our primary challenge is learning zero-shot speech-to-text without explicit speech recognition training. We introduce two novel approaches, using contrastive learning and latent variable modeling, to tackle this issue. The methods we propose allow us to achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot speech-to-text performance on the CommonVoice-to-EN-DE dataset while achieving comparable results on the LargeMVST dataset. Our work lays the groundwork for zero-shot speech-to-text research and paves the way for exploring other speech-to-text language pairs. The code and models have been made publicly available. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. Our method also enables the disruption of optical binding forces by adjusting the multipoles in semiconductor particles. We propose that spherical multipoles could serve as a powerful tool for tailoring optical forces across various applications and systems. Furthermore, this method offers a straightforward approach for comparing the electromagnetic properties of different materials within a broad range of wavelengths. This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both displaying remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Schur elements/quantum immanants bypasses reliance on irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Column and row Schur elements correspond to Capelli and Nazarov-Umeda elements, with duality within these categories stemming from dual combinatorial descriptions of their eigenvalues. Further, algebraic limit passage towards U(gl(n)) is attainable through Olshanski decomposition and filtered algebra direct and inverse limits. Alongside, the study explores connections to quantum immanants, shifted Schur positivity, and the former's relationship to the latter. Lastly, several open problems and conjectures are posed. By directly comparing low-lying many-body energy levels to a $t_{2g}$-only model, we investigate how the magnitude of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing varies with different materials and temperatures. We find that even in cases where the direct $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ hopping is small, strong correlations can induce substantial $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, often exceeding 20%. Furthermore, we find that the spin-orbit coupling generally enhances $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, with the largest effect seen in Cu, where the magnitude of mixing is as high as 50%. Given that experimental branching ratios are often interpreted assuming no $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, our results caution that this assumption may not always hold, and that the actual $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, potentially altering these interpretations. Our findings have important implications for understanding and interpreting experimental data in transition metal oxides, particularly those with low-lying excited states that may be accessed by electron or hole doping. We conclude by highlighting the need for future studies to take $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing into account when analyzing experimental data, and when exploring new materials with exciting low-lying excitations.
